assessment.decision: Ship the Civic Intelligence Engine's own stack for Pilot 1; align with Comhairle at the protocol layer afterward. The stacks diverge (Rust/Svelte versus TypeScript/Python), the Civic Intelligence Engine is already validated and tuned to the campaign, and GNU Affero General Public License §13 rules out the fork-and-software-as-a-service path. Interoperate, don't fork.
assessment.agpl: Running a modified Comhairle as a network service (GNU Affero General Public License, version 3.0, §13) obliges you to release the complete corresponding source, including your adapter, branding, and every change, to every user of the hosted instance. And a clean dual-license escape is unlikely: copyright is spread across the Crown Shy team with no contributor agreement pooling the rights, so a proprietary exception would need sign-off from every contributor. The Civic Intelligence Engine's own clean-room stack carries none of this, which is why the engine stays the product core and Comhairle is an interop partner, not a base to hide inside a paid product.

items.name: Scope banner on every surface
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine stamps an un-removable scope banner on every result and export; Comhairle has no claim-framing layer.
items.cie: A 'scope banner' is a short, always-visible disclaimer stamped on every screen, chart, and downloaded file, reminding the reader what the data is and is not: a community-listening snapshot, not a scientific opinion poll. CIE requires this exact banner to appear verbatim on every result surface, export, and communication, and to be removable by no role, not even an admin or the candidate (spec R1). The point is that a number can never drift out of context and be mistaken for a representative poll, because its framing travels with it everywhere it goes.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no claim-framing layer at all; it orchestrates tools and renders their raw output. The Pol.is report it builds in api/src/wiki_poll_service/polis_service.rs hands back consensus and divisiveness values with no wrapper text, no disclaimer, and no methods framing. Even Bloom, a shipped Pol.is-style product, frames its public results with an editorial 'where people agree and diverge' narrative (bloom-04) but still does not stamp an unremovable, system-enforced scope banner.
items.meaning: This is a pure CIE addition with no hook in Comhairle. If CIE data is exported into Comhairle, the banner obligation stays on the CIE side, on its own dashboard and exports, because Comhairle offers nowhere to attach a system-enforced, unremovable banner. For a decision-maker: integration does not threaten the banner as long as CIE remains the presentation surface, but handing raw numbers to Comhairle to render would silently drop it.
items.cie_s: The scope banner stamps an unremovable community-listening disclaimer verbatim on every screen, chart, and export, so a number's framing always travels with it and can never be mistaken for a representative poll.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no claim-framing layer at all, rendering the raw Pol.is consensus and divisiveness values with no wrapper text or disclaimer.
items.meaning_s: Because Comhairle offers nowhere to attach a system-enforced banner, the obligation stays on the Civic Intelligence Engine side, so integration is safe only while Civic Intelligence Engine remains the presentation surface.

items.name: Copy linter bans polling language
items.note: A linter fails the build on margin-of-error language absent a polling frame; Comhairle has no such guard.
items.cie: A 'copy linter' is an automated check that runs when the software is built and scans all user-facing wording for forbidden phrases, here the statistical-polling language of 'margin of error', 'statistically significant', or 'X percent of the district'. CIE fails the build loudly if such language appears unless a genuine polling frame is confirmed and the sample reaches n=384 with a documented audit (spec R2). It is a guardrail that stops a well-meaning copywriter from accidentally over-claiming what community listening can support.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no equivalent guard. Text is authored freely by hosts and tools, and nothing in its build pipeline inspects wording for over-claiming. The language-related machinery in the codebase is about translation and internationalisation (api/src/translation_service.rs), not claim discipline, so there is simply no stage where polling language would be caught and rejected.
items.meaning: Another pure claim-discipline gap. This is a continuous-integration control that would have to be re-implemented from scratch if CIE content were ever authored inside Comhairle. The integration payoff is clear: keep content authoring and linting inside CIE's own pipeline, because Comhairle cannot enforce this rule and will not inherit it from a data export.
items.cie_s: The copy linter scans all user-facing wording at build time and fails the build loudly on statistical-polling phrases like 'margin of error' unless a genuine polling frame with n=384 and a documented audit is confirmed.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no such guard; text is authored freely by hosts and tools, and its only language machinery is translation and internationalisation, not claim discipline.
items.meaning_s: This continuous-integration control would have to be rebuilt from scratch inside Comhairle, so content authoring and linting should stay inside Civic Intelligence Engine's own pipeline.

items.name: Single badge, fixed vocabulary
items.note: Every result carries one badge from a three-value taxonomy; Comhairle surfaces raw Pol.is numbers with no badge.
items.cie: A 'badge' is a small standardised label on each result that tells the reader how much to trust it. CIE mandates exactly one badge per result drawn from a fixed three-value vocabulary, representative-enough / directional / below-bar, with identical words on every surface and no aliasing or softening (spec R3). In the proof of concept, this badge is computed in analysis/bridging.py and rendered consistently across views, so a reader always sees the same three words carrying the same three meanings.
items.comhairle: Comhairle surfaces the raw Pol.is numbers with no badge layer. polis_service.rs returns group_informed_consensus and divisiveness as bare floating-point values (Option<f64>), and deciding whether a given number is trustworthy is left entirely to the reader or the host. There is no controlled vocabulary anywhere along its report path.
items.meaning: The badge is the visible tip of CIE's whole gating discipline (see R8), so it has no Comhairle counterpart. If integrated, CIE must compute and attach the badge before any number is shown, and because Comhairle's data model has no field to carry a trust badge, an export would have to smuggle it through metadata or lose it. The clean division for a decision-maker: CIE owns interpretation, Comhairle owns raw numbers.
items.cie_s: The single badge attaches exactly one label per result drawn from a fixed three-value vocabulary of representative-enough, directional, or below-bar, worded identically on every surface.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle surfaces the raw Pol.is numbers as bare floats with no badge layer, leaving trustworthiness entirely for the reader to judge.
items.meaning_s: Since Comhairle's data model has no field to carry a trust badge, Civic Intelligence Engine must compute and attach it before any number is shown, keeping Civic Intelligence Engine the owner of interpretation and Comhairle the owner of raw numbers.

items.name: Validity card on every result
items.note: Per-group counts, smallest-group margin, coverage, and knife-edge flags have no analog in Comhairle.
items.cie: A 'validity card' is a compact nutrition-label attached to every result showing the diagnostics that reveal how solid it is: how many people are in each opinion group, the margin for the smallest group, coverage, the count of flagged records, and 'knife-edge' flags whenever a number sits within 0.05 of a decision threshold. CIE requires this card on every result (spec R4), and bridging.py already computes the per-group counts and Wilson bounds that populate it. It turns hidden statistical fragility into something a lay reader can actually see.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no analog; it renders the Pol.is math live and ungated, with no per-group margin, coverage figure, or knife-edge surfacing. The report structure in polis_service.rs carries vote breakdowns per statement but nothing that flags borderline reliability or smallest-group risk, so a fragile result and a robust one look identical to the reader.
items.meaning: This is core to CIE's trust layer and entirely absent from Comhairle. It reinforces that Comhairle can consume CIE's headline numbers but not its reliability apparatus. For integration, the validity card stays a CIE-rendered artifact, because nothing in Comhairle's schema.json interchange grammar has a place to hold it.
items.cie_s: The validity card attaches a nutrition-label of diagnostics to every result, showing per-group counts, the smallest-group margin, coverage, flagged-record counts, and knife-edge flags whenever a number sits within 0.05 of a decision threshold.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no analog, rendering the Pol.is math live and ungated so a fragile result and a robust one look identical to the reader.
items.meaning_s: With nothing in Comhairle's interchange grammar to hold it, the validity card stays a Civic Intelligence Engine-rendered artifact, so Comhairle can consume headline numbers but not the reliability apparatus behind them.

items.name: Plain-language methods note
items.note: A methods note reachable from every surface; Comhairle ships none.
items.cie: A 'methods note' is a short, jargon-free explanation of how the results were produced, how opinion groups are found, what 'bridging' means, and what each badge means, reachable from every results surface and understandable by a reader with no prior briefing (spec R5). It is the show-your-work page that lets a skeptical reader audit the process rather than just the numbers.
items.comhairle: Comhairle ships no such note. Its context-facing text is host-authored conversation framing, not a standardised methods explainer. Bloom is useful prior art here: its 'What is an Open Poll?' and 'How it works' tabs (bloom-02) show that a plain-language methods explainer is product-viable, but that is Bloom's own editorial content, not a Comhairle platform feature enforced per surface.
items.meaning: A pure gap, a documentation and user-experience artifact that CIE must supply itself. Integration neither helps nor hurts: as long as CIE renders the results, it carries the note. Bloom demonstrates the concept sells well, but neither Bloom nor Comhairle enforces it as a per-surface requirement the way CIE's spec does.
items.cie_s: The plain-language methods note is a jargon-free explainer of how opinion groups are found, what bridging means, and what each badge means, reachable from every results surface.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle ships no such note, offering only host-authored conversation framing rather than a standardised, per-surface methods explainer.
items.meaning_s: This documentation-and-user-experience artifact must be supplied by Civic Intelligence Engine itself, and integration neither helps nor hurts as long as Civic Intelligence Engine renders the results that carry it.

items.name: Candidate claim-language briefing
items.note: A pre-launch briefing and usage agreement with the candidate: a program step, not a platform feature.
items.cie: This is a program and operations step, not a software feature: before launch the candidate receives a briefing on what the tool can and cannot claim, and signs a results-usage agreement so they do not present community-listening data as a scientific poll (spec R6). It is the human-process complement to the technical claim-discipline items R1 through R5, closing the loop on the humans who will speak about the numbers.
items.comhairle: Because this is an offline agreement between the operator and the candidate, Comhairle neither provides it nor lacks it in any code sense; no platform implements a person-to-person briefing and signature. It is marked N/A precisely because it lives outside both codebases entirely.
items.meaning: Integration is irrelevant to this item; it is carried by whoever runs the pilot, regardless of which stack renders the data. For a decision-maker it is a reminder that several of CIE's trust guarantees are governance and process rather than features, and they travel with the operator, not with the software.
items.cie_s: The candidate claim-language briefing is a pre-launch program step in which the candidate is briefed on what the tool can and cannot claim and signs a results-usage agreement.
items.comhairle_s: Because this is an offline agreement between operator and candidate, Comhairle neither provides nor lacks it, since no platform implements a person-to-person briefing and signature.
items.meaning_s: Integration is irrelevant here, as the guarantee is carried by whoever runs the pilot, a reminder that several Civic Intelligence Engine trust guarantees are governance and process rather than software features.

items.name: Aggregates from real votes only
items.note: Comhairle aggregates real Pol.is votes; simulated agreement never enters, which is the measurement-integrity floor the Civic Intelligence Engine requires.
items.cie: This is CIE's measurement-integrity floor: every reported aggregate must be computed exclusively from real human votes and self-codes, and agreement simulated or generated by artificial intelligence must never enter them, verified by test (spec R7). In the proof of concept, artificial intelligence is used only as a listening aid for labeling and phrasing, while every number is computed from the human vote matrix in bridging.py; as the cie-lab README puts it, 'artificial intelligence is a listening aid, never the measurement.'
items.comhairle: Comhairle satisfies this on the vote path: its Pol.is integration aggregates real participant votes, and the group-aware consensus it reports (polis_service.rs, where consensus is read from math_pca.group_aware_consensus) is computed by the wrapped Pol.is math server over actual votes, never synthesised. This is one of the few genuine SATISFIES, the shared Pol.is spine both systems trust.
items.meaning: This is common ground. Both systems agree that reported numbers must come from real votes, so a CIE-to-Comhairle export of vote-derived aggregates preserves this integrity on both sides. It is a foundation the two stacks already share and can safely build interoperability on without conflict.
items.cie_s: The real-votes-only rule requires every reported aggregate to be computed exclusively from human votes and self-codes, with simulated or artificial-intelligence-generated agreement never entering, verified by test.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle satisfies this on the vote path, aggregating real participant votes through the wrapped Pol.is math server so the reported consensus is never synthesised.
items.meaning_s: This is shared common ground, so a Civic Intelligence Engine-to-Comhairle export of vote-derived aggregates preserves measurement integrity on both sides and is a safe foundation to build interoperability on.

items.name: Gated bridging badge
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine's badge needs group-informed consensus of at least 0.5, each group's Wilson score above 0.5, and 25 votes; Comhairle exposes Pol.is's raw consensus float.
items.cie: 'Bridging' statements are ones that every opinion group agrees on, the common ground across a divided public. CIE refuses to call something a bridge on a raw number alone; its badge requires all of: group-informed consensus at or above 0.5, each group's Wilson 95% lower bound above 0.5 (a conservative floor that guards against small-sample flukes), and at least 25 votes per group, with the Seattle dataset kept as a regression test that must keep producing zero badges (spec R8). bridging.py implements exactly this gate (gic_headline 0.5, wilson_z 1.96, an all-groups-pass check), turning a number into a defensible claim.
items.comhairle: Comhairle exposes Pol.is's raw group_informed_consensus float directly (polis_service.rs, the Option<f64> at line 105 populated around line 366) with no Wilson lower bound, no minimum-votes gate, and no regression discipline. It is the same underlying quantity CIE starts from, but published ungated, the exact 'a number, not a claim' distinction the assessment flags.
items.meaning: This is the single most important divergence: both systems compute the same consensus quantity, but only CIE wraps it in a defensible statistical gate before calling it common ground. In an export, CIE can send Comhairle either the raw float (which Comhairle already understands) or the gated badge (for which Comhairle has no field). The decision-maker takeaway: CIE's core value-add lives precisely in this gate, so CIE must remain the arbiter of what counts as a bridge.
items.cie_s: The gated bridging badge refuses to call a statement common ground on a raw number alone, requiring group-informed consensus at or above 0.5, each group's Wilson 95% lower bound above 0.5, and at least 25 votes per group.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle exposes Pol.is's raw group-informed-consensus float directly, with no Wilson lower bound, no minimum-votes gate, and no regression discipline.
items.meaning_s: This is the single most important divergence, since both systems compute the same quantity but only Civic Intelligence Engine wraps it in a defensible statistical gate, so Civic Intelligence Engine must remain the arbiter of what counts as a bridge.

items.name: Groups from response patterns only
items.note: Comhairle's Pol.is clusters on vote patterns with no demographic input, exactly the Civic Intelligence Engine's rule.
items.cie: Opinion groups, or clusters, must be derived only from how people voted, never from demographics or any external attribute, so the groups reflect shared opinion rather than identity (spec R9). The proof of concept runs principal component analysis followed by k-means on the vote matrix alone (bridging.py), with the number of groups k chosen by a silhouette score; no demographic feature ever enters the clustering.
items.comhairle: Comhairle satisfies this because its Pol.is clustering operates purely on vote patterns via the wrapped math server, and demographics, where collected, are stored separately and do not feed the clustering. This is the second genuine SATISFIES on the shared Pol.is spine, alongside votes-only aggregation.
items.meaning: Another point of agreement: both cluster in a demographic-blind way. But note the latent tension the assessment flags, that Comhairle also stores joinable demographics (ethnicity, age, party, zip) which CIE deliberately quarantines. So the algorithms agree, yet Comhairle keeps identity data adjacent in a way CIE's privacy model would not. It is safe to interoperate on the clustering itself, but a decision-maker should watch the surrounding demographic data.
items.cie_s: The response-patterns-only clustering derives opinion groups solely from how people voted, running principal component analysis then k-means on the vote matrix alone, never from demographics or any external attribute.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle satisfies this, clustering purely on vote patterns via the wrapped math server while storing any demographics separately from the clustering.
items.meaning_s: The algorithms agree, but Comhairle keeps joinable identity data adjacent in a way Civic Intelligence Engine's privacy model would not, so interoperating on the clustering itself is safe while the surrounding demographic data warrants watching.

items.name: Bounded, re-derived cluster search
items.note: Comhairle runs Pol.is clustering but doesn't pin a re-derived k-range as a versioned thresholds commit.
items.cie: The 'cluster-count search' is how the system decides how many opinion groups actually exist in the data. CIE bounds this search to a small calibrated range, re-derives it on real district text before pinning it for production, and treats any change as a documented 'thresholds commit', a versioned, reviewed change to the thresholds file that serves as the single source of truth (spec R10, reinforced by R40). In the proof of concept, k is searched over the range [2..5] by silhouette in bridging.py; the production discipline adds the re-derivation-and-pin ceremony on top.
items.comhairle: Comhairle runs Pol.is clustering, so a bounded k-search does happen inside the wrapped math server, which is why this scores PARTIAL rather than gap. But Comhairle does not pin a re-derived k-range as a versioned thresholds commit; the parameters live in the upstream Pol.is service rather than in a governed, auditable thresholds file under Comhairle's own control.
items.meaning: The mechanism exists on both sides; the governance around it does not. Comhairle gives you clustering but not CIE's reproducible, versioned parameter discipline. For integration this is a 'same engine, different rigor' item: CIE can consume Comhairle's clustering, but it would still need its own threshold governance to keep results defensible.
items.cie_s: The bounded cluster-count search limits the number of opinion groups to a small calibrated range, re-derives it on real district text, and pins any change as a versioned, reviewed thresholds commit that is the single source of truth.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's wrapped Pol.is does perform a bounded k-search, but it does not pin a re-derived k-range as a governed, auditable thresholds file under its own control.
items.meaning_s: The mechanism exists on both sides but the governance does not, so Civic Intelligence Engine can consume Comhairle's clustering yet still needs its own threshold discipline to keep results reproducible and defensible.

items.name: Stability gate fails loudly
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine blocks artifacts on a failed stability gate; Comhairle renders results live and ungated.
items.cie: A 'stability gate' checks whether the opinion groups are robust, asking in effect: if you re-ran the clustering, would you get roughly the same groups back? CIE requires that a run failing this gate fails loudly, producing no manifest, no artifact, and no dashboard path to unstable results at all (spec R11). Fragile structure is blocked from ever being shown, rather than shown with a caveat and left for the reader to notice.
items.comhairle: Comhairle renders Pol.is results live and ungated, so there is no stability gate that could block publication. The report path in polis_service.rs produces output whenever the math server returns, with no reproducibility check standing between computation and display.
items.meaning: This belongs to CIE's quality-gate ladder, which the assessment scores as an entire GAP in Comhairle (the T1 through T6 gates are all gap). It means Comhairle will happily display fragile results that CIE would suppress. For integration, CIE must gate before it exports; if Comhairle instead renders live from its own Pol.is instance, no gate applies, so this discipline cannot be delegated to Comhairle.
items.cie_s: The stability gate checks whether re-running the clustering would return roughly the same groups and fails loudly, producing no manifest, no artifact, and no dashboard path to unstable results at all.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle renders Pol.is results live and ungated, with no reproducibility check standing between computation and display.
items.meaning_s: Comhairle will happily display fragile results that Civic Intelligence Engine would suppress, so Civic Intelligence Engine must gate before it exports and this discipline cannot be delegated to Comhairle.

items.name: Per-cluster stability → directional
items.note: Marking unstable sub-clusters directional has no counterpart in Comhairle's output.
items.cie: Even within a run that passes overall, some sub-groups are shakier than others. CIE measures stability per cluster and marks the less-stable, non-headline clusters as 'directional', meaning suggestive rather than firm, so readers weight them accordingly (spec R12). The proof of concept's badge vocabulary already carries a 'directional' tier (bridging.py assigns it when consensus is moderate) for exactly this kind of down-weighting.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no per-cluster stability marking and no directional tier in its output; every cluster the math server returns is presented on equal footing. There is no field in its report structure to say 'this particular group is less reliable than the others.'
items.meaning: A fine-grained trust nuance unique to CIE. It compounds R11: not only does CIE gate whole runs, it grades individual clusters within a run. Comhairle cannot express this distinction, so it would flatten on export. For a decision-maker, CIE's per-cluster honesty is a differentiator with no Comhairle equivalent.
items.cie_s: The per-cluster stability marking measures robustness for each group and tags the shakier, non-headline clusters as directional so readers weight them accordingly.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no per-cluster stability marking and no directional tier, presenting every cluster the math server returns on equal footing.
items.meaning_s: This fine-grained trust nuance would flatten on export, since Comhairle has no field to express that one particular group is less reliable than the others.

items.name: Local embeddings, no network
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine embeds locally with no egress; Comhairle makes external per-record calls to artificial intelligence services.
items.cie: An 'embedding' turns a piece of text into a list of numbers that a computer can compare for meaning. CIE records which embedding model each run used, runs it locally on the same machine with no network calls, and re-evaluates it on real data before pinning (spec R13), a data-sovereignty stance ensuring raw constituent text never leaves the box. (The cie-lab proof of concept uses free TELUS embeddings for experimentation, but explicitly on synthetic and public data only; the production requirement is local and no-egress.)
items.comhairle: Comhairle makes external, per-record artificial-intelligence calls: it has a bot service, RAGFlow document question-answering, categorization, and translation services (api/src/bot_service/ragflow_bot.rs, api/src/translation_service.rs, api/src/categorization_service/) that send data out to external providers. This is the opposite posture, many per-record egress calls versus CIE's zero-egress rule.
items.meaning: A direct architectural conflict, not merely a missing feature. CIE's privacy guarantee depends on data not leaving the machine, while Comhairle's enrichment features assume that it does. Integration must keep the boundary explicit: CIE can export scrubbed aggregates to Comhairle, but routing raw text through Comhairle's artificial-intelligence services would violate CIE's egress rule. This is a governance line a decision-maker must hold firmly.
items.cie_s: The local-embeddings rule records which embedding model each run used and runs it on the same machine with no network calls, ensuring raw constituent text never leaves the box.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle makes external, per-record artificial intelligence calls through its bot, RAGFlow document question-and-answer service, categorization, and translation services, the opposite egress-heavy posture.
items.meaning_s: This is a direct architectural conflict, so the boundary must stay explicit: Civic Intelligence Engine can export scrubbed aggregates, but routing raw text through Comhairle's artificial intelligence services would violate its zero-egress rule.

items.name: Divisive shown beside bridging
items.note: Comhairle can display divisive Pol.is results, but without the Civic Intelligence Engine's guarantee they sit un-subordinated and unsuppressible.
items.cie: To prevent cherry-picking only the feel-good common ground, CIE requires that divisive and majority-only results display right beside the bridging results on the same surface, never hidden or visually subordinated, and that the candidate cannot suppress them from their own view (spec R14). It is an anti-spin guarantee baked directly into the interface.
items.comhairle: Comhairle can display divisive results; polis_service.rs computes and returns a divisiveness value alongside consensus, which is why this scores PARTIAL. But Comhairle offers no guarantee that divisive results sit un-subordinated and unsuppressible; layout and emphasis are left to hosts and tools, and nothing prevents a candidate view from hiding them. Bloom similarly surfaces where people 'differ' (bloom-04) as editorial content, without any suppression guarantee.
items.meaning: The capability exists in Comhairle; the enforced fairness contract does not. Both can show divisiveness, but only CIE promises it cannot be buried. For a decision-maker this is a 'data yes, guarantee no' item: interoperation preserves the divisive numbers themselves, but CIE's no-suppression pledge only holds while CIE controls the presentation surface.
items.cie_s: The divisive-beside-bridging rule requires majority-only and divisive results to display un-subordinated on the same surface as bridging results, unsuppressible even by the candidate.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle can compute and return a divisiveness value, but offers no guarantee those results sit un-subordinated and cannot be hidden from a candidate view.
items.meaning_s: The capability exists but the enforced fairness contract does not, so Civic Intelligence Engine's no-suppression pledge only holds while Civic Intelligence Engine controls the presentation surface.

items.name: Genuine pass / not-sure option
items.note: Pol.is offers a pass, though not recorded as the Civic Intelligence Engine's distinct, non-gating value on every item.
items.cie: A 'genuine pass / not-sure' option means that when a participant is shown a short opinion statement, they can vote agree or disagree but also explicitly say 'pass' or 'I'm not sure' as a real, recorded answer rather than being forced to pick a side or being blocked from moving on. CIE treats this pass as its own distinct value on every single item and never lets any item gate progress, so uncertainty is captured as real signal instead of noise. In the cie-lab proof-of-concept the voting surface (web/src/views/Converse.tsx) presents agree/disagree/pass as co-equal choices, matching the spec requirement (R15) that pass is a non-gating, first-class response.
items.comhairle: Comhairle drives its voting through Pol.is, which does offer a pass button, so the raw capability to skip a statement exists (api/src/tools/polis.rs wires votes and statements to the Pol.is engine). What is not guaranteed at Comhairle's layer is CIE's stricter promise that pass is stored as a distinct, analyzable value on every item and that no item ever blocks progress. Bloom, a shipped Pol.is-style Open Poll product used here as prior art (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), demonstrates the mature version of this: it co-displays a genuine UNSURE/pass choice alongside free-text entry, showing the pattern is well established in the field.
items.meaning: For integration this is a 'partial' item: the underlying pass mechanic already flows through Comhairle via Pol.is, so the two systems are close. The work is not building a pass button but hardening it to CIE's standard, ensuring pass is persisted as its own value and auditable per item, and confirming no item can gate a participant. This is a low-risk alignment task rather than net-new construction.
items.cie_s: The genuine pass / not-sure option lets participants vote agree, disagree, or explicitly pass as a co-equal, recorded value on every item, with no item ever gating progress.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Pol.is integration offers a pass button, but does not guarantee Civic Intelligence Engine's stricter promise that pass is stored as a distinct, analysable value on every item with no gating.
items.meaning_s: This is a low-risk alignment task rather than net-new construction, since the pass mechanic already flows through Comhairle and the work is hardening it to Civic Intelligence Engine's standard.

items.name: Instrument under seven minutes
items.note: A completion-time timing study with a test posse: a field-research step, not a codebase capability.
items.cie: This requirement says the entire instrument (the full set of questions a participant answers) must be completable in under seven minutes on a mid-range phone, verified by an actual timing study run with the human 'test posse' rather than the engineers who built it. It is a field-research and usability standard about respondent burden, not a piece of software: keeping the survey short protects completion rates and data quality. CIE's spec (R16) deliberately assigns the verification to independent testers so the timing reflects real people, not developers who already know the flow.
items.comhairle: Because this is a human timing study and a process gate, it is not something that lives in Comhairle's codebase at all; no repository file can satisfy 'run a stopwatch study with real testers.' Comhairle can host and serve an instrument of any length, but it has no notion of a certified completion-time budget or an external timing sign-off. Bloom's short, mobile-first Open Poll flow (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md) is a useful reference for what a sub-seven-minute experience looks like in practice, but it too is a design outcome rather than an enforced check.
items.meaning: This is marked 'na' (not applicable) to a code comparison because it is a research and quality-assurance activity that sits outside both platforms' software. When integrating, the takeaway is that whichever system hosts the instrument, a separate operational step must schedule and record the timing study. Neither adopting Comhairle nor CIE removes the need for this human verification.
items.cie_s: The under-seven-minute instrument requirement caps the full question set at seven minutes on a mid-range phone, verified by an actual timing study run with the independent test posse rather than the engineers who built it.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle can host an instrument of any length but has no notion of a certified completion-time budget or an external timing sign-off, since this human study lives in no codebase.
items.meaning_s: Whichever system hosts the instrument, a separate operational timing study must still be scheduled and recorded, and neither platform removes that need.

items.name: Validated item banks + neutral audit
items.note: Wording sourced from validated banks and neutral-audited, a content and process gate.
items.cie: This item requires that the wording of survey questions starts from 'validated election-survey item banks' (question sets that academics or pollsters have already tested for neutrality and reliability) and then passes a neutral-language audit by the instrument owner, with that audit logged before the go/no-go decision. The point is to prevent leading or biased wording from skewing which opinions surface. In CIE this is a content-provenance and review discipline captured in the spec (R17); it governs where question text comes from and who signs off on its neutrality, upstream of any code.
items.comhairle: Comhairle stores statement text and themes (api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs holds statement_text and a themes vector) but has no concept of a validated source bank or a recorded neutral-language audit; a statement is just a string with a moderation status. There is no field or workflow that ties wording back to a vetted item bank or logs an owner's audit finding. Bloom provides statement-submission moderation guidelines as prior art (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), but that is moderation of user submissions, not sourcing from validated academic banks.
items.meaning: Classified 'na' because it is a content and process gate rather than a platform feature, this shows a gap that no software swap resolves. Integrating CIE-grade rigor means adding an editorial pipeline and an audit log around whichever tool holds the questions. Comhairle could store the resulting vetted text, but the vetting itself is human governance that must be layered on.
items.cie_s: The validated-item-banks rule sources question wording from tested academic election-survey banks and passes a neutral-language audit by the instrument owner, logged before the go/no-go decision.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle stores statement text and themes but has no concept of a validated source bank or a recorded neutral-language audit, since a statement is just a string with a moderation status.
items.meaning_s: This content-and-process gate is unresolved by any software swap, so reaching Civic Intelligence Engine's rigor means adding an editorial pipeline and audit log around whichever tool holds the questions.

items.name: Named instrument owner
items.note: A named, resourced instrument owner confirmed before collection: a staffing gate.
items.cie: This requirement is a staffing control: before any field data collection begins, there must be a named 'instrument owner' (a specific accountable person) with a signed deliverable and confirmed working hours, and collection is hard-blocked until that is in place. The intent is to ensure a real, resourced human is answerable for the quality and neutrality of the survey, rather than an anonymous or unowned instrument going live. CIE's spec (R18) makes this an explicit precondition on launch, not a nicety.
items.comhairle: This is an organizational/governance gate, so it has no direct analog in Comhairle's code; the repo has organizations and users (api/src/models/organization.rs, users.rs) but nothing that binds a named, hours-confirmed instrument owner to a hard block on data collection. Comhairle will happily run a workflow whether or not such a person has been designated. There is no Bloom prior art for this either, since it is an internal accountability practice rather than a participant-facing feature.
items.meaning: Marked 'na' as a staffing gate, this reminds integrators that CIE's trust model depends on human accountability that lives in project governance, not in either platform. Whichever system is adopted, someone must enforce the 'no named owner, no collection' rule administratively. It is a checklist item for launch readiness, not a build task.
items.cie_s: The named-instrument-owner rule hard-blocks data collection until a specific accountable person with a signed deliverable and confirmed working hours is in place.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has organizations and users but nothing binding a named, hours-confirmed owner to a hard block on collection, so it will run whether or not one is designated.
items.meaning_s: This staffing gate lives in project governance rather than either platform, so someone must enforce the 'no named owner, no collection' rule administratively.

items.name: Curator identity + timestamp
items.note: Comhairle stores statement authorship, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's enforced curator-identity-before-display check.
items.cie: This requirement says every statement, whether drafted by artificial intelligence or submitted by a participant, must carry a curator identity (who vetted or authored it) and a timestamp before it is ever displayed, and this must be enforced both in the ingest validator (the code that accepts new statements) and in the rendering query (the code that pulls statements to show). The goal is provenance: no statement reaches a reader without a traceable, time-stamped human curator behind it. CIE's spec (R19) enforces this at two points so nothing slips through unattributed.
items.comhairle: Comhairle does store the raw materials for this: api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs records user_id (authorship), is_seed, created_at/updated_at timestamps, and a moderation_status drawn from ModerationStatus (wiki_poll_service.rs). What it lacks is CIE's enforced 'curator identity must exist before display' check woven into the rendering path; authorship is captured but not gated on. Bloom's statement-submission moderation guidelines (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md) show the same moderation-before-display intent as product prior art.
items.meaning: This is a 'partial' item: the data model already carries author and timestamp, so Comhairle is meaningfully ahead here compared to items with no analog. Integration work is to add the enforcement, a validator and a filtered render query that refuse to surface any statement lacking a curator identity, on top of fields Comhairle already has. It is an enhancement of an existing schema, not a from-scratch build.
items.cie_s: The curator-identity rule requires every statement to carry a curator identity and timestamp before display, enforced in both the ingest validator and the rendering query.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle already stores authorship, seed flags, timestamps, and moderation status, but does not gate on curator identity before a statement is shown.
items.meaning_s: This is a partial where the data model is already ahead, so integration adds a validator and a filtered render query that refuse any statement lacking a curator, atop fields Comhairle already has.

items.name: Seed cites research source
items.note: Each seed statement citing swing-theme research: a content-provenance step.
items.cie: This requirement asks that each 'seed' statement (the starter statements an organizer plants to kick off the conversation) cites the swing-theme research source it came from, stored in the statement catalog. Swing themes are the contested topics research suggests could move opinion, and citing the source keeps organizers honest about why a given seed was chosen. In CIE this is a content-provenance step in the spec (R20): the catalog entry for a seed should point back to the evidence that justified it.
items.comhairle: Comhairle marks whether a statement is a seed (is_seed in api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs) and tags themes, but it has no field to cite a research source behind a seed; the provenance link simply does not exist in the schema. A curator could stuff a citation into free text, but nothing models or requires it. There is no specific Bloom prior art for research-sourced seeds, as this is an internal sourcing discipline rather than a participant-facing element.
items.meaning: Marked 'na' as a content-provenance step, this is another governance/editorial gap rather than a platform capability. To reach CIE's standard, integrators would extend the seed record with a source citation and require it at authoring time. Comhairle's is_seed and themes fields are a natural place to hang that citation, so the extension is small, but the discipline of sourcing is human.
items.cie_s: The seed-source-citation rule requires each starter seed statement to cite the swing-theme research source it came from, stored in the statement catalog.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle marks whether a statement is a seed and tags its themes, but has no field to cite the research source behind a seed.
items.meaning_s: This content-provenance step is a small schema extension, since Comhairle's seed and theme fields are a natural home for the citation, though the sourcing discipline itself remains human.

items.name: Dial decision recorded
items.note: Recording the elicitation-dial decision before launch: a process artifact.
items.cie: The 'dial' is CIE's term for how the elicitation is tuned, how many seed statements to plant, what the participant-submission policy is, and the cross-pollination criteria (rules for carrying statements between groups or conversations). This requirement demands that the dial setting be recorded as a closed, deliberate decision, with those parameters fixed, before the engagement begins. CIE's spec (R21) treats this as a pre-launch decision artifact so the configuration is intentional and auditable rather than improvised mid-stream.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has the moving parts a dial would configure, seed statements (is_seed), submission handling through Pol.is (api/src/tools/polis.rs), required_votes settings, but no single recorded 'dial decision' artifact that freezes and documents these choices before launch. The configuration is scattered across live settings rather than captured as one signed-off decision. This is an internal process artifact with no Bloom analog, since it concerns how organizers document their setup, not what participants see.
items.meaning: Classified 'na' as a process artifact, this highlights that CIE wants configuration decisions to be explicit and frozen, a governance habit rather than a feature either platform ships. In an integration, one would produce this decision record alongside whatever Comhairle configuration is used. The parameters map onto Comhairle's existing knobs, but the act of recording the closed decision is procedural.
items.cie_s: The dial-decision record freezes the elicitation tuning, including seed count, submission policy, and cross-pollination criteria, as a closed and documented pre-launch decision artifact.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has the configurable moving parts a dial would set but no single recorded decision artifact that freezes and documents those choices before launch.
items.meaning_s: The parameters map onto Comhairle's existing knobs, but the act of recording the closed decision is a procedural governance habit neither platform ships.

items.name: Config empty until owner sign-off
items.note: Gating the instrument config on the owner's deliverable: a process control.
items.cie: This requirement is a process control on configuration: the instrument's configuration file must stay empty until the instrument owner's deliverable (from R18) actually lands, and populating that file requires the owner's sign-off recorded in the commit itself. In plain terms, nobody gets to fill in the live survey settings until the accountable owner has delivered and explicitly approved, with that approval traceable in version control. CIE's spec (R22) uses the commit history as the enforcement mechanism, tying config changes to owner authorization.
items.comhairle: This is a development-process and source-control discipline, so it has no representation inside Comhairle's application code; the repo can hold configuration, but it has no rule that a config file stays empty pending an owner's signed deliverable or that commits must carry owner sign-off. Enforcement would live in the team's git workflow and review policy, not in any Rust module. There is no Bloom prior art, as this is purely an internal build-governance control.
items.meaning: Marked 'na' because it is a process control on how the team commits configuration, this is orthogonal to which platform is chosen. Integrating CIE's discipline means adopting a commit/review convention around config, regardless of whether Comhairle or the CIE proof of concept hosts the instrument. It is a way of working, enforced by people and git, not by either codebase.
items.cie_s: The config-sign-off rule keeps the instrument's configuration file empty until the owner's deliverable lands and requires the owner's sign-off recorded in the commit that populates it.
items.comhairle_s: This source-control discipline has no representation in Comhairle's application code, so enforcement would live in the team's git workflow and review policy rather than any Rust module.
items.meaning_s: Adopting this means a commit-and-review convention around config, enforced by people and git, orthogonal to which platform hosts the instrument.

items.name: Two-tier unbundled consent
items.note: Comhairle has a single consent boolean; the Civic Intelligence Engine's two independent tiers with contact-off-by-default have no analog.
items.cie: This is CIE's two-tier unbundled consent model. 'Two-tier' means participation consent and contact/recontact consent are asked as two separate, independent choices rather than bundled into one checkbox; 'unbundled' means agreeing to one does not force agreeing to the other. Contact defaults to off, and if someone declines, CIE stores no participant row, no consent event, no code linkage, only an anonymous daily counter, so a decliner leaves essentially no trace. The spec (R23) makes this the heart of CIE's privacy stance: minimal data, granular and revocable consent.
items.comhairle: Comhairle models consent as a single boolean: api/src/models/user_profile.rs has one `consented: bool`, and routes/user_profile.rs simply reads request.consented (defaulting to false). Demographics like age and gender sit in the same profile and are gated by that one flag (queries filter on consented = true). There is no separation of a participation tier from a contact tier, no contact-off-by-default second choice, and declining still implies an ordinary user/profile row rather than CIE's trace-free anonymous counter. Bloom's consent-forward optional demographics at the end of its flow, 'share only what you're comfortable with' (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), is closer in spirit but still not two independent tiers.
items.meaning: This is a true 'gap' (sourced): CIE's granular two-tier, minimal-trace consent has no analog in Comhairle's single boolean. Integration would require reworking Comhairle's user_profile consent model into two independent flags, defaulting contact off, and, harder, changing how declines are stored so no linkable row is created. That touches the data model and the participation flow, making it substantive rather than cosmetic work.
items.cie_s: The two-tier unbundled consent asks participation and contact consent as separate independent choices with contact off by default, storing only an anonymous daily counter, no row, event, or code linkage, when someone declines.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle models consent as a single boolean with demographics gated by that one flag, with no separation of participation from contact and an ordinary profile row even for decliners.
items.meaning_s: This true gap requires reworking Comhairle's consent model into two independent flags and, harder, changing how declines are stored so no linkable row is created, which is substantive data-model work.

items.name: Artificial intelligence disclosure at start
items.note: Comhairle uses artificial intelligence services and can disclose them, but without the Civic Intelligence Engine's red-teamed standalone-screenshot standard.
items.cie: This requirement mandates that artificial intelligence involvement be disclosed to participants at the very start of the conversation and again on the visualization (the results view), in wording the candidate has approved and that has been 'red-teamed as a standalone screenshot', meaning someone adversarially checked that a single screenshot of the disclosure, seen out of context, still reads as honest and clear. The aim is that no one is misled about where artificial intelligence is in the loop. CIE's spec (R24) sets a high bar: not just any disclosure, but one stress-tested to survive being screenshotted and shared.
items.comhairle: Comhairle does use artificial-intelligence services in its stack (for example around Pol.is orchestration and thinking-space summaries, e.g. api/src/models/thinking_space_summary.rs), so it has artificial intelligence to disclose and could show a notice. What it lacks is CIE's specific standard: an approved, red-teamed, standalone-screenshot-proof disclosure placed at conversation start and on the visualization. There is no code enforcing where or how the artificial-intelligence disclosure appears. Bloom shows artificial-intelligence-style disclosure as product prior art (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), demonstrating the pattern exists in shipped products.
items.meaning: Marked 'partial': the raw ability to display a disclosure is trivially present, and Comhairle genuinely uses artificial intelligence, so the gap is about rigor and placement, not capability. Integration means authoring the approved copy, running the red-team screenshot test, and pinning the disclosure to the right two moments (start and visualization). This is more of a content-and-review task than an engineering one.
items.cie_s: The artificial-intelligence-disclosure rule discloses artificial intelligence involvement at conversation start and again on the visualization, in candidate-approved wording red-teamed to read honestly even as a standalone screenshot.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle uses artificial intelligence services and could show a notice, but lacks Civic Intelligence Engine's approved, red-teamed, screenshot-proof disclosure pinned to those two specific moments.
items.meaning_s: The gap is about rigor and placement rather than capability, so integration is mostly authoring the copy, running the screenshot red-team, and pinning the disclosure, a content-and-review task.

items.name: Consent event pins copy version
items.note: Versioning every consent event to the exact copy shown is absent from Comhairle's model.
items.cie: This requirement says every consent event must pin the exact version of the consent copy the participant actually saw. Because consent language changes over time, recording only 'consented: true' is not enough; you must know precisely which wording that person agreed to, so the consent is legally and ethically defensible later. CIE's spec (R25) treats each consent as an immutable event bound to a specific copy version, fitting its append-only, auditable data philosophy.
items.comhairle: Comhairle's model has no version pinning: consent is the single `consented: bool` in api/src/models/user_profile.rs, with no field capturing which consent-copy version was shown, and the profile is ordinary mutable Postgres rather than append-only event history. If the consent wording changed, there would be no way to reconstruct what any given user agreed to. There is no Bloom prior art specifically for consent-copy versioning, as this is a back-end compliance concern.
items.meaning: This is a sourced 'gap': versioning consent to exact copy is simply absent from Comhairle's design. Closing it means adding a consent-copy version reference to each consent record and, ideally, moving to append-only consent events so history is preserved. That is a meaningful schema and data-lifecycle change, since Comhairle's mutable single-boolean approach is structurally the opposite of what R25 needs.
items.cie_s: The consent-copy-version rule pins every consent event to the exact version of the consent copy the participant actually saw, recorded as an immutable append-only event.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's single consent boolean captures no consent-copy version and lives in mutable Postgres, so a past agreement cannot be reconstructed if the wording changed.
items.meaning_s: Closing this gap means adding a consent-copy version reference to each record and ideally moving to append-only consent events, a meaningful schema and data-lifecycle change.

items.name: Consent compliance review
items.note: A privacy and electoral-compliance sign-off before go/no-go: a governance step.
items.cie: This requirement is a governance sign-off: the consent language must pass a privacy and electoral-compliance review before the go/no-go launch decision, with the written finding kept on file. Electoral-compliance matters because CIE is used in campaign/community contexts where election law and privacy law both apply. CIE's spec (R26) requires a documented legal/privacy review artifact, not just internal confidence, before collection can proceed.
items.comhairle: This is a governance and legal review step, so it has no home in Comhairle's codebase; there is no module that represents a compliance finding or blocks launch pending a written review. Comhairle can run regardless of whether such a review happened. There is no Bloom prior art, since this is an internal legal/compliance process rather than any product feature.
items.meaning: Classified 'na' as a governance step, this underscores that CIE's trust posture leans heavily on human review artifacts that neither platform enforces. In any integration, a privacy/electoral-compliance review and its filed finding remain a manual precondition to launch. The platform choice does not affect this obligation.
items.cie_s: The consent-compliance review requires the consent language to pass a documented privacy and electoral-compliance sign-off, kept on file, before the go/no-go decision.
items.comhairle_s: This governance and legal review step has no home in Comhairle's codebase, which will run regardless of whether such a review happened.
items.meaning_s: A filed privacy and electoral-compliance review remains a manual precondition to launch that the platform choice does not affect.

items.name: 11-participant suppression floor
items.note: Server-side cell suppression below 11, with complementary suppression, is not in Comhairle's ungated render.
items.cie: This requirement is a suppression floor: no quote, drill-down, or demographic cut may be displayed if fewer than 11 participants underlie it, the suppression is executed server-side at the artifact layer (when the shareable result is built, not just hidden in the user interface), and 'complementary suppression' is applied so that a hidden small cell cannot be inferred by subtracting the visible ones. The point is to protect small groups from being re-identified. CIE's spec (R27) enforces this at the server so the raw small-n data never even leaves the building.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no server-side suppression floor: its demographic reporting (api/src/models/user_profile.rs get_demographic_report / get_demographics_for_export) aggregates age, gender, and ethnicity for consented users and returns the breakdowns without any minimum-cell-size gate or complementary suppression. Rendering is ungated, so a cut with only a handful of people would be shown as-is. There is no Bloom prior art for statistical suppression, which is a back-end privacy safeguard rather than a visible feature.
items.meaning: This is a sourced 'gap': the k-anonymity-style 11-participant floor with complementary suppression is entirely missing from Comhairle's report layer. Integration requires inserting server-side suppression logic into the export/artifact path, checking cell sizes and blanking or coarsening anything under 11, including the second-order inference protection. This is real defensive engineering added to Comhairle's currently open aggregation queries.
items.cie_s: The 11-participant suppression floor blocks any quote, drill-down, or demographic cut backed by fewer than 11 people, executed server-side at the artifact layer with complementary suppression so hidden cells cannot be inferred by subtraction.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's demographic reporting aggregates and returns breakdowns with no minimum-cell-size gate or complementary suppression, so a handful-sized cut is shown as-is.
items.meaning_s: This sourced gap requires inserting server-side suppression logic into Comhairle's export path, blanking or coarsening anything under 11 including the second-order inference protection.

items.name: Paraphrase-only quotes
items.note: Comhairle stores and serves verbatim statement text, the opposite of the Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase-only egress rule.
items.cie: This requirement is CIE's paraphrase-only egress rule: any quote shown to readers must be a human-reviewed paraphrase, labeled as such, and the original verbatim participant text must never leave the raw store, enforced at the export layer by an automated test. Paraphrasing plus review reduces the risk that a distinctive verbatim phrase re-identifies or exposes a participant. CIE's spec (R28) makes this a hard egress boundary, with a test guarding the export so verbatim text cannot escape.
items.comhairle: Comhairle does the opposite: it stores and serves verbatim statement text. api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs holds statement_text as the literal string, and the Pol.is flow ingests and returns that verbatim text (api/src/tools/polis.rs maps comment.txt straight into statement_text). There is no paraphrase step, no 'paraphrase' label, and no export-layer test preventing raw text from leaving. Bloom co-displays genuine free-text with votes (/tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), again reflecting a verbatim-forward norm rather than CIE's paraphrase discipline.
items.meaning: This is a sourced 'gap', arguably the sharpest one: Comhairle's verbatim-serving default is the direct inverse of CIE's paraphrase-only rule. Integration cannot be a small patch; it requires inserting a human paraphrase-and-review stage between the raw store and any display, labeling outputs, and adding an export-layer test that fails if verbatim text escapes. Reconciling these two opposite egress philosophies is one of the more consequential pieces of joining the systems.
items.cie_s: The paraphrase-only egress rule requires every displayed quote to be a human-reviewed, labeled paraphrase, with verbatim participant text never leaving the raw store, guarded by an export-layer test.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle does the opposite, storing and serving verbatim statement text with no paraphrase step, no 'paraphrase' label, and no export-layer test.
items.meaning_s: Reconciling these opposite egress philosophies is one of the more consequential integration pieces, requiring a human paraphrase-and-review stage and an export test between the raw store and any display.

items.name: Recontact tier live at launch
items.note: A live recontact consent tier has no counterpart in Comhairle.
items.cie: A 'recontact tier' is a separate, opt-in permission that lets the project email a participant again later (for example, to invite them into a follow-up pilot), kept distinct from permission to merely analyze their votes. CIE treats consent as two independent, unbundled switches (R23): one to include your responses in analysis, and a separate contact switch that defaults to OFF. R29 insists the recontact switch be built and working the day the first pilot launches, because if it is missing at launch you can never go back and ask that first wave of participants for permission you didn't collect: the chance to re-engage them across pilots is permanently foreclosed.
items.comhairle: Comhairle records consent as a single boolean, `user_profile.consented` (see `api/src/models/user_profile.rs`), rather than as separate analysis-vs-contact tiers, so there is no dedicated, independently-toggled recontact permission. It does have the plumbing to email people (notification models in `api/src/models/notification.rs`, scheduled email in `api/src/models/scheduled_email.rs`, and per-conversation recipient lists in `api/src/models/conversation_email_notification_recipients.rs`), but nothing that captures a standalone, versioned 'you may contact me for future rounds' consent. Bloom, the shipped Open-Poll product, shows this tier is product-viable: its 'Stay in touch' screen (bloom-07) is exactly an opt-in email signup for future 'opportunities to share your voice.'
items.meaning: Because the recontact permission is a CIE-specific consent concept with no matching field in Comhairle's model, an integration cannot rely on Comhairle to store or honor it: CIE must remain the system of record for consent. When exporting to Comhairle's interchange grammar the recontact flag simply has no target, so it stays behind in CIE's quarantined store; this is one of the 'no-analog' consent items the compare/contrast doc flags (§10.2), and it reinforces why CIE keeps its own consent ledger rather than delegating it.
items.cie_s: The recontact tier is a separate opt-in, defaulting off, that permits emailing a participant for future rounds, and must be live the day the first pilot launches or that first wave's permission is permanently foreclosed.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle records consent as a single boolean with plenty of email plumbing but no standalone, versioned recontact permission.
items.meaning_s: Because this consent concept has no matching field in Comhairle, Civic Intelligence Engine must remain the system of record for consent, and the recontact flag stays behind in Civic Intelligence Engine's quarantined store on export.

items.name: Post-results comms to completers
items.note: Comhairle has notifications, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's session-state rule of 'completed submitters only, after analysis'.
items.cie: This capability sends the 'here are the results' message only to people who actually finished the session, and only after the analysis run has completed, not to everyone who clicked in, and not before the numbers are final. Crucially, CIE enforces the 'completed submitters only' rule through session state (a flag the system sets when a participant genuinely reaches the end), not through a fragile manual process a staffer could get wrong. This protects both accuracy (no half-finished sessions get told 'you shaped the outcome') and trust (nobody is emailed results that later change).
items.comhairle: Comhairle has a real notification and email subsystem: `NotificationType` and delivery models in `api/src/models/notification.rs`, plus `scheduled_email.rs`, so it can send post-event messages. What it lacks is CIE's specific gating rule: there is no built-in constraint that ties a results email to 'this user's session reached the completed state AND the analysis run is done.' Comhairle's notifications are general-purpose and event/workflow triggered rather than bound to a per-participant completion plus post-analysis condition. Bloom's completion screen (bloom-08: 'Get on the email list') shows the recruitment side of this but likewise not the completed-only gating.
items.meaning: This is a 'partial' rather than a gap: an integrated system could reuse Comhairle's mailer as the delivery pipe while CIE supplies the eligibility decision (who counts as completed, and whether analysis is finished). The rule itself lives in CIE session state, so any integration must let CIE compute the recipient set and hand Comhairle a finalized list, rather than letting Comhairle broadcast on its own event triggers.
items.cie_s: The completers-only comms rule sends the results message only to participants whose session reached the completed state and only after the analysis run finishes, enforced through session state rather than a fragile manual process.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has a real notification and email subsystem but no built-in constraint tying a results email to per-participant completion plus post-analysis readiness.
items.meaning_s: This partial lets an integrated system reuse Comhairle's mailer as the delivery pipe while Civic Intelligence Engine computes the eligible recipient set and hands over a finalized list.

items.name: Contract in schema + validator
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine implements one record contract in both app schema and pipeline validator; Comhairle has no dual-checked contract.
items.cie: A 'record contract' is the single agreed definition of what a stored response looks like: its fields, types, and rules. R31 requires that identical definition to be enforced in two places at once: the application's database schema (what the app writes) and the pipeline's validator (what the analysis code refuses to read if malformed). If the two ever need to differ, that difference must be written down as a numbered entry in a README, never as a silent drift. This double-checking means a bad or unexpected row is caught coming in the front door and again before analysis, so the two halves of the system can never quietly disagree about the shape of the data.
items.comhairle: Comhairle also has a storage schema (its SQLx models plus 92 Structured Query Language migrations under `api/migrations/`) and, separately, an interchange grammar at `data_model/schema.json`, but these are not two cross-checked copies of one contract. The compare/contrast doc (§10.2) verified the `data_model` crate is essentially a stub: no model is actually a `Statement`/`Reaction`/`Group` table and no tool overrides `sync_data`, so the interchange schema is unwired rather than a live validator enforced against the database. There is no equivalent of a pipeline-side validator that would reject rows failing to match the app schema.
items.meaning: CIE's dual-enforced contract is exactly the seam that makes interoperability with Comhairle possible, since its record contract is elicitation-agnostic and already speaks Comhairle's Statement/Reaction vocabulary. But because Comhairle's own interchange schema is a stub, an integration means CIE serializing outward into that grammar (Path 1 export, §10.3), knowing the mapping is lossy; Comhairle cannot round-trip and re-validate CIE's contract, so CIE stays the authoritative definition.
items.cie_s: The dual-enforced record contract enforces one identical response definition in both the app's database schema and the pipeline's validator, with any divergence written down as a numbered README entry rather than allowed to drift.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has a storage schema and a separate interchange grammar, but these are not cross-checked copies of one contract, since the interchange schema is an unwired stub with no pipeline-side validator.
items.meaning_s: This contract is the seam that makes interoperability possible, but because Comhairle's interchange schema is a stub, integration means Civic Intelligence Engine serializing outward into that grammar as a lossy, one-way export with Civic Intelligence Engine staying authoritative.

items.name: No update/delete of raw rows
items.note: Append-only enforced in database roles; Comhairle uses ordinary mutable Postgres.
items.cie: 'Append-only' means raw response rows can be inserted but never updated or deleted: the historical record is immutable. CIE enforces this at the database-permission level: no role available to the app or the candidate is granted UPDATE or DELETE on the raw tables, and the requirement demands a live proof of this at the very first database bring-up, logged in the go/no-go checklist. This is CIE's 'one structural choice': by making tampering physically impossible rather than merely against policy, every downstream trust claim (hash chain, validity cards) rests on a foundation that cannot be quietly rewritten.
items.comhairle: Comhairle runs ordinary, mutable Postgres with no append-only roles or guard triggers; records can be updated or deleted like any normal database. The compare/contrast verification specifically found that `polis_statement_aux` (`api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs`) exposes `update`/`upsert` operations, and none of the 92 migrations install append-only enforcement. This isn't an oversight so much as a different priority: Comhairle optimizes for flexible orchestration of many tools, not for a tamper-evident constituent-data vault.
items.meaning: This is a foundational architecture divergence, not a feature toggle: CIE's immutability guarantee has no counterpart to inherit if data lived in Comhairle. It is a core reason the recommended posture keeps CIE as the system of record (§10.4), since Comhairle can at best be a downstream interop consumer, because pushing CIE's data into mutable storage would silently drop the very guarantee that makes the trust layer meaningful.
items.cie_s: The append-only rule makes raw rows insert-only, granting no role UPDATE or DELETE on the raw tables, proven live at first database bring-up and logged in the go/no-go checklist.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle runs ordinary mutable Postgres with no append-only roles or guard triggers, and its statement aux table exposes update and upsert operations.
items.meaning_s: This foundational architecture divergence has no counterpart to inherit, a core reason Civic Intelligence Engine stays the system of record while Comhairle can at best be a downstream interop consumer.

items.name: Analysis can't read contacts
items.note: A permission-audited wall between analysis and the contact store; Comhairle stores joinable data without it.
items.cie: This is a deliberate wall between the analysis engine and the contact store: the database role the pipeline uses to compute results has no read access whatsoever to the table holding people's contact details, and that separation is confirmed by a permission audit rather than trusted on faith. The point is personally identifiable information quarantine: even if the analysis code were buggy or compromised, it structurally cannot pull names, emails, or joinable identifiers into the results. Who someone is and how they voted are kept in separate compartments by design.
items.comhairle: Comhairle stores demographic and contact-adjacent data (ethnicity, age range, gender, political affiliation) in `user_profile` and joins it directly into analysis queries: `api/src/models/user_profile.rs` contains breakdown queries that filter `WHERE consented = true` and aggregate ethnicity, age, and gender by workflow. That joinability is a feature there (representativeness/demographic breakdowns), the exact opposite of CIE's wall. There is no analysis role isolated from the contact/profile store.
items.meaning: The compare/contrast doc flags this as a direct tension (§10.1): Comhairle's demographic joinability is precisely what CIE deliberately quarantines. For integration this means CIE must never export the joinable personally identifiable information into Comhairle's model. The Path 1 export explicitly emits no personally identifiable information (§10.3), and the two systems embody opposing philosophies about whether identity and opinion may be linked, which is a values conversation to surface with the Comhairle team, not just a schema detail.
items.cie_s: The wall quarantining personally identifiable information gives the analysis database role no read access to the contact table, confirmed by a permission audit, so buggy or compromised analysis code structurally cannot pull identifiers into results.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle stores demographic and contact-adjacent data in one profile and joins it directly into analysis queries, so joinability is a feature there, the exact opposite of the wall.
items.meaning_s: This is a direct values tension, so Civic Intelligence Engine must never export joinable personally identifiable information into Comhairle's model, and the opposing philosophies about linking identity and opinion should be surfaced with the Comhairle team.

items.name: Nightly off-box hash chain
items.note: A tamper-evident hash chain that blocks reads on mismatch, absent from Comhairle.
items.cie: A hash chain is a tamper-evidence device: each night the system computes a cryptographic fingerprint (hash) of the data, chained to the previous night's fingerprint, so that any later alteration of a past record breaks the chain and is instantly detectable. CIE requires this chain to be initialized before any real constituent data is ingested, to write its fingerprints off-box (to separate storage the app can't reach), and to block dashboard reads entirely if a mismatch is found. In plain terms: if anyone tampers with the history, the dashboards go dark rather than show data that can no longer be trusted.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no hash chain or equivalent tamper-evidence mechanism anywhere in the codebase; combined with its mutable Postgres (R32), there is nothing that would detect or block on a silent alteration of past rows. This is consistent with its design as a general orchestration platform rather than a high-assurance data vault: integrity-by-cryptographic-attestation simply isn't part of its threat model.
items.meaning: Tamper-evidence is a CIE-only guarantee with no target in Comhairle's model, so it cannot survive a move into Comhairle storage. It layers on top of append-only (R32) and hash-registered run artifacts (R36) as part of CIE's integrity stack, and it is another reason the mapping is lossy in exactly the direction that matters: Comhairle can consume CIE's outputs but cannot reproduce the assurance that those outputs were never altered.
items.cie_s: The nightly off-box hash chain fingerprints the data each night chained to the prior night, writes those fingerprints to storage the app cannot reach, and blocks dashboard reads entirely on any mismatch.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no hash chain or equivalent tamper-evidence, which combined with its mutable Postgres means a silent alteration of past rows would go undetected.
items.meaning_s: This Civic Intelligence Engine-only tamper-evidence cannot survive a move into Comhairle storage, another reason the export mapping is lossy in exactly the direction that matters.

items.name: Two-class moderation
items.note: Comhairle has a moderation status, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's two semantics: toxicity hides yet counts, while integrity excludes the session.
items.cie: CIE splits moderation into two distinct meanings, and the distinction changes the math. A 'toxicity' flag hides a statement from display but its votes still count in the aggregates (the person's opinion remains valid data even if their wording was unacceptable); an 'integrity' flag, for a bad-faith or fraudulent session, excludes that whole session from the counts. These flags write only to a separate enrichment table, never altering the raw rows, and both behaviors are verified by test. Keeping the two semantics apart matters because collapsing them would either throw away legitimate votes or let bad-faith votes pollute the results.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has a single moderation axis: `ModerationStatus` with `Accepted` / `Rejected` / `Pending` values, stored as an integer (-1 / 0 / 1) in `api/src/wiki_poll_service.rs`. A rejected statement is simply rejected: there is no notion of 'hide from display but still count the votes' versus 'exclude the whole session,' so the two CIE semantics fold into one accept/reject decision. This is a genuine partial: moderation exists, but not with CIE's two-behavior separation.
items.meaning: The compare/contrast doc (§10.2) singles this out as a place where collapsing CIE's two-class moderation into Comhairle's single status 'silently corrupts the statistics the spec explicitly warns about.' For integration, an export into Comhairle must state its moderation-filter policy up front in the export README, and one of the two proposed upstream 'gifts' to Crown Shy is a richer moderation/provenance entity for the interchange schema (§10.4), turning this gap into a contribution.
items.cie_s: The two-class moderation separates a toxicity flag, which hides a statement from display while its votes still count, from an integrity flag, which excludes a whole bad-faith session, writing only to a separate enrichment table that never alters raw rows.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has a single accept/reject/pending moderation axis, so both Civic Intelligence Engine semantics collapse into one decision that would either discard legitimate votes or admit bad-faith ones.
items.meaning_s: Collapsing the two classes silently corrupts the statistics the spec warns about, so an export must state its moderation-filter policy up front, and a richer moderation entity is one proposed upstream contribution.

items.name: Hash-registered run artifacts
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine renders immutable per-run artifacts under a versioned run id; Comhairle renders live data.
