items.cie: This capability makes every analysis result reproducible and immutable. Each pipeline run writes its outputs as fixed artifacts stamped with a run identifier that encodes the exact code version, instrument version, parameters, and an input 'watermark' (a marker of exactly which data went in), and those artifacts are hash-registered so they can't be silently changed. The dashboard then renders these frozen runs, never the live database. The effect: a result you saw last week is the same result today, traceable to precisely the code and inputs that produced it, so nobody can quietly re-run and swap the numbers under you.
items.comhairle: Comhairle renders live data drawn from its mutable Postgres store; there is no concept of a frozen, hash-registered run artifact under a versioned run id encoding code/instrument/parameters/watermark. Because analysis is served straight from the current database state, re-running or editing upstream data changes what the dashboard shows, with no immutable snapshot to compare against. This follows directly from the absence of append-only storage (R32) and a hash chain (R34).
items.meaning: Reproducible, versioned run artifacts are a CIE-core capability Comhairle entirely lacks (§10.1), and it's tightly coupled to CIE's other integrity guarantees. For integration it means the thing CIE would export is a specific, identified run, not a live feed, and Comhairle, rendering live data, has no place to preserve that run's identity or immutability, reinforcing CIE-as-system-of-record.
items.cie_s: The hash-registered run artifacts capability writes every pipeline run's outputs as fixed, hash-registered files stamped with a run id encoding code version, instrument version, parameters, and an input watermark, and the dashboard renders these frozen runs rather than the live database.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle renders live data straight from its mutable Postgres store and has no concept of a frozen, hash-registered run artifact, so re-running or editing upstream data silently changes what the dashboard shows.
items.meaning_s: Because Civic Intelligence Engine would export a specific, identified run rather than a live feed and Comhairle has nowhere to preserve that run's identity or immutability, this reinforces Civic Intelligence Engine staying the system of record.

items.name: Theme labels from a large language model, human-confirmed
items.note: Comhairle auto-categorizes with artificial intelligence, but without the Civic Intelligence Engine's recorded human confirmation and 20-contributor floor.
items.cie: Theme labels are the short human-readable names put on clusters of related statements ('housing costs,' 'school safety'). CIE has a large language model propose these labels but requires a human to confirm each one, with the reviewer's identity recorded; no label ships unreviewed. It also applies a floor: any theme supported by fewer than 20 contributors is shown only as 'emerging' and 'directional,' never as a firm finding, so thin themes aren't over-claimed. The combination keeps the speed of artificial-intelligence labeling while ensuring a named person stands behind every published label and small themes are honestly hedged.
items.comhairle: Comhairle auto-categorizes contributions with artificial intelligence via its categorization service, `api/src/categorization_service/tttc_categorizer.rs` (a 'Talk to the City'-style categorizer), but there is no recorded human-confirmation step tied to reviewer identity, and no 20-contributor floor that downgrades thin themes to emerging/directional. The categories it produces are used without the mandatory human sign-off and small-N hedging CIE requires, making this a partial rather than a full match.
items.meaning: Integration-wise, CIE's labels carry provenance (which human confirmed, and whether the theme cleared the 20-contributor floor) that Comhairle's model has nowhere to store. CIE would map cluster labels to Comhairle `Group` entities with `Generator::Algorithm` provenance (§10.2), but the human-confirmation and directional-only status are CIE-side metadata. It's another case where CIE's discipline is finer-grained than the interchange grammar can express.
items.cie_s: The large-language-model-plus-human-confirmed theme labels capability has a large language model propose cluster labels but records a named human's confirmation of each one, and hedges any theme with fewer than 20 contributors as merely emerging and directional.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle auto-categorizes contributions with its artificial intelligence categorization service but records no human-confirmation step tied to reviewer identity and applies no 20-contributor floor, making this a partial rather than full match.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's label provenance and directional-only status are Civic Intelligence Engine-side metadata that Comhairle's interchange grammar cannot express, so labels map to Comhairle Group entities with algorithm provenance but lose the human-confirmation detail.

items.name: Label/publish held for provider
items.note: A deliberate hold on the label/publish stage until the provider decision lands: a Civic Intelligence Engine build-discipline choice.
items.cie: This is a build-discipline rule rather than a runtime feature: the pipeline's 'label' and 'publish' stages are deliberately left unimplemented until the decision about which large-language-model provider to use has actually landed, and no placeholder or fake large-language-model output is ever written in the meantime. The reasoning is that writing throwaway machine text now risks it leaking into real artifacts or setting expectations before the provider (and its data-handling terms) is approved. CIE would rather ship an honest empty stage than a stub that pretends to work.
items.comhairle: Comhairle is a mature production system that already ships labeling, summarization, and question-answering backed by artificial intelligence against real providers: the RAGFlow bot (`api/src/bot_service/ragflow_bot.rs`), the categorization service, and translation/transcription services are all live. So it does not have (or need) a deliberate hold on these stages; the provider question was settled long ago in its lifecycle. This item is therefore less a Comhairle 'lack' than a snapshot of CIE's earlier build stage and its refusal to write placeholder output.
items.meaning: For integration this is mostly a sequencing note: CIE's label/publish path won't emit anything, real or placeholder, until its provider decision is made, so any export or adapter work that depends on labeled themes must wait for that gate. It signals to the Comhairle/Liz collaboration that CIE's artificial-intelligence-output surface is intentionally not-yet-wired, which is a discipline choice, not a capability Comhairle needs to supply.
items.cie_s: The hold-label-and-publish-for-provider rule deliberately leaves the pipeline's label and publish stages unimplemented, writing no placeholder or fake large language model output, until the decision about which large language model provider to use has actually landed.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle is a mature production system already shipping artificial-intelligence-backed labeling, summarization, and question-and-answer services against real providers, so it has no such hold, making this item less a Comhairle lack than a snapshot of Civic Intelligence Engine's earlier build stage.
items.meaning_s: This is mainly a sequencing note: any export or adapter work depending on labeled themes must wait for Civic Intelligence Engine's provider decision, signaling that Civic Intelligence Engine's artificial-intelligence-output surface is intentionally not-yet-wired by discipline rather than by a gap Comhairle must fill.

items.name: Single batch large language model call over aggregates
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine makes one batch pass over aggregates scrubbed of personally identifiable information; Comhairle makes many per-record external calls.
items.cie: This governs data egress: what leaves the box to an external artificial intelligence. CIE makes exactly one external large-language-model call: a single batch pass over aggregates scrubbed of personally identifiable information (summary data with personal identifiers already stripped) sent to the approved provider, verified by both code review and actual network-traffic capture. There are deliberately no per-record calls. The design keeps constituent data sovereign: instead of streaming thousands of individual responses to a third party, it sends one carefully-scrubbed summary, minimizing both privacy exposure and dependence on outside services.
items.comhairle: Comhairle makes many per-record external artificial-intelligence calls across several services: the RAGFlow bot (`api/src/bot_service/ragflow_bot.rs`), the categorization service (`categorization_service/tttc_categorizer.rs`), plus `translation_service` and `transcription_service`, which is the opposite pattern, numerous outbound calls, often on individual items, as a normal part of orchestration. The compare/contrast doc (§10.1) frames this as a data-sovereignty divergence: CIE uses local, processor-based embeddings plus one scrubbed batch call, while Comhairle routes many per-record items to external artificial intelligence.
items.meaning: This is a genuine gap with real privacy implications for integration: routing CIE data through Comhairle's per-record artificial-intelligence paths would violate CIE's single-scrubbed-egress guarantee. It's a strong argument for the export-first, CIE-as-system-of-record posture (§10.4): CIE controls exactly what, if anything, reaches an external model, and would not delegate that boundary to Comhairle's more liberal outbound-call architecture.
items.cie_s: The single-batch-large-language-model-over-aggregates rule makes exactly one external large language model call, a single batch pass over aggregates scrubbed of personally identifiable information, with deliberately no per-record calls, verified by both code review and network-traffic capture.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle takes the opposite posture, making many per-record external artificial intelligence calls across its RAGFlow bot, categorization, translation, and transcription services as a normal part of orchestration.
items.meaning_s: Routing Civic Intelligence Engine data through Comhairle's per-record artificial intelligence paths would violate Civic Intelligence Engine's single-scrubbed-egress guarantee, making this a strong argument for the export-first, Civic Intelligence Engine-as-system-of-record posture where Civic Intelligence Engine controls exactly what reaches an external model.

items.name: Thresholds single source of truth
items.note: Comhairle has config, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's linted single-source thresholds file with generated constants.
items.cie: A 'threshold' is any tuning number the analysis depends on (minimum votes per group, the 0.5 bridging cutoff, cluster-count bounds). R40 requires all of them to live in one file that is the single source of truth; from it, code constants are generated and checked in, never hand-edited, and a linter rejects any threshold literal hardcoded elsewhere in the codebase. This prevents the classic bug where a magic number is changed in one place but not another, and it makes every tuning decision auditable in one spot, which is essential when the numbers drive published civic claims.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has configuration (a top-level `api/src/config.rs` plus per-service config modules for the bot, categorization, etc.), but not CIE's linted single-source thresholds discipline: there is no one authoritative thresholds file whose constants are code-generated and guarded by a lint against stray literals. Configuration is present and reasonable for its purpose, which is why this rates partial, but the specific 'one file, generated constants, lint-enforced' guarantee is absent.
items.meaning: This is largely an internal-quality property rather than an interoperability seam, so it affects integration mainly by keeping CIE's analytic parameters coherent and auditable regardless of any Comhairle collaboration. If CIE's bridging analysis were ever contributed as a Comhairle adapter (§10.3 Path 2), CIE's thresholds file would remain the authority for those numbers, since Comhairle offers no equivalent single-source discipline to adopt them into.
items.cie_s: The thresholds single-source-of-truth rule keeps every tuning number in one authoritative file from which code constants are generated and checked in, with a linter rejecting any threshold literal hardcoded elsewhere.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has reasonable configuration in a top-level config module plus per-service configs but not Civic Intelligence Engine's linted single-source thresholds discipline with code-generated, lint-guarded constants, so it rates partial.
items.meaning_s: This is largely an internal-quality property rather than an interoperability seam, so even if Civic Intelligence Engine's bridging analysis became a Comhairle adapter its thresholds file would remain the authority for those numbers.

items.name: Unique codes + redemption log
items.note: Comhairle issues participation codes, though not to the Civic Intelligence Engine's 45-bit-entropy + append-only-redemption spec.
items.cie: These are the participation codes handed out (e.g., printed on a mailer) so a specific invited person can enter the poll. CIE specs them tightly: each code carries at least 45 bits of entropy (making them practically unguessable), redemption uses first-redemption-counts semantics (the first valid use is what registers), and every redemption is written to an append-only log so the record of who-redeemed-when can't be altered. Print feasibility must be confirmed in writing before proofs, with a per-batch fallback specified. The goal is codes that resist fraud and a redemption history that is tamper-evident.
items.comhairle: Comhairle issues invites via its `Invite` model (`api/src/models/invites.rs`), but they are keyed by a Universally Unique Identifier with a mutable `status` and an `accept_count`, plus `expires_at` and tags, not the 45-bit-entropy, first-redemption-counts, append-only-redemption specification CIE requires. Universally Unique Identifiers provide uniqueness but aren't the same as CIE's entropy-and-fraud-resistance contract, and the mutable status field means redemption state can change rather than being an immutable log. So participation codes exist (partial), but not to CIE's spec.
items.meaning: For integration, code issuance and redemption is another place where CIE's trust properties (entropy floor, append-only redemption log) have no matching enforcement in Comhairle's invite model, so CIE would keep ownership of code generation and redemption logging. Comhairle's invite/accept mechanism could coexist as a separate participation path, but it can't stand in for CIE's fraud-resistant, tamper-evident redemption requirements.
items.cie_s: The unique-codes-and-redemption-log capability specs each participation code to carry at least 45 bits of entropy, uses first-redemption-counts semantics, and writes every redemption to an append-only, tamper-evident log, with print feasibility confirmed in writing beforehand.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle issues invites keyed by a Universally Unique Identifier with a mutable status and accept count rather than Civic Intelligence Engine's entropy floor, first-redemption semantics, and append-only redemption log, so participation codes exist but not to Civic Intelligence Engine's fraud-resistant spec.
items.meaning_s: Because Civic Intelligence Engine's entropy floor and append-only redemption log have no matching enforcement in Comhairle's invite model, Civic Intelligence Engine keeps ownership of code generation and redemption logging while Comhairle's invite mechanism could at most coexist as a separate path.

items.name: Funnel report by channel/batch
items.note: Comhairle has participation analytics, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's delivered/redeemed/consented/completed funnel.
items.cie: A funnel report tracks how many people made it through each stage of participation: delivered (codes/invites sent), redeemed (entered), consented (agreed to participate), and completed (finished the instrument), broken out by channel (how they were reached) and batch (which mailing wave). CIE requires this four-stage funnel because it feeds the representativeness audit: knowing where people drop off, and whether some channels or batches over- or under-perform, is what lets the project judge whether the responding sample fairly reflects the district rather than a self-selected slice.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has participation analytics but not this specific funnel. It offers `DailyResponseStats` (accept/reject counts per day per invite, in `api/src/models/invites.rs`), `RecruitmentTarget` (target counts per metric/bucket, in `api/src/models/recruitment_target.rs`), and demographic breakdowns (`user_profile.rs`), useful pieces, but not a delivered→redeemed→consented→completed funnel segmented by channel and batch. Bloom's recruitment/share screens (bloom-06) show the top-of-funnel intent but likewise not the staged funnel report. Hence partial.
items.meaning: Because CIE's funnel is defined around its own stages, including 'consented' (tied to CIE's two-tier consent) and 'completed' (tied to CIE session state), it depends on data Comhairle doesn't model the same way, so CIE would compute the funnel from its own records. Comhairle's recruitment targets and daily stats could complement a representativeness view, but the authoritative funnel and the representativeness audit it feeds remain CIE-side.
items.cie_s: The funnel-report-by-channel-and-batch capability tracks participation through delivered, redeemed, consented, and completed stages broken out by outreach channel and mailing batch, feeding the representativeness audit.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle offers useful pieces such as daily response stats, recruitment targets, and demographic breakdowns but not the staged delivered-to-completed funnel segmented by channel and batch, so it rates partial.
items.meaning_s: Because Civic Intelligence Engine's funnel is defined around its own consented and completed stages, Civic Intelligence Engine computes the authoritative funnel from its own records while Comhairle's recruitment stats could at most complement a representativeness view.

items.name: Contact-list provenance documented
items.note: Documenting contact-list provenance before print: an operations step.
items.cie: R43 is an operations requirement, not a piece of software: before anyone prints a mailer with a Quick Response code, the campaign must write down where the contact list came from, whether the people on it agreed to be contacted, and the rule used to pick them. In plain terms, 'provenance' just means a paper trail answering 'who are these people, and are we allowed to reach them this way?'. CIE treats this as a launch gate because a listening exercise that recruits from a tainted or non-consented list poisons every downstream statistic no matter how good the math is; the requirement (catalog R43) forces that honesty conversation before money is spent on print.
items.comhairle: Comhairle is orchestration software that spins up and wires together polling tools like Pol.is and HeyForm; it has no concept of who was invited or how a contact list was assembled, because recruitment happens entirely outside the platform. So there is nothing in the codebase to check here, and no equivalent gate. Bloom, the shipped 'Open Poll' product, handles recruitment similarly as an off-platform program step, sharing links and Quick Response codes without recording list provenance in the tool itself.
items.meaning: For integration this is a reminder that CIE's rigor is not only in code: even if Comhairle produced a flawless opinion map, a candidate could not stand behind the result unless the human process that fed it (who was invited, with what consent) was documented first. Comhairle can be the engine, but the campaign still owes the provenance record that CIE's acceptance checklist demands before launch.
items.cie_s: The contact-list-provenance capability is an operations gate requiring the campaign, before printing any Quick Response code mailer, to document where the contact list came from, whether those people consented to contact, and the rule used to select them.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle is orchestration software with no concept of who was invited or how a contact list was assembled, because recruitment happens entirely outside the platform, so there is no equivalent gate to check.
items.meaning_s: This reminds integrators that even a flawless Comhairle-produced opinion map cannot be stood behind unless the human recruitment process feeding it is documented first, an obligation that stays with the campaign regardless of engine.

items.name: Quick Response code domain warmed, fast landing
items.note: Warming the domain behind the Quick Response code and latency-testing the landing page: a deployment step.
items.cie: R44 says the web address behind the Quick Response code must be chosen, 'warmed', and speed-tested before the campaign commits to a print vendor, with the landing page loading in under three seconds on a mid-range phone over a normal cellular connection. 'Warming' a domain means using it enough ahead of time that spam filters and security scanners recognize it as legitimate rather than flagging a brand-new link; a cold domain can get silently blocked, so scanning constituents never even reach the survey. CIE ties this to participation because every second of load time and every filter block shaves off respondents, and the whole system's validity depends on getting enough people in the door (it directly feeds the T1 participation floor).
items.comhairle: Comhairle serves its SvelteKit frontend and an Axum-based application programming interface, but the choice of public Quick Response domain, its reputation warming, and landing-page latency are deployment and infrastructure concerns that live outside the application logic; the repo does not encode a three-second budget or a domain-warming step. Bloom likewise treats share links and Quick Response codes as a distribution task the organizer handles, not a platform-enforced performance gate.
items.meaning: Integrating the two systems means someone still has to own the operational plumbing around Comhairle: registering and warming the domain, and confirming fast mobile loads. CIE's spec makes this a precondition rather than an afterthought, so a Comhairle-hosted pilot would need this latency-and-deliverability work wrapped around it before print, or the participation numbers that every quality gate assumes will never materialize.
items.cie_s: The warmed-Quick-Response-domain-and-fast-landing capability requires the public web address behind the Quick Response code to be chosen, reputation-warmed against spam filters, and speed-tested to load in under three seconds on a mid-range phone before committing to print.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle serves its frontend and application programming interface, but the choice, warming, and latency of the public Quick Response code domain are deployment and infrastructure concerns outside its application logic, so the repo encodes no such budget or warming step.
items.meaning_s: Integrating means someone must still own the operational plumbing of registering and warming the domain and confirming fast mobile loads, since without it the participation numbers every quality gate assumes will never materialize.

items.name: Staging walkthrough
items.note: A production-identical staging walkthrough: a launch-readiness step.
items.cie: R45 requires a full dress rehearsal on a staging environment that is identical to production, where the team deliberately views the system in its genuine low-participation state, so they see cells that are suppressed (hidden for privacy/insufficient data) and results wearing their honest confidence badges, and then resolves or explicitly waives any feedback before launch. The point is to make the campaign confront early reality: at 50 participants most breakdowns will be blank, not because the tool is broken but because it is being honest. CIE's spec (AC-B4.1) treats this walkthrough as the moment the abstract quality gates become visible to non-technical stakeholders, so launch day holds no surprises.
items.comhairle: Because Comhairle renders Pol.is output live and ungated, it has no 'low-N honest state' to rehearse: it simply shows whatever number the analysis returns regardless of how few people voted, with no suppression chips or badges to preview (the raw group-informed-consensus float is surfaced directly, per api/src/tools/polis.rs and the wrapped Pol.is server). There is therefore nothing to walk through in the CIE sense. Bloom similarly publishes raw agree/diverge tallies without a gated staging preview of suppressed cells.
items.meaning: A Comhairle-based pilot would need CIE's gating layer added just so a meaningful staging walkthrough could exist, because you cannot rehearse the suppression-and-badge experience on a system that never suppresses or badges anything. This item shows the integration gap concretely: the walkthrough is a rehearsal of CIE's honesty machinery, which Comhairle does not yet have.

items.comhairle_s: Because Comhairle renders Pol.is output live and ungated, it has no low-N honest state to rehearse, showing whatever number the analysis returns with no suppression chips or badges to preview.

items.name: Load test at 5–10k
items.note: A concurrency load test confirming zero loss: a testing step.
items.cie: R46 is a load test: push 5,000 to 10,000 fake submissions through the production configuration and confirm three things stay true under heavy simultaneous traffic: no data is lost, the append-only store stays intact (records are only added, never overwritten, so no one can quietly alter what constituents said), and the landing page stays within its speed budget. 'Concurrency' just means many people acting at the same moment, which is exactly what happens when a mailer lands and thousands scan the Quick Response code within an hour. CIE cares because data integrity under load is a foundational honesty guarantee (AC-A4.2): if submissions vanish or get clobbered during a rush, the results are corrupt before any statistics run.
items.comhairle: Load and concurrency behavior are properties of a specific deployment, not something visible in the Comhairle source; the repo does not ship a load-test harness or an append-only integrity assertion of the kind CIE specifies. Whether Comhairle's Axum backend loses data under a 10k burst would have to be measured against a real deployment. Bloom, as a hosted product, handles scaling operationally rather than exposing an integrity-under-load acceptance test.
items.meaning: If Comhairle were the runtime, this test would still need to be run against that stack, and its storage layer would need to prove append-only integrity to satisfy CIE's data-honesty commitment. The item underlines that CIE's guarantees include operational resilience, not just statistics, so wrapping CIE gates around Comhairle results only matters if the underlying store provably keeps every vote.
items.cie_s: The load-test-at-5-to-10k capability pushes thousands of simultaneous submissions through the production configuration and confirms no data is lost, the append-only store stays intact, and the landing page holds its speed budget under heavy traffic.
items.comhairle_s: Load and concurrency behavior are properties of a specific deployment rather than the Comhairle source, which ships no load-test harness or append-only integrity assertion of the kind Civic Intelligence Engine specifies.
items.meaning_s: If Comhairle were the runtime this test would still need running against that stack, and its storage layer would need to prove append-only integrity under load to satisfy Civic Intelligence Engine's data-honesty commitment.

items.name: Milestone gates signed
items.note: Funder-signed milestone gates and go/no-go: a governance step.
items.cie: R47 is a governance gate: the funder signs off on a sequence of milestones, and the final go/no-go decision requires every MUST-level criterion to be green, a review of scope against the budget cap, and a current decision log with no OPEN item still blocking a MUST. In plain terms it is a structured checklist of approvals so that launch is a deliberate, signed decision rather than a drift into going live. CIE builds this as six sequential funder-signed gates (spec E1-E3) precisely so a candidate and funder gain confidence at intervals and no one can later claim the launch bar was fuzzy.
items.comhairle: This is a project-management and funder-governance process, entirely outside any software; Comhairle neither tracks milestones nor enforces sign-offs, and there is nothing in the codebase that corresponds to it. Bloom likewise leaves program governance to the organizing team rather than the tool.
items.meaning: Whatever software runs the pilot, the milestone-gate process belongs to the program, so Comhairle-as-engine changes nothing here except that the 'every MUST green' check would include the missing CIE quality gates (T1-T10). In other words, a Comhairle deployment could not truthfully pass this governance gate until the statistical guardrails it currently lacks were added and shown green.
items.cie_s: The signed-milestone-gates capability is a governance process where the funder signs off on a sequence of milestones and the final go/no-go requires every MUST-level criterion green, a scope-versus-budget review, and a decision log with no open blocking item.
items.comhairle_s: This is a project-management and funder-governance process entirely outside any software, so Comhairle neither tracks milestones nor enforces sign-offs and has nothing in its codebase corresponding to it.
items.meaning_s: Whatever software runs the pilot, the milestone-gate process belongs to the program, and a Comhairle deployment could not truthfully pass the every-MUST-green check until the statistical guardrails it currently lacks were added and shown green.

items.name: Replication playbook
items.note: A playbook authored alongside the build: a deliverable, not a platform feature.
items.cie: R48 requires a replication playbook written alongside the build, not after it, that separates pilot-specific details from generally reusable steps, carries the protocol for communicating with the candidate, and measures deployment time across pilots as the key replication metric. The idea is that the real product is not one campaign's dashboard but the repeatable ability to stand up another one quickly and correctly; writing the playbook in parallel keeps it honest because it captures decisions while they are fresh. CIE treats faster deployment-per-pilot as the yardstick that the method actually generalizes.
items.comhairle: A playbook is a written deliverable about how to run the program, not a platform feature, so Comhairle has no analog; however, Comhairle's value proposition as reusable open-source orchestration (GNU Affero General Public License, version 3.0, Rust/SvelteKit) is exactly the kind of asset a replication playbook would lean on to cut deployment time. Bloom's existence as a packaged Open Poll product is itself a form of replication, contrasting with CIE's documented-playbook approach.
items.meaning: For integration, Comhairle could become the reusable technical substrate the playbook points to, shrinking per-pilot setup time, but the playbook must also document the CIE gating that Comhairle does not provide out of the box. The item frames Comhairle as a potential accelerator of replication while making clear the honesty layer still has to travel with it from pilot to pilot.
items.cie_s: The replication-playbook capability requires a playbook written alongside the build that separates pilot-specific details from reusable steps, carries the candidate-communication protocol, and measures deployment time per pilot as the key replication metric.
items.comhairle_s: A playbook is a written deliverable rather than a platform feature, so Comhairle has no analog, though its reusable open-source orchestration is exactly the kind of asset such a playbook would lean on to cut deployment time.
items.meaning_s: Comhairle could become the reusable technical substrate the playbook points to, shrinking per-pilot setup time, but the playbook must still document the Civic Intelligence Engine gating that Comhairle does not provide out of the box.

items.name: Participation gate
items.note: A minimum-participation floor before any result renders; Comhairle shows Pol.is math live.
items.cie: T1 is the participation floor: no result renders until a minimum number of people have taken part (the spec uses roughly 100 participants for the opinion map). The reason is intuitive: opinions computed from a handful of people are noise dressed up as signal, and showing them invites a candidate to over-read a dozen votes as 'what the district thinks'. CIE enforces this as a hard gate before any analysis output is displayed, so the map simply does not appear until enough voices are present; below it, the honest statement-level fallback view is shown instead.
items.comhairle: Comhairle applies no participation floor: it surfaces Pol.is's group-informed-consensus numbers live regardless of how few people have voted (the raw float is passed straight through the polis integration in api/src/tools/polis.rs with no minimum-N check). A three-person conversation would render a full-looking result. Bloom similarly publishes tallies from whoever has responded so far without a participation gate.
items.meaning: This is the first and most basic gate Comhairle lacks, so a Comhairle result at low turnout would look authoritative while resting on almost nothing. Before a candidate could stand behind a Comhairle-produced map, CIE's participation floor would have to be wrapped around it to withhold display until the sample is large enough to mean anything.
items.cie_s: The participation gate renders no result until a minimum number of people (roughly 100 for the opinion map) have taken part, showing an honest statement-level fallback below that floor so a handful of votes are never over-read as the district's view.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle applies no participation floor, surfacing Pol.is's group-informed-consensus numbers live regardless of how few people have voted, so a three-person conversation renders a full-looking result.
items.meaning_s: This is the first and most basic gate Comhairle lacks, so before a candidate could stand behind a Comhairle-produced map Civic Intelligence Engine's participation floor would have to be wrapped around it to withhold display until the sample is large enough to mean anything.

items.name: Cell suppression floor
items.note: The 11-participant server-side suppression floor is absent from Comhairle's ungated display.
items.cie: T2 is small-cell suppression: any breakdown (say, a demographic cross-tab) computed from fewer than 11 people is hidden rather than shown. 'Cell suppression' comes from health-data privacy practice (the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services n<11 standard) and protects individuals, because a group of two or three is small enough that an outsider could deduce who said what. CIE enforces this server-side at the artifact-serving layer so no chart component ever receives sub-threshold data; you can see it in bridging.py where min_cell = 11 and per-group self-code overlays are marked suppressed when n < 11.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no suppression floor: its ungated display would render a cell built from two respondents exactly as it renders one built from two thousand, since it forwards Pol.is output without a privacy threshold. There is no server-side min-cell filter in the rendering path. Bloom likewise shows raw agree/diverge counts without a small-cell privacy cutoff.
items.meaning: Integrating Comhairle safely would require inserting CIE's suppression floor between the analysis and any client, because otherwise a tiny subgroup's data could be exposed and re-identified. This is a privacy-and-liability gate a candidate genuinely cannot skip, so it must be added around Comhairle before results are published.
items.cie_s: The cell suppression floor hides any breakdown computed from fewer than 11 people, enforced server-side at the artifact-serving layer so no chart component ever receives sub-threshold data.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no suppression floor, rendering a cell built from two respondents exactly as it renders one built from two thousand because it forwards Pol.is output without a privacy threshold.
items.meaning_s: Integrating Comhairle safely requires inserting Civic Intelligence Engine's suppression floor between the analysis and any client, since otherwise a tiny subgroup's data could be exposed and re-identified, a privacy-and-liability gate a candidate cannot skip.

items.name: Coverage / representativeness gate
items.note: A coverage threshold before results: Comhairle applies no such gate.
items.cie: T3 is a coverage / representativeness gate: it asks whether enough of the relevant themes or slices of the conversation have accumulated enough data to be worth showing, rather than presenting a sparse, lopsided picture as if it were complete. In practice several themes will sit below this bar early in a pilot, and CIE's response is to withhold or clearly mark those thin areas rather than imply full coverage. It protects against the subtle dishonesty of a dashboard that looks comprehensive when in fact only one or two topics have real support behind them.
items.comhairle: Comhairle applies no coverage threshold: it displays whatever the underlying analysis returns for every theme regardless of how thinly populated, because it renders live and ungated. Nothing in the codebase gauges whether a slice is well-enough covered to display. Bloom similarly surfaces all results without a representativeness gate.
items.meaning: A Comhairle dashboard would present under-covered themes with the same visual authority as well-supported ones, so CIE's coverage gate would need to be layered on to distinguish 'we have a real read here' from 'barely anyone spoke to this'. Without it, a candidate risks acting on a theme that only a few participants ever touched.
items.cie_s: The coverage and representativeness gate asks whether enough themes or slices of the conversation have accumulated enough data to be worth showing, withholding or clearly marking thin areas rather than implying full coverage.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle applies no coverage threshold, displaying whatever the analysis returns for every theme regardless of how thinly populated because it renders live and ungated.
items.meaning_s: A Comhairle dashboard would present under-covered themes with the same visual authority as well-supported ones, so Civic Intelligence Engine's coverage gate would need to be layered on to distinguish a real read from barely anyone speaking to a topic.

items.name: ≥25 votes per group
items.note: The 25-votes-per-group floor for a group-level claim has no analog in Comhairle.
items.cie: T4 requires at least 25 votes from each opinion group on a given statement before any group-level claim about that statement is allowed (the proof of concept scales this to 15 for demo data; see min_votes_per_group in bridging.py). The logic is that a claim like 'both camps agree on this' is only trustworthy if each camp actually cast enough votes on that specific statement; with a handful of votes per group, apparent agreement is a coin-flip artifact. CIE enforces the floor per statement and per group, and if a statement falls short it can be shown as a bridging candidate with the exact vote deficit displayed rather than as a settled result.
items.comhairle: Comhairle enforces no per-group vote minimum: it would report a cross-group consensus number even if one group cast only two or three votes on the statement, because the raw Pol.is figure is surfaced without a votes-per-group check. There is no analog to min_votes_per_group in its display path. Bloom, publishing raw tallies, similarly has no per-group sufficiency floor.
items.meaning: For a candidate to trust a Comhairle 'the groups agree' claim, CIE's 25-votes-per-group floor would have to gate it, because agreement computed from too-few votes per group is not a finding. This gate is a building block of the bridging badge, so its absence in Comhairle undermines the very cross-group claims that make the tool politically useful.
items.cie_s: The at-least-25-votes-per-group gate requires each opinion group to cast at least 25 votes on a statement before any group-level claim about it is allowed, showing short statements as bridging candidates with the exact vote deficit rather than settled results.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle enforces no per-group vote minimum, reporting a cross-group consensus number even if one group cast only two or three votes on the statement.
items.meaning_s: Because this floor is a building block of the bridging badge, its absence in Comhairle undermines the very cross-group claims that make the tool politically useful, so Civic Intelligence Engine's 25-votes-per-group gate would have to sit in front of any such claim.

items.name: Opinion-map stability gate
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine blocks an unstable opinion map; Comhairle renders whatever Pol.is returns.
items.cie: T5 is the opinion-map stability gate: the clustering that finds opinion groups is re-run across several random seeds, and the map is only shown if the groupings agree with each other across runs (the spec requires median pairwise ARI >= 0.8; ARI, the Adjusted Rand Index, is a 0-to-1 score of how similarly two runs sort people into groups). If the map reshuffles every time you run it, it is measuring noise, not real opinion structure, and CIE blocks it. The evaluation found the vote-plane map stable at n=300 but the text-plane clustering could still fail T5 at n=150, which is exactly when CIE falls back to the honest per-statement view.
items.comhairle: Comhairle renders whatever grouping Pol.is returns on a single run, with no multi-seed stability check, so an unstable map that would reshuffle on re-computation is displayed as if it were solid. Nothing in the codebase re-runs clustering across seeds or compares ARI. Bloom does not present a seed-stability-gated opinion map either.
items.meaning: A Comhairle opinion map could show groups that are essentially arbitrary, and the viewer would have no way to know. To stand behind it, CIE's stability gate would need to wrap the clustering so an unstable map is withheld in favor of the fallback, meaning Comhairle's headline feature (the opinion map) is precisely the one most in need of CIE's guardrail.
items.cie_s: The opinion-map stability gate re-runs the clustering across several random seeds and shows the map only if the groupings agree across runs (median pairwise Adjusted Rand Index at least 0.8), falling back to the honest per-statement view otherwise.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle renders whatever grouping Pol.is returns on a single run with no multi-seed stability check, so an unstable map that would reshuffle on re-computation is displayed as if it were solid.
items.meaning_s: A Comhairle opinion map could show essentially arbitrary groups with no way for the viewer to know, so Civic Intelligence Engine's stability gate would need to wrap the clustering, meaning Comhairle's headline feature is precisely the one most in need of the guardrail.

items.name: Per-cluster stability gate
items.note: Per-cluster stability gating (sub-headline → directional) is absent from Comhairle.
items.cie: T6 is per-cluster stability: beyond checking that the whole map is stable (T5), it checks each individual group by resampling the data many times (bootstrap) and measuring how consistently the same people stay grouped together (Jaccard overlap >= 0.75, where Jaccard is the share of members two versions of a group have in common). A cluster that passes gets to carry a headline claim; one that is only moderately stable is demoted to a weaker 'directional' statement. This graceful degradation lets CIE say more about the groups it is sure of and less about the shaky ones, rather than treating every cluster as equally solid.
items.comhairle: Comhairle performs no per-cluster stability assessment and has no notion of demoting a shaky group's claim to 'directional'; every group Pol.is returns is presented with equal confidence in the live, ungated view. There is no bootstrap-Jaccard step in its path. Bloom likewise does not tier group claims by per-cluster stability.
items.meaning: Wrapping CIE around Comhairle would add this nuance the raw display lacks: some groups are trustworthy enough to headline, others only to hint at. Without T6, a Comhairle result invites a candidate to over-trust a fragile subgroup, so the gate is part of the honesty layer that would need to sit between Comhairle's analysis and any published claim.
items.cie_s: The per-cluster stability gate resamples the data many times to measure how consistently each individual group holds together (Jaccard overlap at least 0.75), letting stable clusters carry headline claims while demoting shaky ones to directional.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle performs no per-cluster stability assessment and has no notion of demoting a shaky group's claim, presenting every group Pol.is returns with equal confidence in the live, ungated view.
items.meaning_s: Without this gate a Comhairle result invites a candidate to over-trust a fragile subgroup, so per-cluster stability is part of the honesty layer that would need to sit between Comhairle's analysis and any published claim.

items.name: Per-group Wilson lower bound
items.note: Requiring each group's Wilson 95% lower bound above 0.5 is not enforced by Comhairle.
items.cie: T7 requires that each opinion group's Wilson 95% lower bound on its agreement with a statement exceeds 0.5. A 'Wilson lower bound' is a careful way to state the worst-case end of a confidence interval for a proportion: instead of saying '60% of this group agreed', it asks 'given how few votes there were, how low could the true agreement plausibly be?' and uses that pessimistic figure. Requiring the lower bound (not just the raw 60%) to clear 50% is the difference between 'the groups probably agree' and 'we are confident they agree even accounting for uncertainty'; bridging.py computes this in wilson_lower() and only lets a bridge pass when all group lower bounds exceed 0.5, which is why the polarized Seattle dataset correctly earns zero bridges.
items.comhairle: Comhairle surfaces Pol.is's point-estimate group-informed-consensus float directly and applies no Wilson interval or lower-bound test, so a statement whose raw agreement merely looks above half would display as consensus even if the uncertainty band dips well below 0.5. The interval math never runs in Comhairle's path (the bridging computation lives in the wrapped Pol.is Clojure server, out of the clone, and is surfaced ungated). Bloom similarly reports raw agreement without a lower-bound confidence test.
items.meaning: This is the statistical heart of a defensible bridging claim, and Comhairle omits it, so its consensus numbers can fire on shaky majorities that CIE would reject. Before a candidate could publicly claim 'these opposed groups actually agree', CIE's Wilson-lower-bound gate would have to be computed on top of Comhairle's raw output; the number Comhairle shows is a starting ingredient, not a vetted claim.
items.cie_s: The per-group Wilson lower bound gate requires each opinion group's Wilson 95% lower bound on its agreement with a statement to exceed 0.5, using the pessimistic end of the confidence interval so that only genuinely confident agreement passes.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle surfaces Pol.is's point-estimate consensus float directly and applies no Wilson interval or lower-bound test, so a statement whose raw agreement merely looks above half displays as consensus even when the uncertainty band dips below 0.5.
items.meaning_s: This is the statistical heart of a defensible bridging claim that Comhairle omits, so before a candidate could publicly claim opposed groups agree, Civic Intelligence Engine's Wilson-lower-bound gate would have to be computed on top of Comhairle's raw output.

items.name: Bridging / representativeness badge
items.note: The gated badge itself, the claim rather than the number, has no Comhairle equivalent.
items.cie: T8 is the gated badge itself: every result surface carries exactly one confidence label from a fixed vocabulary ('representative-enough', 'directional', or 'suppressed'), and a bridging badge is awarded only when the underlying gates (enough votes per group, group agreement >= 0.5, and all Wilson lower bounds above 0.5) all pass. The badge is the claim, not the number: it translates a pile of statistics into one honest word a non-statistician can read, deliberately replacing 'margin of error' language (which is not even computable for opt-in samples) with a term about what the data can support. bridging.py assigns exactly this badge, labeling a statement 'representative-enough' only when the full gate stack passes and 'directional' or 'below-bar' otherwise.
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no badge concept at all: it shows the raw consensus figure with no label describing how much confidence it deserves, because it renders live and ungated with no gate stack behind a claim. There is nothing in the codebase that stamps a result 'representative-enough' versus 'directional'. Bloom, publishing raw agree/diverge results, likewise offers no gated confidence badge, which is the sharpest contrast with CIE's validity-carded presentation.
items.meaning: The badge is the single most visible thing CIE adds and Comhairle lacks: it is the difference between handing a candidate a bare number and handing them a vetted claim they can repeat in public. Integrating the two means CIE's entire gate stack (T1-T7) would need to run behind Comhairle's output to earn a badge, so that a candidate is never standing behind an unlabeled figure that the statistics do not actually support.
items.cie_s: The bridging and representativeness badge stamps every result surface with exactly one confidence label from a fixed vocabulary, awarding a bridging badge only when the full gate stack of vote counts, group agreement, and Wilson lower bounds all pass, so the badge is the claim rather than the bare number.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no badge concept at all, showing the raw consensus figure with no label describing how much confidence it deserves because it renders live and ungated with no gate stack behind a claim.
items.meaning_s: The badge is the single most visible thing Civic Intelligence Engine adds and Comhairle lacks, so integrating means Civic Intelligence Engine's entire gate stack would run behind Comhairle's output to earn a badge and ensure a candidate never stands behind an unlabeled figure the statistics do not support.

items.name: Claim-type gate
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine's pipeline claim-type gate plus scope banner; Comhairle has no claim-discipline gate.
items.cie: T9 is CIE's 'claim-type gate': a hard rule that the product may never say things like 'X% of the district believes Y' unless a real representative sample exists (the spec pins this at n>=384 with a documented sampling frame, and even then only if the funder confirms a polling-style claim). The reason is that opt-in civic responses are self-selected, so no margin of error is even computable; calling them a district-wide percentage would be a false statistical claim. CIE enforces T9 mechanically with a copy-linter that scans every dashboard string, export, and communication for forbidden 'percent-of-district' language before the go/no-go gate, and the cie-lab Ask prototype (web/src/views/Ask.tsx) carries the same discipline into chat by refusing premises the votes don't support (e.g. 'prove everyone opposes new taxes' returns 'the evidence does not answer this').
items.comhairle: Comhairle has no claim-type gate. Its wrapped Pol.is tool (api/src/tools/polis.rs) computes and returns opinion groups and per-statement agreement, but nothing in the pipeline inspects or constrains how those numbers are described to a reader, and there is no copy-linter over output strings. Bloom, the shipped Open Poll product, is the same: it publishes results publicly as 'where Americans agree, where we differ' (bloom-04) but presents them raw, with no gate distinguishing a theme-map claim from a representativeness claim.
items.meaning: Integrating the two systems means T9 has to be added as a layer on top of whatever Comhairle emits, because Comhairle will happily hand over cluster percentages with no vocabulary discipline attached. In practice CIE would wrap or post-process Comhairle's output and run its copy-linter before anything reaches a candidate or the public, so the claim-type gate lives in CIE's presentation/export layer rather than in the shared analysis substrate.
items.cie_s: The claim-type gate is a hard rule that the product may never say a percentage of the district believes something unless a real representative sample exists, enforced mechanically by a copy-linter that scans every dashboard string, export, and communication for forbidden polling language.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has no claim-type gate, computing and returning opinion groups and per-statement agreement with nothing in the pipeline inspecting or constraining how those numbers are described to a reader.
items.meaning_s: Integrating means this gate has to be added as a layer on top of whatever Comhairle emits, so Civic Intelligence Engine would wrap or post-process Comhairle's output and run its copy-linter before anything reaches a candidate or the public.

items.name: Paraphrase / verbatim-egress gate
items.note: The export-layer block on verbatim text (substituting a paraphrase) is the opposite of Comhairle's verbatim serving.
items.cie: T10 is the 'paraphrase / verbatim-egress' gate: constituents' exact words (free-text comments) must stay inside the raw store and never appear on a dashboard, export, or vendor file; any displayed quote must be a human-reviewed paraphrase. The concern is deductive disclosure: in an 80,000-person district a neighbor or opposing campaign can recognize someone from their speech style and incidental detail even with the name removed, so verbatim text is a re-identification risk. CIE builds this as an export-layer block that substitutes a paraphrase for verbatim text, composed with human review before display (AC-N1) and the small-cell suppression floor; notably its conversational prototype (analysis/converse.py) does use verbatim quotes to ground a synthesis, but only in-session with the speaker confirming, never in egress.
items.comhairle: Comhairle serves statements verbatim by design; its Pol.is and statement tooling (api/src/tools/polis.rs, api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs) store and return the exact submitted text, and there is no export-layer paraphrase substitution. This is the direct opposite posture to T10. Bloom likewise co-displays free-text 'Share your perspective' submissions (bloom-01) as first-class content, again showing raw participant words rather than a paraphrase-gated view.
items.meaning: This is a genuine architectural conflict, not just a missing feature: Comhairle's whole statement model assumes verbatim serving, so an integration cannot simply pass Comhairle text through. CIE would have to intercept every egress path from Comhairle, hold verbatim text in a controlled raw store, and emit only reviewed paraphrases, which is exactly the kind of seam the frozen record contract (M6) is meant to create.
items.cie_s: The paraphrase and verbatim-egress gate keeps constituents' exact words inside the raw store and never on a dashboard, export, or vendor file, substituting a human-reviewed paraphrase at the export layer to prevent re-identification through distinctive speech.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle serves statements verbatim by design, storing and returning the exact submitted text with no export-layer paraphrase substitution, the direct opposite posture to this gate.
items.meaning_s: This is a genuine architectural conflict rather than a missing feature, so Civic Intelligence Engine would have to intercept every egress path from Comhairle, hold verbatim text in a controlled store, and emit only reviewed paraphrases, exactly the seam the frozen record contract is meant to create.

items.name: Low-friction web entry
items.note: Comhairle offers web entry and codes, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's proportionate astroturf-integrity layer as specified.
items.cie: M1 is low-friction web entry: a participant can join from a landing page, Quick Response code, or unique invite code with no app install and no login, and be voting in under a minute, plus a 'proportionate integrity layer' that contains astroturfing (fake or coordinated mass responses) without adding friction for real people. CIE treats the entry surface as a funnel that must be frictionless yet defensible; the cie-lab prototypes (web/src/views/Converse.tsx and the vote view) demonstrate the join-and-participate flow that this milestone standardizes.
items.comhairle: Comhairle covers the mechanics of web entry and codes, and Bloom is strong prior art that this pattern is product-viable: Bloom offers a warm no-install voting screen with an 'N LEFT' counter and share-by-text/email/link recruitment (bloom-01, bloom-06). What is not present as CIE specifies is the proportionate astroturf-integrity layer sized to the invite population, which is why this item is marked partial rather than satisfied.
items.meaning: For integration, most of M1's plumbing already exists on the Comhairle/Bloom side, so the work is additive: bolt on the integrity checks (rate limits, code-scoped access, coordinated-response detection) rather than rebuild entry. The shared lesson is that low-friction entry is a solved, shipped pattern; CIE's differentiator is the discipline layered on top, not the front door itself.
items.cie_s: The low-friction web entry milestone lets a participant join from a landing page, Quick Response code, or unique invite code with no install and no login and be voting in under a minute, plus a proportionate integrity layer that contains astroturfing without adding friction for real people.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle covers the mechanics of web entry and codes, but the proportionate astroturf-integrity layer sized to the invite population that Civic Intelligence Engine specifies is not present, so this rates partial rather than satisfied.
items.meaning_s: Most of the entry plumbing already exists on the Comhairle side, so the integration work is additive, bolting on rate limits, code-scoped access, and coordinated-response detection rather than rebuilding the front door.

items.name: Consent and artificial intelligence disclosure
items.note: Comhairle has a consent boolean and artificial intelligence services; the Civic Intelligence Engine's two unbundled tiers with contact-off default are a stronger form.
items.cie: M2 is plain-language consent plus artificial-intelligence disclosure, structured as two independent (unbundled) tiers with contact turned off by default. 'Unbundled' means a participant can agree to have their votes analyzed without also agreeing to be contacted later, and 'contact off by default' means silence never becomes permission. This is the policy boundary set before any input is collected; CIE's disclosure also tells the participant plainly that artificial intelligence is involved, satisfying laws like California's bot-disclosure act. The cie-lab conversational prototype surfaces the free-text-to-large-language-model egress edge honestly, which is the same consent-and-disclosure posture at the interaction level.
items.comhairle: Comhairle records consent as a single boolean on the user profile (api/src/routes/user_profile.rs, field 'consented', defaulting to false), and it does run artificial-intelligence services. That is real but coarser than CIE's design: one all-or-nothing flag cannot express the two-tier unbundling (analyze-yes / contact-no) that CIE requires, hence partial. Bloom shows the stronger consumer pattern CIE wants, gating optional demographics to the end of the flow with explicit 'every question is optional' framing and a separate 'stay in touch' recontact tier (bloom-09/10, bloom-07).
items.meaning: Integration would keep Comhairle's consent record as the storage point but split the single boolean into CIE's independent tiers, defaulting contact off. The good news is the seam is small (a profile-schema change plus disclosure copy); the important part is policy, not code, so the tiers must be wired before any field collection begins.
items.cie_s: The consent-and-artificial-intelligence-disclosure milestone structures consent as two independent unbundled tiers with contact off by default, so a participant can agree to analysis without agreeing to be contacted, and plainly discloses that artificial intelligence is involved.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle records consent as a single boolean on the user profile and does run artificial intelligence services, but one all-or-nothing flag cannot express Civic Intelligence Engine's two-tier unbundling, so it rates partial.
items.meaning_s: Integration would keep Comhairle's consent record as the storage point but split the single boolean into Civic Intelligence Engine's independent tiers with contact defaulted off, a small schema seam whose important part is policy that must be wired before any field collection begins.

items.name: Vote elicitation floor
items.note: Vote agree/disagree/pass on seeded + emergent statements: Comhairle's wrapped Pol.is is exactly this spine.
items.cie: M3 is the vote-elicitation floor: the defensible spine where participants vote agree, disagree, or pass on short statements, seeded from real NC-12 swing-theme research and then expanded as constituents submit their own emergent statements. 'Pass' matters because it lets people abstain without distorting the signal, and the seed-plus-emergent design gives both a defensible starting agenda and organic discovery. CIE builds this in cie-lab's core listening loop (proof of concept #1), encoding votes as agree=+1 / disagree=-1 / pass=0 in the vote matrix that feeds analysis/bridging.py.
items.comhairle: Comhairle satisfies M3 outright: its wrapped Pol.is tool (api/src/tools/polis.rs) is exactly vote-on-statements with participant-submitted statements, verified to do agree/disagree voting over seeded and emergent statements. Bloom demonstrates the same floor in a shipped user interface, with AGREE/DISAGREE/UNSURE buttons plus a statement-submission entry (bloom-01, bloom-13), confirming the pattern is mature and product-ready.
items.meaning: This is the strongest point of agreement between the two systems and the natural integration anchor: both treat vote-on-statements as the substrate. CIE can adopt Comhairle's Pol.is spine directly for M3 rather than rebuild it, which is why the recommended near-term path is export-first over this shared floor, layering CIE's discipline on top of Comhairle's proven elicitation.
items.cie_s: The vote-elicitation floor is the defensible spine where participants vote agree, disagree, or pass on short statements seeded from real swing-theme research and expanded as constituents submit their own emergent statements.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle satisfies this outright, as its wrapped Pol.is tool is exactly vote-on-statements with participant-submitted statements over seeded and emergent content.
items.meaning_s: This is the strongest point of agreement and the natural integration anchor, so Civic Intelligence Engine can adopt Comhairle's Pol.is spine directly rather than rebuild it, layering its discipline on top of this shared, proven elicitation floor.

items.name: Instrument as a budget
items.note: Comhairle's HeyForm covers surveys, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's under-seven-minute ascending-load neutral-wording budget.
items.cie: M4 is 'the instrument as a budget': the whole survey/elicitation instrument is treated like a time and attention budget, four to six mobile items completable in under seven minutes, ordered by ascending cognitive load, worded neutrally with explicit pass options, and using validated survey wording. The point is that completion stays high and bias stays bounded because the instrument is deliberately short and non-leading rather than expanding to fill every question someone wants to ask. CIE encodes these as testable requirements (item count, time ceiling, neutral wording) that the instrument owner enforces.
items.comhairle: Comhairle's HeyForm tool (api/src/tools/heyform.rs) covers general surveys, so the form-building capability exists. What it does not encode is CIE's specific budget discipline, the under-seven-minute ceiling, ascending-load ordering, and validated neutral wording, which is a design constraint on how the instrument is authored, not a feature a form engine provides; hence partial.
items.meaning: Integration can reuse HeyForm as the delivery mechanism while treating CIE's budget as authoring rules the instrument owner applies when building the form. The distinction to keep clear is capability versus discipline: Comhairle gives you a survey tool, but M4's guarantee comes from constraining how that tool is used, which is a human/process commitment layered over the platform.
items.cie_s: The instrument-as-a-budget milestone treats the whole elicitation as a time and attention budget of four to six mobile items completable in under seven minutes, ordered by ascending cognitive load and worded neutrally with explicit pass options and validated wording.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's HeyForm tool covers general survey building, but it does not encode Civic Intelligence Engine's specific budget discipline of the under-seven-minute ceiling, ascending-load ordering, and validated neutral wording, so it rates partial.
items.meaning_s: Integration can reuse HeyForm as the delivery mechanism while treating Civic Intelligence Engine's budget as authoring rules the instrument owner applies, keeping clear that Comhairle gives a survey tool but the guarantee comes from constraining how it is used.

items.name: Named instrument owner
items.note: Resourcing a named instrument owner: a staffing commitment, not a platform capability.
items.cie: M5 is a named, resourced instrument owner: a specific person accountable for the instrument, with their deliverable and hours confirmed before field collection begins. This is a staffing commitment rather than software, and it exists because the make-or-break expertise (writing unbiased items, defending the methodology) has to be assigned to someone, not left implicit. CIE's spec treats this as a hard precondition for going to field, verified by a confirmed owner on record.
items.comhairle: This item is marked N/A for Comhairle because it is not a platform capability at all; no repository can 'contain' a named staff owner. Comhairle neither provides nor precludes it. Bloom's hosted model is a faint analogue (each poll has a named host like 'Central Oregon Civic Action Project', bloom-02), but a host organization is not the same as CIE's accountable instrument owner with confirmed hours.
items.meaning: For integration this milestone is orthogonal to the code: whichever system runs the pilot, a human owner must be named and resourced. The takeaway is that M5 lives in the project's governance and staffing plan, so it carries over unchanged regardless of whether CIE builds fresh or forks Comhairle.

items.name: Frozen v0 record contract
items.note: The Civic Intelligence Engine's normalized append-only record contract is the seam Comhairle's stub data_model never implements.
items.cie: M6 is the frozen v0 record contract: a fixed, agreed data shape for every response, respondent, item, type, value, open text, timestamp, and an item registry, with every column normalized to the unit interval (rescaled to a 0-to-1 range so different item types are comparable). It is append-only, meaning records are added but never edited or deleted, so no one can quietly change what was said after the fact. This frozen schema is the seam that lets the pipeline, dashboard, and analysis all build in parallel against a stable contract; cie-lab expresses this as versioned artifacts (schema 'cie.results.v0', and the 'cie.interop.v0' export) so every consumer reads the same shape.
items.comhairle: This is a gap: Comhairle's data_model/schema.json is a stub-level AllTypes schema (Group, Reaction, Statement, AlgorithmDescriptor) that never implements CIE's normalized, append-only response contract, and the compare/contrast work verified concrete holes such as Reaction having no target-id to tie a reaction to its statement. Comhairle stores data, but not as a frozen, unit-interval-normalized, append-only record contract that downstream components can safely build against.
items.meaning: M6 is the linchpin of any real integration: because Comhairle's data model does not provide CIE's seam, an export-first path must map Comhairle's Group/Reaction/Statement into CIE's frozen v0 contract (the 'cie.interop.v0' export is the first step), and a deeper fork-adapter would add a normalized append-only store. Without pinning this contract, the paraphrase gate (T10), validity card (M8), and dashboard (M10) have nothing stable to consume.
items.cie_s: The frozen v0 record contract is a fixed, agreed data shape for every response, respondent, item, type, value, open text, and timestamp, normalized to the unit interval and append-only, forming the stable seam the pipeline, dashboard, and analysis all build against in parallel.
items.comhairle_s: This is a gap, as Comhairle's data model is a stub-level schema that never implements Civic Intelligence Engine's normalized, append-only response contract and has concrete holes such as a Reaction with no target-id tying it to its statement.
items.meaning_s: This contract is the linchpin of any real integration, so an export-first path must map Comhairle's Group, Reaction, and Statement into Civic Intelligence Engine's frozen v0 contract, without which the paraphrase gate, validity card, and dashboard have nothing stable to consume.

items.name: Proven analysis core
items.note: Principal component analysis feeding k-means with silhouette-bounded k on response patterns: Comhairle's Pol.is core matches, validated on blind data.
items.cie: M7 is the proven analysis core: reduce the vote matrix with principal component analysis, which collapses many statements into a 2-D opinion map, then cluster participants with k-means, choosing the number of groups k by silhouette score within a calibrated bound, so opinion groups come from vote patterns only and nothing else. Bounding k matters because an unconstrained sweep over-fragments short civic text (recovering k=11-12 at an Adjusted Rand Index around 0.4 instead of the true four themes at an Adjusted Rand Index of 0.958). CIE builds exactly this in analysis/bridging.py (principal component analysis to 2D, k-means with silhouette over a bounded k, self-codes deliberately kept out of the clustering), validated on blind synthetic data.
items.comhairle: Comhairle satisfies M7: its wrapped Pol.is tool (api/src/tools/polis.rs) does the same principal-component-analysis-to-k-means clustering on response patterns to produce opinion groups, verified against the repo. This is the second pillar (with M3) where the two systems genuinely agree, and it is a mature, well-understood method rather than anything CIE invents.
items.meaning: Because the analysis core matches, integration does not need to reimplement clustering; CIE can consume Comhairle's group assignments or run its own equivalent over the shared vote floor. The one caution is the calibrated k-bound: CIE's spec insists the bound be re-derived on real pilot data, so even where the algorithm agrees, CIE adds a validation discipline around the parameters that Comhairle does not enforce.
items.cie_s: The proven analysis core reduces the vote matrix with principal component analysis into a 2-D opinion map, clusters participants with k-means choosing the number of groups by silhouette score within a calibrated bound, so opinion groups come from vote patterns only.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle satisfies this, as its wrapped Pol.is tool does the same principal-component-analysis-to-k-means clustering on response patterns to produce opinion groups.
items.meaning_s: Because the analysis core matches, integration need not reimplement clustering and Civic Intelligence Engine can consume Comhairle's group assignments, with the one caution that Civic Intelligence Engine re-derives the calibrated k-bound on real pilot data where Comhairle enforces no such validation.

items.name: Validity card with every result
items.note: The validity card has no counterpart in Comhairle's ungated output.
items.cie: M8 is a validity card attached to every result: per-group vote counts, the smallest-group margin, coverage, a flagged-record count, knife-edge flags (results that would flip with a tiny change), and a non-representative label. Its purpose is that the candidate can defend every number in public, because each headline is shipped with the evidence about how solid it is. CIE builds this directly in analysis/bridging.py, which emits a per-statement 'validity' block (smallest_group_seen, coverage, groups meeting the vote floor) plus Wilson lower bounds and a gated badge (representative-enough / directional / below-bar) so weak results are visibly marked, not hidden.
items.comhairle: This is a gap with no counterpart in Comhairle: its Pol.is tool outputs clusters and agreement but attaches no validity card, no confidence badge, and no non-representative label; the output is ungated. Bloom is the same, publishing results as agree/diverge/common-ground (bloom-04) but with no per-result validity or gated badge, which is precisely the contrast CIE draws: shipped products show raw numbers where CIE ships numbers-plus-their-warrant.
items.meaning: Integrating means CIE must compute and bind a validity card onto whatever Comhairle produces, which requires the per-group counts and coverage that only the frozen record contract (M6) reliably exposes. This is one of the core things CIE adds that Comhairle lacks, so it lands in CIE's analysis/presentation layer downstream of Comhairle's clustering, not inside Comhairle itself.
items.cie_s: The validity card attaches to every result the per-group vote counts, smallest-group margin, coverage, flagged-record count, knife-edge flags, and non-representative label, so a candidate can defend every number in public with the evidence of how solid it is.
items.comhairle_s: This is a gap with no counterpart in Comhairle, whose Pol.is tool outputs clusters and agreement but attaches no validity card, confidence badge, or non-representative label.
items.meaning_s: Integrating means Civic Intelligence Engine must compute and bind a validity card onto whatever Comhairle produces, which requires the per-group counts and coverage that only the frozen record contract reliably exposes, landing in Civic Intelligence Engine's downstream analysis and presentation layer.

items.name: Local embeddings + one batch call
items.note: Sovereign local embeddings and one scrubbed batch call; Comhairle's per-record external artificial intelligence is the opposite posture.
items.cie: M9 is the artificial-intelligence sovereignty posture: run embeddings locally, and make at most a single-pass batch large-language-model call over scrubbed, aggregated text, never over individual response records. 'Embeddings' turn text into vectors so statements can be grouped by meaning; doing that locally means constituent text never leaves controlled infrastructure for that step. The spec confirms the default local model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 384-dimensional, running on ordinary processor hardware) hits an Adjusted Rand Index of 0.958 in under 10 seconds, so sovereignty costs nothing in quality; the one batch call sees only aggregates scrubbed of personally identifiable information and theme labels, giving one auditable egress point and flat cost. cie-lab implements local embeddings plus narrow large-language-model jobs (routing and phrasing only) in analysis/serve.py and kg.py, with every displayed number coming from votes, not the model.
items.comhairle: Comhairle takes the opposite posture: it calls external artificial-intelligence services per record rather than embedding locally and making one scrubbed batch pass. That per-record external-artificial-intelligence flow is exactly the sovereignty and auditability gap M9 is written against, since it multiplies egress points and sends individual text outward. There is no local-embedding, single-egress architecture in the Comhairle tooling.
items.meaning: This is a posture conflict, not just a missing library: a compliant integration would have to route embeddings to a local model and collapse Comhairle's per-record artificial-intelligence calls into CIE's one batch-over-aggregates step, so that the funder can truthfully say where constituent data goes. It reinforces the M6 dependency, because 'scrubbed aggregates' presuppose a normalized store you can aggregate and scrub before the single egress.
items.cie_s: The local-embeddings-plus-one-batch-call milestone runs embeddings locally so constituent text never leaves controlled infrastructure and makes at most a single batch large language model call over scrubbed, aggregated text, giving one auditable egress point at flat cost.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle takes the opposite posture, calling external artificial intelligence services per record rather than embedding locally, which multiplies egress points and sends individual text outward.
items.meaning_s: This is a posture conflict, so a compliant integration would route embeddings to a local model and collapse Comhairle's per-record calls into Civic Intelligence Engine's one batch-over-aggregates step, reinforcing the record-contract dependency since scrubbed aggregates presuppose a normalized store.

items.name: Candidate bridging dashboard
items.note: Comhairle has participation and admin user interfaces, but not the Civic Intelligence Engine's bridging-ranked candidate dashboard with per-group support beside every label.
items.cie: M10 is the candidate dashboard: it ranks statements by bridging score (how broadly a statement is accepted across the different opinion groups, not just overall), shows per-group support beside every statement label, and displays divisive results honestly rather than hiding them. The point is a decision aid the candidate can trust, where a 'consensus' statement is only surfaced because every group actually supports it. CIE builds this in cie-lab's Dashboard (web/src/views/Dashboard.tsx), sorting by the gated bridging badge and group-informed-consensus score with per-group agreement shown for each statement, driven by the artifact from analysis/bridging.py.
