items.comhairle: Comhairle has participation and admin user interfaces, and its Pol.is core computes the group data such a dashboard would need, but it does not ship CIE's bridging-ranked candidate dashboard with per-group support beside every label; hence partial. Bloom again shows the public-results half of this well (agree/diverge/common-ground framing, bloom-04) but as a participant-facing summary rather than a bridging-ranked decision surface with per-group breakdowns and honest divisive panels.
items.meaning: Integration can source the underlying group-by-statement numbers from Comhairle's clustering, but the ranking-by-bridging view, the per-group columns, and the honest divisive display are CIE's to build on top. Because the dashboard reads bridging scores and validity data, it depends on M7's clustering, M8's validity card, and M6's record contract all being in place, so it is best treated as CIE's presentation layer over Comhairle's analytical output.
items.cie_s: The candidate bridging dashboard ranks statements by bridging score, shows per-group support beside every statement label, and displays divisive results honestly, giving the candidate a decision aid where a consensus statement surfaces only because every group actually supports it.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has participation and admin UIs and its Pol.is core computes the needed group data, but it does not ship Civic Intelligence Engine's bridging-ranked candidate dashboard with per-group support beside every label, so it rates partial.
items.meaning_s: Integration can source the underlying group-by-statement numbers from Comhairle's clustering, but the bridging ranking, per-group columns, and honest divisive display are Civic Intelligence Engine's to build as a presentation layer depending on the analysis core, validity card, and record contract.

items.name: Scope banner + methods note
items.note: The scope-banner claim-discipline surface is absent from Comhairle.
items.cie: M11 is the scope banner on every surface plus a plain-language methods note. The banner is load-bearing claim discipline and must appear verbatim, 'what engaged, responding constituents told us, not what the district believes', on the dashboard, in every export, and in any communication that cites results. It draws the exact line the T9 gate enforces: theme-map claims (here is what respondents said) versus percent-of-district claims (which would need a representative sample). cie-lab surfaces this scope-banner-and-methods discipline in the Dashboard view (web/src/views/Dashboard.tsx, proof of concept #1's scope banner and methods note) so no result is ever shown context-free.
items.comhairle: This is a gap: there is no scope banner or standing claim-discipline surface in Comhairle; results are presented without a persistent 'not what the district believes' caveat. Bloom, like Comhairle, shows raw results (bloom-04) without CIE's scope banner, which is the recurring contrast, the elicitation and clustering are shared, but the discipline surface that bounds what the numbers mean is uniquely CIE's.
items.meaning: Integrating means CIE must inject the verbatim scope banner and methods note into every surface that renders Comhairle-derived results, including exports, and enforce it with the same copy-linter that backs T9. Since Comhairle emits ungated output, this banner has to be added at CIE's presentation/export boundary and cannot be assumed to come along with Comhairle's data.
items.cie_s: The scope-banner-and-methods-note milestone stamps every surface with a verbatim banner clarifying that results are what engaged responding constituents told us and not what the district believes, alongside a plain-language methods note, drawing the exact line the claim-type gate enforces.
items.comhairle_s: This is a gap, as Comhairle has no scope banner or standing claim-discipline surface and presents results without a persistent not-what-the-district-believes caveat.
items.meaning_s: Integrating means Civic Intelligence Engine must inject the verbatim scope banner and methods note into every surface rendering Comhairle-derived results including exports, enforced by the same copy-linter behind the claim-type gate, since Comhairle's ungated output will not carry it along.

items.name: Contract deltas vs signed agreement
items.note: Checking the build against the signed agreement's contract deltas: a governance gate.
items.cie: M12 is the contract-deltas check: before launch, the build is audited against the signed funder agreement across four deltas, claim-type (does the language match what was agreed), representation (does it make district-level claims the contract does not authorize), data-handling (does the data flow match what was disclosed), and budget (does it stay under the $45,000 cap). The representation and claim-type delta is a hard red gate: go/no-go cannot proceed if it is out of alignment, because over-claiming representativeness is the highest reputational and legal risk. CIE realizes this as a signed delta-review document on file at go/no-go, with the scope banner (M11) and validity badges (M8) as the technical mechanisms it verifies are actually present.
items.comhairle: This is N/A as a platform capability: a governance gate against a signed agreement is not something Comhairle's code provides or blocks, it is a launch-time audit process. Comhairle offers no such check, but nothing about it prevents one either; the audit sits outside the software entirely.
items.meaning: For integration, M12 is the umbrella that verifies the other guarantees are wired before launch, so it carries over unchanged regardless of build-vs-fork. Its practical effect on a Comhairle integration is that it forces the claim-type gate (T9), scope banner (M11), and validity card (M8) to actually be present in whatever surfaces Comhairle-derived results reach, because the hard red gate is checking exactly those mechanisms against the signed language.
items.cie_s: The contract-deltas check audits the build against the signed funder agreement across claim-type, representation, data-handling, and budget deltas before launch, with the representation and claim-type delta a hard red go/no-go gate.
items.comhairle_s: This is not applicable as a platform capability, since a governance audit against a signed agreement is not something Comhairle's code provides or blocks, though nothing about it prevents one either.
items.meaning_s: This milestone is the umbrella verifying the other guarantees are wired before launch, so its practical effect on a Comhairle integration is to force the claim-type gate, scope banner, and validity card to actually be present in whatever surfaces Comhairle-derived results reach.

coverage.finding: The two systems agree on the Pol.is spine and diverge on everything the Civic Intelligence Engine adds around it. The only items Comhairle fully satisfies (votes-only aggregation, demographic-blind clustering, the Pol.is tool, the principal-component-analysis-to-k-means core) are the Pol.is-derived substrate the Civic Intelligence Engine already re-implements clean-room.

cie_gaps: Bridging as a gated claim: group-informed consensus of at least 0.5, a per-group Wilson lower bound above 0.5, and a vote floor. Comhairle shows Pol.is's raw consensus float, a number rather than a defensible claim.
Database-enforced append-only trust + off-box hash chain. Comhairle uses ordinary mutable Postgres.
Two-tier consent and quarantine of personally identifiable information. Comhairle has a single consent boolean and stores joinable demographics.
The quality-gate ladder + validity cards. Comhairle renders Pol.is math live and ungated.
Paraphrase-only quotes. Comhairle stores and serves verbatim statement text, the opposite policy.
Claim discipline: scope banner, copy linter, badge vocabulary, methods note.
Data-sovereignty egress: local embeddings plus one batch call to a large language model over scrubbed aggregates; Comhairle makes many per-record calls to external artificial intelligence.
assessment.comhairle_has: Composable multi-tool workflows (quadratic-vote prioritization, ranking, ThinkingSpace), RAGFlow document Q&A, multi-org tenancy, i18n, ScotAccount OpenID Connect + anonymous→account upgrade, audio transcription, and demographic / representativeness breakdowns. (That last one is exactly what the Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately quarantines: a tension to flag.)

paths.name: Path 1 · Interop-export
paths.note: A pipeline stage that serializes the Civic Intelligence Engine's data into Comhairle's schema.json shape. No Comhairle code, reversible, personally identifiable information stays quarantined. It's the literal artifact to bring to the July call: 'the Civic Intelligence Engine speaks Comhairle's grammar.'

paths.name: Path 2 · Custom adapter (fork)
paths.note: A Civic Intelligence Engine ToolImpl inside a Comhairle fork. Buys little today, since Comhairle's interchange ingest is unwired, and carries fork-maintenance plus GNU Affero General Public License §13 exposure. Fund it once there's a live consumer.

assessment.posture: Export-first, adapter-later. The Civic Intelligence Engine stays the system of record in every scenario: the mapping is lossy in exactly the direction that matters. The Civic Intelligence Engine's trust, consent, moderation, and bridging-badge guarantees have no target in Comhairle's model. So Comhairle is at best a downstream interop consumer, never a replacement store.

gifts.d: So 'participant P voted + on statement S' can be expressed at all: a real hole this mapping surfaced.
So the two-class moderation policy (hide-but-count vs exclude-session) survives the handoff instead of silently corrupting the statistics.

reverse.finding: Read the other direction, Comhairle is broad where the Civic Intelligence Engine is deep. Studying its codebase surfaces 57 capabilities the Civic Intelligence Engine has no answer for: a full identity and multi-org stack, a suite of elicitation tools beyond voting, an operational engagement layer (transcription, events, notifications, jobs), a localization pipeline, and a tool-agnostic interchange grammar. Most are things the Civic Intelligence Engine deferred by staying narrow (24 worth adopting, 22 worth watching); 11 are ones the Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately refuses on principle: demographic quotas, mutable storage, verbatim serving, and per-record external artificial intelligence, where the divergence is the design, not a gap.

items.name: Proposal prioritization scoring
items.comhairle: The Prioritization tool (api/src/tools/prioritization.rs) lets admins attach a set of typed questions to each user-submitted proposal and collect a rich, per-question score rather than a single agree/disagree. Question types include free Text, a discrete LikertScale with admin-defined value/label categories, and a Continuous slider with configurable min/max values, min/max labels, and sub-steps (defaulting to a -? to 10 range with 10 sub-steps). Each participant's answer set is stored as QuestionResponses tied to (proposal, user), responses upsert so a re-vote replaces the prior one, and a randomize_order flag shuffles proposal presentation to blunt ordering bias. Proposal titles and bodies are localized TextContentIds, and admins can pull raw translation data via withTranslations=true.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has no equivalent. Its only elicitation primitive is the Pol.is-style vote matrix of agree/disagree/pass on short statements (spec 07-the-system-by-layer.md, 08-the-build-core.md); there is no notion of a participant-authored proposal carrying multiple scored dimensions, no Likert or continuous-slider capture, and no order-randomization control.
items.meaning: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch, and likely borrow, the idea that a single deliberation item can carry several scored dimensions instead of one ternary vote: Likert and continuous scales express intensity and trade-offs that binary voting flattens. Adopting it would require extending Civic Intelligence Engine's vote-matrix math (its principal component analysis/k-means pipeline assumes ternary cells), so this is a medium-effort gain rather than a drop-in, but the randomize-order bias control and per-question localization are cheap, principled wins Civic Intelligence Engine lacks today.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Prioritization tool collects multi-dimensional, per-question scores (free text, discrete Likert categories, and a configurable continuous slider with min/max labels and sub-steps) against each participant-submitted proposal, with an order-randomization flag to reduce presentation bias.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine offers only ternary agree/disagree/pass voting on short statements and has no proposal object, no Likert or continuous-slider scoring, and no order-randomization control.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should treat Comhairle's Likert-plus-continuous proposal scoring as a gain worth adopting, since intensity and trade-off scales capture signal that binary voting flattens, even though wiring it into Civic Intelligence Engine's ternary principal component analysis/k-means pipeline is a medium-effort change.

items.name: Quadratic & comparative ranking
items.comhairle: The Ranking tool (api/src/tools/ranking.rs) defines a distinct modality where participants rank a fixed set of admin-authored options rather than vote on statements. Its RankingType enum offers three sub-modes: Basic ordinal ranking, Quadratic(QuadraticVoting) where a participant spends a budget of credits across options with quadratically increasing cost, and Comparative (pairwise) ranking. Each RankOption has a title and optional details, and the tool carries a prompt framing the choice. The file is clearly work-in-progress (it has unfinished From impls and a mis-named sanitize), but the design intent (budgeted, preference-intensity-aware ranking of a curated option set) is explicit.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has nothing resembling ranked or budgeted voting. Its listening loop treats every statement independently as an agree/disagree/pass cell; there is no credit budget, no forced ordering, and no pairwise comparison, and the spec's north-star (02-north-star.md) deliberately keeps the flow narrow.
items.meaning: Watch rather than adopt now: quadratic voting is a well-regarded mechanism for surfacing preference intensity and resisting tyranny-of-the-majority, which aligns with Civic Intelligence Engine's consensus goals, but Comhairle's own implementation is unfinished and Civic Intelligence Engine's ternary matrix would need a parallel scoring path. It is worth tracking as a future option for the rare campaign that needs prioritization-under-budget, without disturbing Civic Intelligence Engine's core bridging loop.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Ranking tool lets participants rank a curated option set via Basic ordinal, Quadratic credit-budget, or Comparative pairwise modes, encoding preference intensity that plain voting cannot.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no ranked, budgeted, or pairwise voting at all. Every statement is an independent agree/disagree/pass cell.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch quadratic and comparative ranking as a promising future mechanism for preference-intensity elicitation, while noting Comhairle's implementation is still incomplete and Civic Intelligence Engine's ternary pipeline would need a separate scoring path.

items.name: Artificial intelligence thinking-space deepening
items.comhairle: The Thinking Space tool (api/src/tools/thinking_space.rs) is a guided qualitative-reflection modality. Admins seed root questions, each carrying a hidden intent string that is never shown to participants but is fed to the large language model as question_intent so it can generate sharper follow-ups. A participant answers a root question, the bot (via the bot_service agent) streams artificial-intelligence-generated follow-up questions for a configurable follow_up_rounds_count, and answers accumulate with an AnswerStatus (pending/approved) moderation lifecycle. A dedicated summary agent then distills each user's full question/answer thread into a private, per-user artificial intelligence summary that the participant can edit; summaries are strictly scoped to their author (other users' summaries return 404, not 403).
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately does not do open-ended, artificial-intelligence-driven qualitative elicitation. It collects short statements and ternary votes, paraphrases quotes rather than serving verbatim, and quarantines per-record external artificial intelligence (spec 03-principles-and-commitments.md). There is no Socratic follow-up loop, no per-participant artificial intelligence summary, and no hidden question-intent channel.
items.meaning: This is a genuine capability gap worth watching: laddered follow-up questioning and private per-participant synthesis capture depth and reasoning that a vote matrix cannot. But adopting it collides with two Civic Intelligence Engine commitments (no per-record external artificial intelligence and paraphrase-only serving), so any Civic Intelligence Engine version would need local models and careful consent gating. Track the hidden question-intent pattern and the private-summary scoping as strong design ideas even if the external-large-language-model plumbing diverges.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Thinking Space runs an large-language-model-driven Socratic loop that seeds root questions with a hidden admin intent, streams multiple rounds of artificial intelligence follow-up questions, and produces an editable, strictly-private per-participant artificial intelligence summary.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no open-ended artificial intelligence questioning or per-participant synthesis; it stays on short statements, ternary votes, and paraphrase-only quotes with no per-record external artificial intelligence.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch Thinking Space's laddered follow-up questioning and private per-participant summaries as a real depth gain, while recognizing that any adoption must use local models and consent gating to honor Civic Intelligence Engine's no-external-per-record-artificial-intelligence and paraphrase-only commitments.

items.name: Agentic elicitation chatbot
items.comhairle: The Elicitation Bot tool (api/src/tools/elicitation_bot.rs) is a streamed conversational agent that helps a participant articulate and shape their views on a configured topic. Each participant gets a persistent bot_service_user_session (get_or_create) so conversation history is retained, the /elicitation_bot/workflow_step/{id} POST returns a raw SSE byte stream of the large language model reply, and the whole behaviour is defined by a RAGFlow agent graph shipped as a static template (api/src/agent_templates/ragflow-elicitation-bot.json) whose Begin node injects the topic and greets with 'I am here to help you shape your views and opinions.' Session teardown deletes the upstream agent session on tool delete.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has light self-coding but no participant-facing conversational agent. It never engages a participant in free dialogue to elicit opinions; input is structured statements and votes, and per-record external artificial intelligence is explicitly out of scope (spec 03-principles-and-commitments.md).
items.meaning: Watch, leaning diverge on implementation: a topic-scoped elicitation chatbot can lower the barrier for participants who struggle to author a crisp statement, which serves Civic Intelligence Engine's inclusivity aims (04-who-we-serve.md). But Comhairle backs it with an external RAGFlow large language model per conversation, which cuts directly against Civic Intelligence Engine's no-external-per-record-artificial-intelligence and data-egress commitments. The interaction pattern is worth tracking; the transport (external agent service, verbatim streaming) is where Civic Intelligence Engine would principledly diverge.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Elicitation Bot is a persistent, topic-scoped conversational large language model agent (defined by a shipped RAGFlow graph) that streams replies to help each participant shape and articulate their opinions.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no participant-facing conversational agent and treats per-record external artificial intelligence dialogue as out of scope.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch the topic-scoped elicitation-chatbot interaction as an inclusivity aid while diverging from Comhairle's external-RAGFlow-per-conversation implementation, which conflicts with Civic Intelligence Engine's no-external-per-record-artificial-intelligence and data-egress commitments.

items.name: Video story testimony
items.comhairle: The Stories tool (api/src/tools/stories.rs) is a narrative, media-first elicitation modality: participants record and submit a video Story (each Story links a video_id, an optional transcript_id, a user_id and workflow_step_id), and the tool config carries a max_time cap on recording length and a to_see count controlling how many other participants' stories a user is shown. It pairs with Comhairle's transcription_service so spoken testimony can be transcribed. Handlers are currently stubs but the schema and route surface (get/save story per workflow step) define a peer-to-peer video testimony exchange.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately avoids exactly this: it serves paraphrase-only quotes, never verbatim text, and has no media, video, or transcription pipeline (spec 03-principles-and-commitments.md). Serving one participant's raw recorded testimony to others is antithetical to its minimal-egress, quarantine-demographics, paraphrase-first stance.
items.meaning: This is a principled divergence, not a gap Civic Intelligence Engine should close. Raw video testimony is powerful for community storytelling but carries heavy consent, re-identification, and verbatim-serving risks that Civic Intelligence Engine explicitly designs against. Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase-only, no-media posture is the intentional choice; the value of Stories (surfacing lived experience) is better realized in Civic Intelligence Engine through paraphrased representative quotes than through peer-shared video.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Stories tool collects participant video testimony (with recording-length caps, a peer-viewing quota, and optional transcription) and shares each participant's raw recording with others.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine serves only paraphrased quotes and has no video, media, or transcription pipeline by design.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should treat Comhairle's peer-shared video testimony as a principled divergence, since raw-media sharing conflicts with Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase-only, minimal-egress, re-identification-averse commitments, and the underlying goal is better met through paraphrased representative quotes.

items.name: Conversational survey forms
items.comhairle: The HeyForm tool (api/src/tools/heyform.rs) embeds a full third-party survey/form builder as an elicitation modality, driven through the vendored heyform-rust-sdk (adaptors/heyform-rust-sdk). On setup it programmatically provisions an isolated HeyForm account, workspace, and project, creates a Poll form in conversational (chat-like, one-question-at-a-time) InteractiveMode, injects a hidden comhairle_user_id field so responses tie back to the Comhairle participant, applies custom branded Cascading Style Sheets, and publishes a shareable survey web address. Launch clones the preview form's fields into a fresh live form, and delete tears down the upstream poll: a complete external-form lifecycle.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has no structured survey/form capability at all. It captures statements and votes for the bridging loop and nothing else; there is no questionnaire builder, no conversational form mode, and no external form-service integration in scope.
items.meaning: Watch: conversational, one-question-at-a-time surveys are a proven way to collect structured demographic-free intake and closed questions alongside open deliberation, and the hidden-field participant-binding pattern is a clean idea. But Civic Intelligence Engine's whole value proposition is the bridging analysis, not general survey collection, and pulling in an external form service would add data-egress surface Civic Intelligence Engine avoids. Track it as an adjacent modality, not a core need.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's HeyForm tool provisions and publishes fully branded conversational survey forms via an external service, binding responses back to the participant through a hidden user-id field and managing the form's full create/launch/delete lifecycle.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no survey or questionnaire capability and no external form-service integration.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch conversational survey forms and the hidden-field participant-binding trick as an adjacent intake modality, while noting they sit outside Civic Intelligence Engine's bridging-focused scope and would add external data-egress surface Civic Intelligence Engine avoids.

items.name: Deliberative learn pages
items.comhairle: The Learn tool (api/src/tools/learn.rs) is an informational priming modality that can be dropped into a deliberation as its own step. It holds an ordered list of pages, each page a Markdown block available per-language (LocalizedPage carries a lang plus a requires_validation flag defaulting true, so translated content can be gated on human review before it is shown). Pages reference localized TextContentIds, letting facilitators present balanced background, framing, or educational material to participants before they vote or contribute: an explicit 'read before you deliberate' surface.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has no participant-education surface. The listening loop drops a participant straight into voting and statement contribution; there is no built-in way to present neutral framing or background context as a first-class step, and nothing about staged pre-vote information in the spec.
items.meaning: Adopt-worthy gain: informed deliberation improves signal quality, and a lightweight, localized, review-gated content step is cheap to build and squarely compatible with Civic Intelligence Engine's principles (no external artificial intelligence, no mutable per-record egress, since it's static curated text). Presenting shared framing before voting also reduces the noise Civic Intelligence Engine's clustering has to absorb. The requires_validation-per-locale gate is a nice governance detail Civic Intelligence Engine could reuse for any human-authored content.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Learn tool presents ordered, per-language Markdown priming pages (with a per-locale requires-validation gate) as a first-class 'read before you deliberate' step in a participation flow.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine drops participants straight into voting with no built-in surface for neutral framing or background education.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a lightweight localized, review-gated learn/priming step, since informed deliberation improves signal quality and static curated content fully respects Civic Intelligence Engine's no-external-artificial-intelligence and minimal-egress principles.

items.name: Composable multi-tool workflow
items.comhairle: Comhairle's defining architecture is that a deliberation is not one fixed flow but a composable sequence of heterogeneous elicitation tools. The ToolImpl trait (api/src/tools.rs) defines a uniform lifecycle (setup, sync_data, clone_tool, delete, routes, register_workers, sanitize), and a ToolConfig enum wired with enum_dispatch fans every operation out to the seven concrete tools (Polis, Learn, HeyForm, Stories, ElicitationBot, Prioritization, ThinkingSpace). Each workflow_step (api/src/models/workflow_step.rs) carries one tool's config plus orchestration metadata: step_order, activation_rule, required, is_offline, can_revisit, and request_user_share_permission. A conversation thus chains, say, a Learn page then a Thinking Space then a Polis vote then a Prioritization, as an ordered participant journey.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine is intentionally a single, sharp flow: vote matrix to principal component analysis to k-means to group-informed consensus to bridging badges to validity cards (spec 08-the-build-core.md). It has no concept of pluggable tools, no ordered multi-step participant journey, and no per-step lifecycle or activation rules. That narrowness is a stated design commitment (02-north-star.md).
items.meaning: Watch closely, and treat as the single biggest structural idea Civic Intelligence Engine lacks. Civic Intelligence Engine's narrowness is a virtue for its core mission, but the ToolImpl/enum_dispatch pattern (a uniform trait plus dispatch enum that lets new elicitation modalities plug into a staged journey with per-step lifecycle) is exactly how Civic Intelligence Engine would grow beyond one flow without becoming a monolith. Even if Civic Intelligence Engine keeps its single bridging loop, adopting this composition seam would let Learn priming or a follow-up step wrap the vote cleanly. It is a gain in architecture even where the individual tools diverge.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle composes deliberations as an ordered sequence of interchangeable elicitation tools behind a uniform ToolImpl trait and enum_dispatch ToolConfig, with each workflow step carrying its own lifecycle and activation metadata (order, required, offline, revisitable, share-permission).
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is a single fixed vote-to-bridge-to-validity-card flow with no pluggable tools, staged journey, or per-step lifecycle.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should study Comhairle's ToolImpl/enum_dispatch composition seam as the highest-value architectural gain, because a uniform tool trait plus staged workflow steps is how Civic Intelligence Engine could wrap or extend its bridging loop with additional modalities without abandoning its narrow core.

items.name: Artificial intelligence theme categorization (TTTC)
items.comhairle: The Categorization service (api/src/categorization_service.rs) defines a CategorizationService trait whose one job is to take a batch of free-text Comments (each with id, comment text, and speaker) and asynchronously extract opinion themes and generate a report. The shipped implementation, TttcCategorizer (api/src/categorization_service/tttc_categorizer.rs), posts those comments to an external Talk-to-the-City service configured to run gpt-4o with a 'What are the main themes?' question, then receives the finished report via an authenticated webhook (webhook_url + webhook_secret). It is a per-record, external-large-language-model narrative-clustering pipeline over raw participant text.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine reaches the same 'what are the themes' goal by a deliberately different route: local embeddings with no per-record egress, principal component analysis and k-means clustering on the vote matrix, and paraphrase-only outputs (spec 03-principles-and-commitments.md, 07-the-system-by-layer.md). It explicitly refuses to ship raw participant text to an external artificial intelligence service.
items.meaning: Principled divergence. Comhairle's TTTC path sends verbatim participant comments to a third-party gpt-4o service: precisely the per-record external artificial intelligence and data egress Civic Intelligence Engine forbids. Civic Intelligence Engine should not adopt this mechanism. The useful lesson to watch is the output shape (narrative theme summaries with representative speakers), which Civic Intelligence Engine already approximates locally; the divergence to defend is that Civic Intelligence Engine produces those themes from local embeddings and paraphrase, never by shipping raw text off-box.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Categorization service ships raw free-text participant comments to an external Talk-to-the-City gpt-4o pipeline that extracts opinion themes and returns a report via webhook.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine derives themes locally from vote-matrix clustering and local embeddings with no per-record egress and paraphrase-only output, and refuses to send raw participant text to external artificial intelligence.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should treat TTTC-style external artificial intelligence theme extraction as a principled divergence, since sending verbatim participant comments to a third-party gpt-4o service is exactly the per-record egress Civic Intelligence Engine forbids, even though the narrative-theme output shape is worth noting.

items.name: Document-grounded Q&A (RAGFlow)
items.comhairle: The RAGFlow adaptor (adaptors/ragflow) is a full client for a retrieval-augmented-generation service, exposing datasets, documents, chat sessions, and agent sessions (adaptors/ragflow/src/{dataset,document,chat,agent}). It lets Comhairle upload source documents into a knowledge base and then ground conversational agents (including the Elicitation Bot and Thinking Space bots) in that corpus, so participant-facing chat can answer from and cite campaign materials rather than the model's open weights. The agent templates (api/src/agent_templates/) are RAGFlow graph definitions that stitch this retrieval into the elicitation flow.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine runs local embeddings for its own clustering but has no participant-facing document-Q&A or retrieval-augmented chat. There is no knowledge-base upload, no citation-grounded answering surface, and no agent orchestration over a document corpus in scope.
items.meaning: Watch: grounding an assistant in curated campaign documents so participants can ask 'what does the proposal actually say?' is a legitimately useful facilitation aid and reuses infrastructure (embeddings) Civic Intelligence Engine already has locally. The divergence to hold is that Comhairle's RAGFlow is an external service; a Civic Intelligence Engine version would need to stay on local models and local retrieval to respect its no-egress stance. Track the document-grounded-answering pattern; keep the transport local.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's RAGFlow adaptor uploads campaign documents into a knowledge base and grounds its participant-facing chat agents in that corpus so answers are retrieval-based and citable rather than free-weight generation.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine uses local embeddings only for its own clustering and offers no participant-facing document-Q&A or retrieval-grounded chat.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch document-grounded, citable Q&A as a useful facilitation aid that reuses its local embeddings, while keeping any implementation on local retrieval rather than Comhairle's external RAGFlow service to honor its no-egress stance.

items.name: Contributed-statement moderation
items.comhairle: Comhairle governs participant-contributed content with an explicit moderation lifecycle. The wiki_poll_service (api/src/wiki_poll_service.rs), the orchestration wrapper around the Pol.is-style poll, exposes seed comments plus a moderate_comment call with a ModerationStatus of accepted/rejected/pending (mapped to +1/-1/0), and only accepted comments become active in the poll. The same review pattern recurs in Thinking Space, whose answers carry an AnswerStatus (pending/approved) before they count. Together these give facilitators a gate on which participant-submitted statements and answers enter the shared deliberation, with seed comments to bootstrap discussion.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's spec centers on the vote/bridge/validity-card math and an append-only trust layer, but does not describe a first-class human moderation queue for incoming participant statements before they enter the matrix. Its safeguards are statistical (Wilson gating, validity cards) rather than an explicit accept/reject/pending review step on contributed content.
items.meaning: Watch, tending toward adopt: any listening system that accepts participant-authored statements needs a way to keep spam, abuse, or duplicate statements out of the shared pool, and Comhairle's simple accepted/rejected/pending gate plus seed comments is a proven pattern. Civic Intelligence Engine's append-only trust layer is philosophically different (it records rather than deletes), so the fit is nuanced: Civic Intelligence Engine could add a moderation status flag that hides rather than mutates, preserving append-only provenance while still gating what participants see. Track it as a governance capability Civic Intelligence Engine will eventually need.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle gates participant-contributed statements and answers through an explicit accepted/rejected/pending moderation lifecycle (in wiki_poll_service and Thinking Space) plus seed comments to bootstrap discussion, controlling what enters the shared deliberation.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine relies on statistical safeguards (Wilson gating, validity cards) and an append-only trust layer rather than a first-class accept/reject/pending review queue for incoming statements.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch, and likely adopt, an explicit statement-moderation gate implemented as a hide-not-delete status flag, since any system accepting participant-authored statements needs spam/abuse control while preserving Civic Intelligence Engine's append-only provenance.

items.name: Multi-mode account authentication
items.comhairle: Comhairle ships a full account system with four first-class authentication modes, modelled as the `UserAuthType` enum: `email_password` (Argon2-hashed passwords with a 16-char, 3-of-4-category strength policy enforced by zxcvbn), `one_time_passcode` (email magic-link / code login), `annon` (a randomly-named anonymous account that can still log back in via its generated username), and `scot_account` (a placeholder for Scotland's national identity provider). Each mode issues a signed JWT session cookie (`auth-token`, 7-day expiry, HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite=None). The routing surface is broad: `/auth/login`, `/auth/login_annon`, `/auth/login_otp`, `/auth/signup`, `/auth/signup_annon`, `/auth/signup_otp`, `/auth/create_otp`, logout, email verification and password-reset endpoints all live in `api/src/routes/auth.rs`.
items.cie: Deliberately diverges. Civic Intelligence Engine has no login and no persistent user account at all: constituents enter the conversation through a unique single-use code delivered by mailer or Short Message Service, and a consent decline stores only an anonymous aggregate counter with no participant row (`03-principles-and-commitments.md` 'Anonymous by default'; `04-who-we-serve.md` AC-A2.2). There is no password store, no session identity, and no auth-type concept in the Civic Intelligence Engine record contract.
items.meaning: Diverge, on principle. Civic Intelligence Engine's trust model is built on the constituent never having to create an account or reveal who they are; introducing password/one-time password/identity login would undercut the 'anonymous by default' commitment and add a personally identifiable information surface the append-only, personally-identifiable-information-quarantined store is designed to avoid. The one component worth tracking for a future 'closing-the-loop' pilot is the one-time password magic-link flow, which could re-contact recontact-consented participants without ever storing a password. But even that belongs in the separate contact store, not an account system.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle ships a full account system with four first-class authentication modes in its `UserAuthType` enum (Argon2 email-and-password, one-time-passcode email magic links, re-loggable anonymous accounts, and a ScotAccount placeholder), each issuing a signed seven-day JWT session cookie across a broad set of `/auth/*` login, signup, verification and password-reset routes.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately diverges by having no login or persistent account at all, admitting constituents through unique single-use codes delivered by mailer or Short Message Service with no password store, session identity, or auth-type concept in its record contract.
items.meaning_s: This is a principled divergence because multi-mode account authentication would undercut Civic Intelligence Engine's 'anonymous by default' trust model and add a personally identifiable information surface the append-only store avoids, though the passwordless one-time-passcode magic-link flow is worth tracking for a future recontact pilot if kept in the separate contact store rather than an account system.

items.name: ScotAccount government OpenID Connect identity
items.comhairle: Comhairle reserves a `scot_account` variant in its `UserAuthType` enum (`api/src/models/users.rs`), the hook for integrating ScotAccount: the Scottish Government's national OpenID-Connect identity broker used to give citizens a single verified login across public services. It sits alongside the working password/one-time password/anonymous modes as a planned high-assurance identity path, so a participant could in principle be authenticated as a real, verified Scottish resident rather than a self-asserted account.
items.cie: Deliberately diverges. Civic Intelligence Engine has no OpenID Connect integration and no verified-identity path; the spec's integrity layer is calibrated to 'one-person shared-link scenarios, not coordinated bot attacks' and relies on unique single-use codes with sufficient entropy rather than proving who the participant is (`04-who-we-serve.md`, R11).
items.meaning: Diverge for the pilot, watch for the roadmap. Verified national identity is the opposite of Civic Intelligence Engine's anonymity guarantee and would defeat the small-cell/paraphrase protections that assume no participant is individually identifiable. However, a government-grade identity broker is exactly what a future high-stakes deployment (binding referenda, statutory consultations) might require, so it is worth tracking as the boundary case where Civic Intelligence Engine's anonymity model would have to be renegotiated rather than extended.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle reserves a `scot_account` variant in its `UserAuthType` enum as a planned high-assurance hook for ScotAccount, the Scottish Government's national OpenID-Connect identity broker, so a participant could in principle be authenticated as a real, verified Scottish resident rather than a self-asserted account.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately diverges by having no ScotAccount OpenID-Connect integration or verified-identity path, since its integrity layer relies on high-entropy unique single-use codes calibrated for one-person shared-link scenarios rather than proving who the participant is.
items.meaning_s: Verified national identity via ScotAccount is the opposite of Civic Intelligence Engine's anonymity guarantee and would defeat its small-cell and paraphrase protections, but it is worth watching as the boundary case a future high-stakes deployment such as a binding referendum might require Civic Intelligence Engine to renegotiate its anonymity model to accommodate.

items.name: Anonymous to account upgrade
items.comhairle: Comhairle lets a participant who started anonymously convert into a full, durable account without losing their history. `upgrade_account` in `api/src/models/users.rs` takes an existing `annon` user, validates a new password, and flips the row in-place to `email_password` while attaching a username and email. The same user id (and therefore all their prior participation) carries forward. It is exposed to users and guarded so only accounts currently of type `annon` can be upgraded.
items.cie: Deliberately diverges. Civic Intelligence Engine never links a submission to an identity: the raw layer is append-only and anonymous, and the two-tier consent design keeps any contact detail in a separate, default-off store that is 'never exported alongside response content' (`03-principles-and-commitments.md`). There is no mechanism to attach a name/email back onto an existing participant record.
items.meaning: Diverge, on principle. The whole point of Civic Intelligence Engine's architecture is that an anonymous contribution can never later be de-anonymised, so an in-place 'promote this anonymous person to a named account, keeping their answers' operation is precisely the linkage the record contract forbids. The legitimate need it gestures at (turning a one-off participant into an ongoing relationship) is met in Civic Intelligence Engine by the recontact consent tier, which stores contact info beside a consent flag but structurally apart from response content, never by mutating the response record itself.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's `upgrade_account` function lets a participant who started anonymously convert into a full, durable account by validating a new password and flipping the `annon` row in-place to `email_password` with an attached username and email, so the same user id and all prior participation carry forward.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately diverges by never linking a submission to an identity, keeping the raw layer append-only and anonymous and holding any contact detail in a separate default-off store that is never exported alongside response content, so there is no way to attach a name or email onto an existing participant record.
items.meaning_s: In-place anonymous-to-account upgrade is precisely the de-anonymising linkage Civic Intelligence Engine's record contract forbids, and the legitimate need it gestures at (turning a one-off participant into an ongoing relationship) is instead met by Civic Intelligence Engine's recontact consent tier that stores contact info structurally apart from response content rather than by mutating the response record.

items.name: Resource-scoped role matrix
items.comhairle: Comhairle implements a real role-based access-control matrix. The `resource_role` table (`UserResourceRole`) grants a user one of four roles: `Owner`, `Contributor`, `Translator`, `Moderator`, scoped to a specific resource of kind `Organisation` or `Conversation`. Enforcement is done with a compile-time-typed Axum extractor `RequiredRole<Resource, Roles>` in `api/src/routes/auth.rs`: a handler declares e.g. `RequiredRole<Conversation, (Owner, Moderator)>` and the extractor resolves the current user, reads the `conversation_id` from the path, and rejects with `UserNotAuthorized` unless the user holds one of the listed roles on that resource. A separate config-driven super-admin allowlist (`is_user_admin`) gates platform-wide operations.
items.cie: Absent as an application-layer feature; Civic Intelligence Engine instead enforces authority at the database-role layer. The candidate 'shall be able to publish derived results views and withhold results' but 'shall have no mechanism to delete or alter any raw submission,' and 'this authority model is enforced by database roles, not application-layer access controls' (`04-who-we-serve.md`, D-07). There is no per-user, per-resource permission table.
items.meaning: Watch. Civic Intelligence Engine is intentionally single-campaign, so a full four-role-by-two-resource matrix is overkill today, and Civic Intelligence Engine's database-role enforcement is actually stronger for the one invariant that matters (nobody, including the candidate, can mutate raw data). But the moment Civic Intelligence Engine grows a facilitation/authoring surface with multiple staff (an instrument owner drafting questions, a moderator handling flags, a translator localising prompts), the typed `RequiredRole` pattern is a clean, auditable template to borrow, because it keeps authorization declarative at each endpoint rather than scattered in handler bodies.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle implements a real role-based access-control matrix in which its `resource_role` table grants Owner, Contributor, Translator, or Moderator roles scoped to a specific Organisation or Conversation, enforced by a compile-time-typed `RequiredRole<Resource, Roles>` Axum extractor plus a config-driven super-admin allowlist.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no such application-layer permission table and instead enforces authority at the database-role layer, where the candidate may publish or withhold derived results views but has no mechanism to delete or alter any raw submission.
items.meaning_s: A full four-role-by-two-resource matrix is overkill for single-campaign Civic Intelligence Engine and its database-role enforcement is stronger for the invariant that nobody may mutate raw data, but the typed `RequiredRole` extractor is a clean, auditable template worth watching for the day Civic Intelligence Engine grows a multi-staff facilitation or authoring surface.

items.name: Multi-organisation tenancy
items.comhairle: Comhairle is multi-tenant around a first-class `Organisation` resource. Organizations are create-read-update-delete-managed (`api/src/routes/organizations.rs`), and every conversation and role grant hangs off an organisation or conversation id through the `resource_role` table, so data and permissions are scoped per-tenant: an Owner of Organisation A cannot act on Organisation B's conversations. This lets a single deployed instance host many independent councils/campaigns side by side, each with its own members, roles, conversations and content.
items.cie: Absent by design. Civic Intelligence Engine is scoped to exactly one campaign in one district (NC-12) per deployment; the spec frames replication as standing up a fresh instance from a clean checkout via the playbook, not as adding a tenant to a shared instance (`04-who-we-serve.md`, civic-innovator archetype).
items.meaning: Watch. For the pilot, single-tenant is simpler and reduces the blast radius of any data-isolation bug: a real virtue given Civic Intelligence Engine's privacy stakes. But Civic Intelligence Engine's own north star is a replicable product that many campaigns run, and 'one instance per deployer' does not scale operationally. If Civic Intelligence Engine ever offers a hosted service, the organisation-as-tenant-boundary pattern (every row and every role grant scoped to a tenant id) is the reference design to adopt, and adopting it early is far cheaper than retrofitting tenant isolation onto an append-only store later.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle is multi-tenant around a first-class `Organisation` resource where every conversation and role grant hangs off an organisation or conversation id, so a single deployed instance can host many independent councils and campaigns side by side, each with isolated members, roles, conversations, and content.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is absent this capability by design, scoped to exactly one campaign in one district per deployment and framing replication as standing up a fresh instance from a clean checkout rather than adding a tenant to a shared instance.
items.meaning_s: Single-tenant is simpler and reduces the blast radius of any data-isolation bug for the privacy-sensitive pilot, but because Civic Intelligence Engine's north star is a replicable product that many campaigns run, the organisation-as-tenant-boundary pattern is worth watching and far cheaper to adopt early than to retrofit onto an append-only store later.

items.name: Typed invitations with accept tracking
items.comhairle: Comhairle has a structured invitation system (`api/src/routes/invites.rs`, `api/src/models/invites.rs`). An `Invite` carries a typed target: `Email(address)`, `User(uuid)` for an existing member, `SingleUse` (a link anyone can use but only once), or `Open` (a link many people can accept), and a lifecycle status (`Pending`/`Open`/`Accepted`/`Rejected`). Recipients hit `/accept_invite` or `/reject_invite`, email invites trigger notification mail through the mailer, an invite can auto-register event attendance on accept, and `get_stats_for_invite` reports uptake. Invites are validated (`is_still_valid`, `is_for_user`) so an email invite can only be redeemed by its intended address.
items.cie: Partially present but much narrower. Civic Intelligence Engine's outreach layer delivers unique single-use codes by mailer/Short Message Service and its integrity layer treats shared links as the primary threat (`04-who-we-serve.md`, R11). It has the single-use-code concept but no typed invite object, no accept/reject state machine, and no open/multi-use link type.
items.meaning: Watch, selectively. The `SingleUse` invite maps cleanly onto Civic Intelligence Engine's unique-code model, and the accept-tracking + `get_stats_for_invite` idea is genuinely useful for Civic Intelligence Engine's outreach-sizing story (knowing redemption rate feeds the participation-target math). But the `Open`/multi-use link type directly conflicts with Civic Intelligence Engine's integrity calibration and must not be adopted. An open link is exactly the shared-link attack vector the single-use code is designed to prevent. Adopt the invite-status + stats plumbing; leave open links out.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle has a structured invitation system whose `Invite` carries a typed target: email address, existing user, single-use link, or open multi-use link, plus a Pending/Open/Accepted/Rejected lifecycle, validated redemption, accept/reject endpoints, mailer notifications, optional event-attendance registration, and a `get_stats_for_invite` uptake report.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is only partially present and much narrower here, delivering unique single-use codes by mailer or Short Message Service and treating shared links as its primary threat, so it has the single-use-code concept but no typed invite object, accept/reject state machine, or open multi-use link type.
items.meaning_s: The single-use invite and its accept-tracking `get_stats_for_invite` reporting are worth selectively adopting because redemption-rate data feeds Civic Intelligence Engine's participation-target math, but the open multi-use link type must be left out as it is exactly the shared-link attack vector Civic Intelligence Engine's single-use codes are designed to prevent.

items.name: Multilingual user interface (8 languages, including right-to-left)
items.comhairle: Comhairle's participant user interface is fully internationalised. Its inlang/Paraglide project (`ui/packages/comhairle/project.inlang/settings.json`) declares eight language tags: `en`, `gd` (Scottish Gaelic), `cy` (Welsh), `zh`, `es`, `fr`, `ar` (Arabic, right-to-left), `pt`, with a per-language message catalogue under `ui/packages/comhairle/messages/{lang}.json` and lint rules for missing/empty/identical patterns. Every static string in the interface is a keyed message resolved at build/render time against the visitor's chosen language.
items.cie: Absent / open decision. Civic Intelligence Engine is English-only, and Spanish support (decision D-31) is explicitly unresolved and 'blocked on district confirmation,' flagged as 'a constituent-archetype equity issue with legal dimensions' under Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act (`04-who-we-serve.md`, OQ-04-02). There is no i18n framework in the Civic Intelligence Engine build.
items.meaning: Adopt. This is a clear gain, not a divergence: Civic Intelligence Engine's own spec names an English-only instrument as a systematic exclusion of non-English constituents and an open ethical/legal risk, so multilingual user interface is a capability Civic Intelligence Engine wants rather than one it declines. Comhairle demonstrates a production-proven approach (keyed message catalogues, a source language, missing-translation linting, and even right-to-left support) that Civic Intelligence Engine could lift almost wholesale to resolve D-31 and make the consent gate and conversation reachable in a participant's own language, which the spec notes matters for statistical validity as well as equity, because a confusing or foreign-language screen suppresses exactly the underrepresented voices Civic Intelligence Engine most needs.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's participant user interface is fully internationalised through an inlang/Paraglide project that declares eight language tags including Scottish Gaelic, Welsh, and right-to-left Arabic, with per-language keyed message catalogues and lint rules for missing, empty, or identical translations resolved against the visitor's chosen language.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is English-only with no i18n framework, and its Spanish-support decision is explicitly unresolved and blocked on district confirmation, flagged as a constituent-archetype equity issue with legal dimensions under Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act.
items.meaning_s: Multilingual user interface is a clear gain to adopt because Civic Intelligence Engine's own spec names an English-only instrument as a systematic exclusion and legal risk, and Comhairle's production-proven keyed-catalogue, source-language, missing-translation-linting, and right-to-left approach could be lifted almost wholesale to make the consent gate and conversation reachable in a participant's own language for both equity and statistical validity.

items.name: Localizable persistent content model
items.comhairle: Beyond static user interface strings, Comhairle localises author-created database content. A `TextContent` row holds a canonical string plus its `primary_locale`, and a one-to-many `TextTranslation` set holds per-locale renderings (`api/src/models/translations.rs`). Any localisable field is stored as a `TextContentId` reference rather than a raw string: for example a `Region`'s `name` field is a `TextContentId`, and `region::get_localized_by_id` / `list` resolve the right translation for the request locale. The chosen locale is read from a `COMHAIRLE_LOCALE` cookie by the `LocaleExtractor` and threaded through queries so list/detail endpoints return content already localised (`api/src/routes/regions.rs`, `api/src/routes/translations.rs`).
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine has no localised-content data model; its content (questions, statements, consent copy) is authored and served in a single language, consistent with the English-only instrument posture (`04-who-we-serve.md`).
items.meaning: Adopt if Civic Intelligence Engine localises. Static-user-interface i18n (I7) only covers chrome; the substance Civic Intelligence Engine serves (the consent disclosure, the questions, the statements a constituent votes on) is author-created content that must also be translatable if the equity goal is to be met. Comhairle's 'store an id, resolve a translation per request locale' pattern is the missing half, and it composes well with Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase-only and append-only rules because translations are additive rows keyed to an immutable source. This is a genuine gain: without it, a multilingual user interface would still present English questions.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle localises author-created database content by storing every localisable field as a `TextContentId` reference to a canonical `TextContent` row with a `primary_locale` and a one-to-many set of per-locale `TextTranslation` renderings, resolved for the request locale read from a `COMHAIRLE_LOCALE` cookie and threaded through queries so endpoints return content already localised.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is absent this capability, having no localised-content data model and authoring and serving its questions, statements, and consent copy in a single language consistent with its English-only instrument posture.
items.meaning_s: Because static-user-interface translation alone would still present English questions, Comhairle's 'store an id, resolve a translation per request locale' content model is the genuine gain to adopt if Civic Intelligence Engine localises, and it composes cleanly with Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase-only and append-only rules since translations are additive rows keyed to an immutable source.

items.name: Machine translation with human-validation gate
items.comhairle: Comhairle can auto-translate content and track how trustworthy each translation is. `auto_translate` / `auto_translate_all` (`api/src/routes/translations.rs`) call a pluggable `TranslationService`; the shipped implementation `GoogleTranslateService` POSTs each string to the Google Cloud Translation application programming interface (`api/src/translation_service.rs`). Every `TextTranslation` records two governance flags: `ai_generated` and `requires_validation`, so machine output is marked and can be routed to a human (the `Translator` role from the role-based access control matrix) for sign-off before it is trusted. Admin-only endpoints let a staffer generate all languages for a piece of content in one call.
items.cie: Absent, and the mechanism partly diverges. Civic Intelligence Engine runs no translation service; more importantly its principles forbid per-record external artificial intelligence egress: it uses local embeddings 'so no per-record egress' happens and keeps verbatim text in the raw store only (`02`/`03` principles; T10 paraphrase-only). Shipping each string to Google's application programming interface is exactly the per-record external call Civic Intelligence Engine avoids.
items.meaning: Watch, with a caveat. The valuable, adoptable idea is the human-validation gate: marking machine output `ai_generated`/`requires_validation` and requiring a human to confirm before it goes live is precisely the disclosure-and-oversight discipline Civic Intelligence Engine already applies to its large language model conversation layer, and it fits Civic Intelligence Engine's culture of structural safeguards. The delivery mechanism, however, should diverge: rather than Google Translate's per-record egress, a Civic Intelligence Engine localisation feature would want a local or batch-translated pipeline so participant-adjacent content is not streamed to a third-party application programming interface, preserving the no-per-record-egress commitment.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle can auto-translate content through a pluggable `TranslationService` (shipped as `GoogleTranslateService` POSTing each string to the Google Cloud Translation application programming interface) while marking every machine-produced `TextTranslation` with `ai_generated` and `requires_validation` flags so it can be routed to a human Translator for sign-off before it is trusted.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is absent this and the mechanism partly diverges, since it runs no translation service and its principles forbid the per-record external artificial intelligence egress that shipping each string to Google's application programming interface entails, relying instead on local embeddings and keeping verbatim text in the raw store only.
items.meaning_s: The adoptable idea is the human-validation gate of marking machine output `ai_generated`/`requires_validation` and requiring human confirmation, which matches Civic Intelligence Engine's disclosure-and-oversight discipline, but the delivery mechanism should diverge toward a local or batch-translation pipeline rather than Google's per-record egress to preserve Civic Intelligence Engine's no-per-record-egress commitment.

items.name: Demographic recruitment targets
items.comhairle: Comhairle records recruitment quotas per demographic bucket. A `RecruitmentTarget` (`api/src/models/recruitment_target.rs`) stores, per workflow, a `metric` (a demographic dimension, e.g. age band or region), a `bucket` (a value within that dimension), and a `target_count`: the number of participants wanted from that bucket. It upserts on the `(workflow_id, metric, bucket)` key so targets can be revised, and admin endpoints (`api/src/routes/recruitment_targets.rs`) manage them, with the OpenAPI summary describing it as 'the target number of participants for a given demographic.' This lets organisers steer outreach toward a demographically balanced sample.
items.cie: Deliberately diverges. Civic Intelligence Engine quarantines demographics from the analysis lane and explicitly does not claim to represent the district: participation is 'opt-in, invitation-only, and self-selected,' the constituent archetype is 'explicitly non-representative,' and a scope banner states this on every surface (`04-who-we-serve.md`). Civic Intelligence Engine has no per-demographic recruitment-quota model.
items.meaning: Diverge, on principle, with a narrow watch. Steering recruitment by demographic bucket implies the deployment is trying to build a representative sample, a claim Civic Intelligence Engine's methodology (AAPOR non-probability guidance, Meng's Big Data Paradox) refuses to make, so importing quota-steering wholesale would invite exactly the over-claiming the scope banner exists to prevent. The one adjacent thing Civic Intelligence Engine does care about is representativeness *auditing* (the Validity Card, T2 small-cell floor) and outreach *sizing* (hitting an overall n): a stripped-down 'how many invitations to send' target is compatible, but per-demographic quotas that shape who is recruited are not.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle records recruitment quotas per demographic bucket via a `RecruitmentTarget` that stores a metric, a bucket, and a target_count per workflow (upserting on the workflow/metric/bucket key and managed by admin endpoints) so organisers can steer outreach toward a demographically balanced sample.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately diverges by quarantining demographics from the analysis lane and having no per-demographic recruitment-quota model, explicitly declaring participation opt-in, invitation-only, self-selected, and non-representative on a scope banner shown on every surface.
items.meaning_s: Per-demographic recruitment quotas are a principled divergence because steering toward a representative sample makes exactly the claim Civic Intelligence Engine's non-probability methodology refuses, though a stripped-down overall 'how many invitations to send' sizing target is compatible with Civic Intelligence Engine's representativeness auditing and outreach sizing and worth a narrow watch.

items.name: Geographic region entities
items.comhairle: Comhairle models geography as first-class, localised, filterable data. A `Region` (`api/src/models/region.rs`) has a localised `name` (a `TextContentId`, so it renders in the visitor's language) and a `region_type` of `Official` (a recognised administrative area) or `Custom` (a bespoke boundary an organiser draws). Regions are create-read-update-delete-managed, paginated, filterable and orderable (`api/src/routes/regions.rs`, `RegionFilterOptions`/`RegionOrderOptions`), letting conversations and recruitment be scoped to defined places and letting the same instance operate across many council areas.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine operates within a single fixed district (NC-12, ~80,000 people) and hard-codes that scope into its re-identification thresholds (T2 = 11 per cell, T10 paraphrase-only are 'calibrated to this district scale specifically'); there is no region entity or geographic hierarchy (`04-who-we-serve.md`).
items.meaning: Watch. Single-district is correct for the pilot and is baked into Civic Intelligence Engine's privacy calibration, so a general region model adds nothing today. But Civic Intelligence Engine's spec itself notes that 'district size changes re-identification risk thresholds' for future deployers, which means a replicable product eventually needs a way to declare its geographic scope and adjust thresholds accordingly. Comhairle's `Official`/`Custom` region typing and localised region names are a useful reference for that future 'where does this deployment operate' primitive: worth tracking, not building now.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle models geography as first-class, localised, filterable data through a `Region` entity carrying a localised name and an Official-or-Custom region type, create-read-update-delete-managed and paginated with filter and order options so conversations and recruitment can be scoped to defined places across many council areas.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is absent this capability, operating within a single fixed district whose scale is hard-coded into its re-identification thresholds, with no region entity or geographic hierarchy.
items.meaning_s: A general region model adds nothing to the single-district pilot whose scope is baked into Civic Intelligence Engine's privacy calibration, but because the spec notes that district size changes re-identification thresholds for future deployers, Comhairle's Official/Custom region typing and localised names are worth watching as a reference for a future 'where does this deployment operate' primitive.

items.name: Application programming interface keys for programmatic access
items.comhairle: Comhairle issues application programming interface keys for machine-to-machine access. An admin calls `POST /api_keys` (`api/src/routes/api_keys.rs`) to mint a key; the key is hashed at rest and, on each request, the `resolve_user_from_request` path in `api/src/routes/auth.rs` accepts an `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, hashes it, looks up the owning user, and authenticates the request as that user, so external scripts and integrations can act through the same role-based access control checks as a logged-in session. Key creation is deliberately un-traced to keep secrets out of logs.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine exposes no programmatic third-party application programming interface surface; its data-sharing story is a one-way export of derived, suppressed artifacts, and there is no bearer-token/application-programming-interface-key auth path in the record contract (`03-principles-and-commitments.md`, one-way export).
items.meaning: Watch, low priority. Civic Intelligence Engine's narrowness means it has little need for machine clients today, and adding a bearer-token surface widens the attack surface against an append-only, personally-identifiable-information-quarantined store, so declining it is reasonable. The pattern becomes relevant only if Civic Intelligence Engine later needs trusted automation (e.g. a scheduled representativeness audit or an export pipeline pulling derived artifacts); at that point Comhairle's hash-at-rest, admin-gated, log-suppressed key model is a sound reference, and any Civic Intelligence Engine version should be scoped to derived/export data only, never to the raw store.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle issues admin-minted application programming interface keys for machine-to-machine access that are hashed at rest and, when presented as an `Authorization: Bearer` token, hashed and resolved to the owning user so external scripts act through the same role-based access control checks as a logged-in session, with key creation deliberately un-traced to keep secrets out of logs.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is absent this capability, exposing no programmatic third-party application programming interface surface and no bearer-token auth path, since its data-sharing story is a one-way export of derived, suppressed artifacts.
items.meaning_s: Declining programmatic application programming interface keys is reasonable and low priority because Civic Intelligence Engine has little need for machine clients and a bearer-token surface would widen the attack surface against its append-only, personally-identifiable-information-quarantined store, though Comhairle's hash-at-rest, admin-gated, log-suppressed key model is a sound reference if Civic Intelligence Engine later needs trusted automation scoped strictly to derived or export data.

items.name: Audio-to-sensemaking pipeline
items.comhairle: Comhairle turns a recorded meeting or breakout room into an analysable transcript automatically. The admin route in routes/audio_recordings.rs mints signed upload web addresses for a main room plus any number of breakout rooms and records an audio_recording row. A durable multi-stage worker (worker_service/process_video_call_transcriptions.rs) then runs transcribe_recording, which pulls the file from object storage, calls a pluggable Transcriber (transcription_service.rs, with an Amazon Transcribe implementation) that yields timestamped, speaker-labelled TranscriptEvents, and chains via apalis GoTo into generate_sensemaking_report to distil the transcript into structured Comments/a report.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine is a text-first Pol.is-style vote-on-statements loop; its spec (07-the-system-by-layer.md) covers a vote matrix, principal component analysis, k-means and group-informed consensus, with no audio capture, speech-to-text, or diarization anywhere in the build core.
items.meaning: Civic Intelligence Engine should watch-to-adopt this as the on-ramp for offline and in-person deliberation. Face-to-face community meetings are exactly the settings Civic Intelligence Engine claims to serve, and a transcript pipeline lets spoken input feed the same statement/consensus machinery. The caution is Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase-only and no-per-record-egress commitments: any adopted transcriber would need to run locally or be treated as a trusted subprocessor, and quotes would still be paraphrased rather than served verbatim.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle auto-transcribes recorded meeting and breakout-room audio into timestamped, speaker-labelled transcripts and chains them into a sensemaking report via a staged background worker.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no audio capture, speech-to-text, or diarization at all; its listening loop is entirely text-vote based.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should treat an audio-to-transcript on-ramp as a high-value adoption target for in-person deliberation, provided the transcriber runs locally and quotes stay paraphrased.

items.name: Event lifecycle & attendance
items.comhairle: Comhairle models real-world and video events end-to-end. routes/events.rs and routes/event_attendances.rs create events, register attendees with a role (models/event_attendance.rs stores user_id, event_id, role), and issue confirmations. The mailer (mailer.rs) generates iCal calendar attachments via the icalendar crate and sends event_registration_invite, event_confirmation and event_reminder emails, resolving each event into the attendee's timezone (LocalizedEvent/ResolveTimeZone). Events also link to the transcription pipeline, so a registered video call can be recorded and processed.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec has no concept of scheduled events, attendance confirmations, attendance roles, or calendar invitations; participation is an anonymous asynchronous voting session, not a convened gathering.
items.meaning: This is a genuine gain for Civic Intelligence Engine's outreach layer. The phased Bloom pattern (bloom-03: Open Poll then Live Conversations then Solutions Forum) depends on being able to convene the 30-50 residents for the deliberation stage, which requires exactly this event+attendance-confirmation+reminder scaffolding. Civic Intelligence Engine can borrow the model without compromising its analytical core, since events sit outside the vote/consensus pipeline.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle runs full event scheduling with role-based attendance confirmations, timezone-localized reminders, and iCal calendar attachments, wired to record video calls for transcription.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no events, attendance confirmations, or calendar invitations; participation is anonymous asynchronous voting with no convened gathering.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt an event-and-attendance-confirmation layer to support Bloom's phased poll-to-live-conversation-to-forum civic process, which requires convening named participants.

items.name: Templated transactional mailer
items.comhairle: Comhairle ships a full transactional email subsystem. mailer.rs defines a ComhairleMailer trait sending via lettre/Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, rendering MiniJinja HyperText Markup Language templates (email_templates/: welcome, verify_email, password_reset, one_time_passcode, conversation_invite, event_confirmation, event_reminder, conversation_broadcast) that all extend a shared email_layout.html and have a locals folder for localization. Admins can configure the transactional copy at runtime through routes/email_template_configs.rs, which stores per-type EmailTemplateConfig rows with typed slots and schemas (conversation invite, event registration invite/confirmation).
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec describes no outbound email, no Simple Mail Transfer Protocol integration, and no templating; a clean-room listening loop produces analysis, not correspondence.
items.meaning: Civic Intelligence Engine will need transactional email the moment it does two-tier consent, magic-link auth, or any recontact, so this is a concrete adopt target. The runtime-configurable, per-organization, localizable template store is the part worth borrowing rather than hard-coding, because civic hosts expect to control voice and language. It touches nothing in Civic Intelligence Engine's analytical commitments.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle sends localized, admin-configurable transactional emails (invites, confirmations, verification, password reset, one-time password, broadcasts) via a MiniJinja+Simple-Mail-Transfer-Protocol mailer with a runtime template-config store.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's spec includes no outbound email, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, or templating of any kind.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a templated, localizable mailer since consent, magic-link auth, and recontact all require outbound email the current spec cannot produce.

items.name: Scheduled & automated emails
items.comhairle: Comhairle sends time-based email automatically without an operator in the loop. worker_service.rs registers an apalis-cron CronStream; retrieve_and_enqueue_scheduled_emails (worker_service/scheduled_emails.rs) periodically queries list_upcoming_scheduled_emails and enqueues a SendScheduledEmailJob per due recipient, and send_scheduled_email renders the configured template, attaches any iCal body, marks the scheduled_email row sent, and completes the tracked job. This is what drives event reminders and any future drip/recontact sequence.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine has no scheduler, no cron, and no deferred-send concept; its spec is a synchronous analysis pipeline over a vote matrix with no time-triggered outbound actions.
items.meaning: A scheduled-send loop is the mechanical prerequisite for Bloom's recontact tier (bloom-07 'Stay in touch') and for phased-process nudges reminding participants when Live Conversations open. Civic Intelligence Engine should watch-to-adopt: the value is high for engagement, but any recontact must be gated behind Civic Intelligence Engine's explicit two-tier consent so reminders only reach people who opted into follow-up.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle uses an apalis-cron worker to periodically find due scheduled emails and enqueue-and-send them automatically, powering event reminders and drip/recontact sequences.
