items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no scheduler, cron, or deferred-send mechanism; it is a synchronous analysis pipeline with no time-triggered outbound actions.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a consent-gated scheduled-send loop to enable Bloom-style recontact and phased-process reminders, sending only to opted-in participants.

items.name: In-app notifications over WebSocket
items.comhairle: Comhairle has a first-class in-app notification system plus a realtime transport. routes/notifications.rs exposes unread lists and unread counts per user backed by models/notification_delivery.rs and models/notification.rs (typed Info/Warning/Success/Error, scoped Site or Conversation). websockets.rs runs an Axum WebSocket hub with a DashMap connection registry, an authenticated RequiredUser upgrade, typed WebSocketMessage/NotificationLevel messages, and a pluggable per-domain handler trait, so notifications and other events can be pushed live rather than polled.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec has no per-user notification store and no realtime channel; results are computed and shown, not delivered as an evolving stream of user-addressed events.
items.meaning: For Civic Intelligence Engine this is situational-but-real (watch). A participant surface benefits from 'your group's consensus shifted' or 'new bridging statement' nudges, and a WebSocket hub could also power live result updates during an open poll. It is orthogonal to Civic Intelligence Engine's analytical guarantees, so adopting it carries little principled tension beyond keeping delivered payloads to gated/paraphrased claims rather than raw verbatim.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle stores typed per-user in-app notifications (unread counts, site/conversation scope) and pushes them live through an authenticated Axum WebSocket hub with pluggable per-domain handlers.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no per-user notification store and no realtime channel; it computes and displays results rather than streaming user-addressed events.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine could adopt a WebSocket notification hub to push consensus-shift nudges and live poll updates, keeping delivered payloads to gated, paraphrased claims.

items.name: Durable background job queue
items.comhairle: Comhairle runs heavy and deferred work off the request path on a durable queue. ComhairleWorkerService (worker_service.rs) wraps apalis RedisStorage queues for document processing, transcription, and scheduled email, and every job is mirrored into a tracked Job row (models/job.rs) that admins can list, inspect, and delete via routes/jobs.rs with filter/order/pagination. Failures are recorded against the job (ok_or_record_failure) so operators see why a job died, and multi-step flows chain with apalis GoTo.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec assumes a synchronous, in-process analysis run over the vote matrix; there is no queue, no Redis, no operator-visible job ledger, and no retry/failure-record surface for long-running work.
items.meaning: This is infrastructure Civic Intelligence Engine will need as soon as any step is expensive or asynchronous (embedding batches, re-clustering, report generation, transcription). The operator-facing tracked-job ledger with recorded failure reasons is the borrow-worthy part, since it gives a listening tool auditable, debuggable background processing. It is compatible with Civic Intelligence Engine's append-only leanings if job records are treated as an immutable event log.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle offloads transcription, document, and email work to durable apalis/Redis queues, mirroring each into an admin-visible Job ledger with recorded failure reasons and multi-step chaining.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine assumes synchronous in-process analysis with no queue, no Redis, and no operator-visible job ledger for long-running work.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a durable job queue with an auditable job-ledger once embedding, re-clustering, or report steps become expensive or asynchronous.

items.name: Outcome & impact tracking
items.comhairle: Comhairle records what actually changed as a result of a deliberation and attaches it to the report. routes/report_impacts.rs and models/report_impact.rs let admins create ReportImpact entries (title, details, kind) linked to a report, and FullReportDto (models/report.rs) surfaces impacts alongside the report so participants can see concrete outcomes their input produced. This is the 'you shaped this / here is what happened next' close-the-loop layer.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec ends at validity-carded consensus output; there is no structure for recording downstream decisions, actions taken, or impact attributable to a listening session.
items.meaning: Closing the loop is a strong engagement gain and aligns with Bloom's 'What comes next' framing (bloom-04/08). Showing participants the tangible result of their contribution is a major driver of trust and repeat participation, and impact records pair naturally with Civic Intelligence Engine's append-only trust layer as immutable outcome events. Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt an impact/outcome model as the missing tail of its pipeline.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle records concrete post-deliberation outcomes as titled, typed ReportImpact entries attached to a report, closing the loop so participants see what their input produced.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's pipeline ends at validity-carded consensus with no structure for recording downstream decisions or attributable impact.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt an outcome/impact model as the missing tail of its pipeline, storing impacts as immutable events in its append-only trust layer to build participant trust.

items.name: Facilitator & participant feedback
items.comhairle: Comhairle captures structured feedback on a deliberation from both sides. routes/feedback.rs creates feedback tied to a conversation, and FullReportDto (models/report.rs) splits it into facilitator_feedback and participant_feedback vectors surfaced with the report. This gives a distinct experience/quality self-code channel separate from the substantive vote data, letting hosts learn how the process felt to run and to join.
items.cie: Deferred. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec mentions a light self-code of 'feeling heard' as a participant sentiment signal, but there is no built component for structured, role-split feedback capture on a session; it is an intended-but-unbuilt idea.
items.meaning: This is a build-it gain that operationalizes something Civic Intelligence Engine already wants. Bloom ships the same pattern as an end-of-poll Net Promoter Score self-code (bloom-05), confirming it is product-standard. Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a lightweight feedback capture that stores the experience signal separately from the analytical vote matrix, so 'feeling heard' can be reported without contaminating consensus computation.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle captures role-split facilitator and participant feedback on each conversation as a separate experience/quality channel surfaced alongside the report.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine only sketches a light 'feeling heard' self-code in its spec and has no built structured feedback-capture component.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should build lightweight feedback capture that stores the experience signal separately from the vote matrix, realizing its deferred 'feeling heard' self-code (a Bloom-standard pattern).

items.name: Object storage & media library
items.comhairle: Comhairle has a general blob layer for uploaded files. bulk_storage_service.rs abstracts an object store issuing signed read/write web addresses (get_write_file_url), used by audio recordings, resources.rs (signed upload web addresses for supporting documents), and routes/media.rs, which is a full media library with multipart upload, content-type-typed rows (models/media.rs), and filter/order/pagination listing. This underpins images, attachments, background documents, and recordings across the platform.
items.cie: Absent, and partly by design. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec centers on a vote matrix and derived analysis and avoids mutable storage and per-record external egress; it has no notion of a general file/blob store or a media library.
items.meaning: This is watch-with-caution. Civic Intelligence Engine genuinely needs somewhere to keep background documents and (if it adopts CS1 transcription) recordings, so a signed-web-address object layer is useful. But Civic Intelligence Engine's discipline around mutable storage and egress means it should scope any blob layer narrowly to non-analytical assets (host-provided materials, media) and keep it well away from the append-only trust layer and the vote data, rather than adopting a broad mutable media create, read, update, delete surface as-is.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle provides a signed-web-address object store and a typed media library (multipart upload, filterable listing) backing recordings, resources, and images platform-wide.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no general blob store or media library and deliberately avoids mutable storage and per-record egress.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt only a narrowly-scoped signed-web-address blob layer for non-analytical host materials and recordings, keeping it separate from its append-only vote and trust data.

items.name: Mass participant broadcast email
items.comhairle: Comhairle can send an announcement to a conversation's participants at once. The conversation_broadcast.html template (email_templates/) renders host-authored body copy inside the shared email_layout, and the mailer plus email_template_config machinery supply the recipient resolution and consented-recipient handling (models/conversation_email_notification_recipients.rs) so a host can reach everyone who joined with updates, next-step invites, or results links.
items.cie: Absent. Civic Intelligence Engine's spec has no broadcast/announcement channel to participants; once analysis is produced there is no built path to proactively email the cohort that took part.
items.meaning: Broadcast is the operational realization of Bloom's 'Stay in touch' and 'What's next' tiers (bloom-07/08): telling participants when results are published or when the next phase opens. Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a consent-gated broadcast, drawing recipients only from those who opted into follow-up, so it can move people through a phased poll-to-conversation process without breaking its two-tier consent model.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle lets a host broadcast a templated announcement email to all consented participants of a conversation for updates, next-step invites, and results links.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no participant broadcast channel; after analysis there is no built path to proactively email the cohort that took part.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt a consent-gated broadcast that emails only follow-up opt-ins, realizing Bloom's 'Stay in touch'/'What's next' tiers within its two-tier consent model.

items.name: Tool-agnostic interchange grammar
items.comhairle: Comhairle defines a small, deliberately generic vocabulary for describing any deliberation regardless of which underlying tool produced it: Statement, Reaction, Group, Participant, plus supporting types (StatementRole, ReactionType, Generator, AlgorithmDescriptor). This is captured as a JavaScript Object Notation Schema in data_model/schema.json ('AllTypes') and is clearly intended to be the common pool that all seven tools normalise into. CRITICAL HEAD CAVEAT: this grammar is DEFINED but entirely UNPOPULATED. The data_model crate itself is a stub (data_model/src/main.rs is a literal 'Hello, world!' with no dependencies in Cargo.toml), the grammar types (Statement, Reaction, Generator, AlgorithmDescriptor) are referenced NOWHERE in api/src, and the ToolImpl::sync_data hook that would move tool output into this pool is a no-op default that NO tool overrides (verified: zero 'fn sync_data' bodies exist in api/src/tools/). In practice each tool persists to its own aux tables instead.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has no single tool-agnostic interchange grammar. Its data lives in a purpose-built vote-matrix / statement / group schema tuned for the one Pol.is-style listening loop it runs, per the spec's system-by-layer and build-core docs. It has never needed to normalise across heterogeneous elicitation tools because it deliberately ships exactly one flow.
items.meaning: Worth tracking rather than adopting today. The IDEA of a universal Statement/Reaction/Group/Participant vocabulary is genuinely attractive as a future north star if Civic Intelligence Engine ever hosts more than one elicitation method, and Comhairle has already done the hard modelling work in schema.json. But because Comhairle's own implementation of it is aspirational and unwired, Civic Intelligence Engine gains a design reference, not a proven component. Civic Intelligence Engine should watch whether Comhairle ever populates it before treating it as validated.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle declares a universal deliberation vocabulary (Statement, Reaction, Group, Participant, Generator, AlgorithmDescriptor) in data_model/schema.json, but the grammar is defined-only: the crate is a hello-world stub, no api code references the types, and the sync_data pooling hook is an unimplemented no-op in every tool.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine runs a single purpose-built listening schema and has no tool-agnostic interchange grammar because it deliberately ships exactly one elicitation flow.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should treat Comhairle's universal Statement/Reaction/Group vocabulary as an inspiring but unproven design reference to watch, not a component to adopt, since Comhairle itself has left the grammar unwired.

items.name: Generator / algorithm provenance model
items.comhairle: Every first-class object in Comhairle's interchange grammar records WHO or WHAT produced it via a Generator tagged union with three arms: Participant(uuid), Host(uuid), or Algorithm(AlgorithmDescriptor). AlgorithmDescriptor carries an id, a free-text 'kind', and a string->string 'metadata' map describing how the algorithm was configured (data_model/schema.json). Statements go further and separate two provenance facts: 'made_by' (who authored the content) and 'role_classified_by' (who or what assigned its role/label), so a human can write a sentence while an algorithm labels it a 'Belief', and both facts are retained. This is a clean, machine-readable answer to 'is this datum human, host, or artificial-intelligence-generated, and under what algorithm configuration?'
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine tracks provenance more narrowly. Its append-only trust layer and light self-coding record system events, but per the spec it does not model a first-class Generator=Participant|Host|Algorithm distinction attached to each statement/reaction, nor an AlgorithmDescriptor capturing the exact algorithm configuration that produced a derived object. Distinguishing human-authored from artificial-intelligence-classified content at the row level is not an explicit Civic Intelligence Engine primitive today.
items.meaning: A strong adopt candidate. As Civic Intelligence Engine adds artificial intelligence assistance (paraphrasing, clustering summaries, group-informed-consensus-derived consensus statements), the ability to stamp each derived object with 'Algorithm{kind, metadata}' and to split authorship from classification is exactly the kind of auditable provenance Civic Intelligence Engine's trust-first posture wants. It is cheap to borrow because it is a pure data-shape idea, and it complements, rather than conflicts with, Civic Intelligence Engine's append-only trust layer.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle stamps each grammar object with a Generator union of Participant, Host, or Algorithm (the latter carrying an AlgorithmDescriptor of kind plus a configuration metadata map), and even splits a statement's content-authorship (made_by) from its role-classification (role_classified_by).
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has an append-only trust layer but no first-class per-row Generator distinction separating human-authored, host, and specific-algorithm-configured content.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt Comhairle's Generator/AlgorithmDescriptor provenance shape so every artificial-intelligence-derived paraphrase, cluster, or consensus statement is auditably tagged with the algorithm and config that produced it, distinct from who authored the underlying text.

items.name: Multi-tool conversation container
items.comhairle: Comhairle models a deliberation as a nested container: a Conversation (api/src/models/conversation.rs) owns one or more Workflows (api/src/models/workflow.rs), each Workflow is an ordered list of WorkflowSteps (api/src/models/workflow_step.rs), and each step embeds a polymorphic ToolConfig. ToolConfig is a tagged enum with seven arms: Polis, Learn, HeyForm, Stories, ElicitationBot, Prioritization, ThinkingSpace (api/src/tools.rs), stored as JSONB via a DbJsonBEnum macro. WorkflowStep also carries orchestration metadata: step_order, an ActivationRule, required/can_revisit flags, is_offline, and a preview_tool_config. So a single civic 'conversation' can chain a survey, then a Pol.is vote, then a prioritisation exercise, as a first-class sequenced object rather than as separate unrelated activities.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's data model is scoped to one campaign-listening flow: a vote matrix feeding principal component analysis -> k-means -> group-informed consensus. Per the spec it has no notion of a multi-step, multi-tool workflow container that sequences heterogeneous elicitation activities under one conversation with activation rules and per-step tool configs.
items.meaning: Watch closely, adopt selectively. Civic Intelligence Engine is intentionally a single sharp flow, so wholesale adoption would violate its 'narrow and sharp' commitment. But the container SHAPE, Conversation -> Workflow -> Step(ToolConfig) with ordering and activation rules, is the natural growth path if Civic Intelligence Engine ever wants to bracket its listening loop with a consent gate, a demographic-light intake, or a results-review step. It is a proven pattern for sequencing civic activities and is worth keeping in the back pocket.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle nests Conversation over Workflow over ordered WorkflowSteps, each embedding one of seven polymorphic ToolConfig variants (Polis, Learn, HeyForm, Stories, ElicitationBot, Prioritization, ThinkingSpace) with per-step activation rules, so one civic conversation can sequence a survey, a vote, and a prioritisation as a single first-class object.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's schema covers only its single vote-matrix listening loop and has no multi-step, multi-tool workflow container sequencing heterogeneous elicitation activities.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should keep Comhairle's Conversation-Workflow-Step container pattern in reserve as the natural way to eventually bracket its core listening loop with consent, intake, and review steps without abandoning its single-flow focus.

items.name: Per-tool aux tables, no common pool
items.comhairle: Despite declaring the universal grammar (CD1), Comhairle in practice persists each tool's data into its own dedicated auxiliary tables rather than a shared Statement/Reaction store. The clearest example is polis_statement_aux (migration 20260611155735), which holds Pol.is-specific rows keyed by workflow_step_id and user_id: zid, polis_conversation_id, polis_statement_id, themes[], statement_text, moderation_status/reason, is_seed, and visible_statement_when_submitted. Other tools have their own tables (thinking_space_answer, thinking_space_summary, thinking_space_follow_up_question, proposal, proposal_response). There is no interchange table; the tool-agnostic pool exists only as an unused schema, so cross-tool analytics must reconcile heterogeneous per-tool tables by hand.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine stores its listening loop in one coherent purpose-built schema rather than a constellation of per-tool aux tables, because it only runs one tool. It therefore does not face the reconciliation tax, but it also has no worked example of federating multiple tools' data.
items.meaning: Instructive as an anti-pattern to avoid. Comhairle demonstrates the failure mode of defining an interchange grammar but never routing tools through it: the aspirational common pool decays into a pile of tool-specific aux tables. If Civic Intelligence Engine ever adds a second elicitation surface, the lesson is to wire the shared model on day one (via something like sync_data) rather than let per-tool tables proliferate first.
items.comhairle_s: In practice Comhairle persists each tool to its own aux tables (for example polis_statement_aux with zid, polis_statement_id, themes, statement_text and moderation_status) with no shared interchange table, so the declared universal pool decays into tool-specific silos.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine keeps its single listening loop in one coherent purpose-built schema and has no per-tool aux-table sprawl, but also no worked multi-tool federation.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should read Comhairle's per-tool aux-table sprawl as a cautionary tale: if a second elicitation surface is ever added, route it through a shared model immediately rather than letting tool-specific tables accumulate first.

items.name: Mutable Postgres with cascade deletes
items.comhairle: Comhairle uses conventional mutable Postgres. Rows carry updated_at columns that are rewritten in place (Conversation, WorkflowStep, UserProfile, polis_statement_aux all have created_at + updated_at), update paths issue Structured Query Language UPDATE mutating existing rows (for example user_profile update by field), and referential integrity is enforced with hard ON DELETE CASCADE (polis_statement_aux references workflow_step and comhairle_user 'ON DELETE CASCADE', so deleting a step or user destroys the dependent statement rows). History is not preserved; the latest write wins and deletes are destructive.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately avoids mutable storage. Per its principles-and-commitments spec it runs an append-only trust layer with a hash-chain, so records are added, never overwritten, and nothing is silently destroyed by a cascade. This is a core, principled Civic Intelligence Engine commitment for auditability and tamper-evidence.
items.meaning: A principled divergence, not a gap. Comhairle's in-place mutation and cascade deletion are a normal, pragmatic web-app choice, but they are exactly what Civic Intelligence Engine rejects to guarantee that a civic record's history is auditable and tamper-evident. Civic Intelligence Engine should NOT adopt mutable Postgres semantics; the contrast is useful mainly to articulate WHY Civic Intelligence Engine pays the cost of append-only + hash-chaining. If interoperating with Comhairle, Civic Intelligence Engine must treat Comhairle rows as mutable snapshots, not immutable facts.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle uses mutable Postgres with in-place updated_at rewrites and hard ON DELETE CASCADE foreign keys (deleting a workflow step or user destroys its polis_statement_aux rows), so history is not preserved and the latest write wins.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately uses an append-only, hash-chained trust layer where records are never overwritten and deletes are never destructive.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should keep diverging from Comhairle's mutable, cascade-deleting Postgres because append-only hash-chaining is a principled choice for tamper-evident civic records, and must treat any imported Comhairle rows as mutable snapshots rather than immutable facts.

items.name: Joinable demographics & reports
items.comhairle: Comhairle stores participant demographics in a user_profile table (api/src/models/user_profile.rs) with ethnicity, age, gender, zipcode, and political_party, gated only by a boolean 'consented' flag, and keyed directly to user_id. These fields are freely JOINed to participation and conversation data to produce reports: get_demographic_report aggregates ethnicity, banded age ranges, and gender counts for a workflow (filtered to consented users), and get_demographics_for_export emits per-user rows (user_id, ethnicity, age, gender, zipcode, political_party) joined across user_profile -> comhairle_user -> user_participation -> workflow. Demographics are thus first-class, row-level joinable attributes of an identifiable participant.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately quarantines demographics. Per its principles/who-we-serve spec, personally identifying and demographic attributes are held apart from the deliberation data and are not joinable per-record to a participant's votes; representativeness is handled without exposing individual demographic rows. This is an explicit privacy commitment, not an unbuilt feature.
items.meaning: A principled divergence. Comhairle's joinable demographics power exactly the kind of representativeness breakdowns civic clients ask for, and the demographic-report aggregation is a nice worked example. But doing it by JOINing identifiable user_profile rows to participation is precisely the personally identifiable information exposure Civic Intelligence Engine refuses. Civic Intelligence Engine should NOT adopt the joinable model; if it wants representativeness, it must reproduce the OUTPUT (aggregate breakdowns) through its personally-identifiable-information-quarantine boundary (e.g. aggregate-only, differential-privacy-style, or unlinkable cohort counts) rather than borrow the schema.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle keeps participant demographics (ethnicity, age, gender, zipcode, political_party) in a consent-flagged user_profile table keyed to user_id and JOINs them to participation to produce demographic reports and per-user demographic exports.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately quarantines demographics so personally identifiable information is not joinable per-record to a participant's votes, as an explicit privacy commitment.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should keep diverging from Comhairle's row-level joinable demographics and, if representativeness output is needed, reproduce only aggregate breakdowns across its personally-identifiable-information-quarantine boundary rather than adopt the identifiable-join schema.

items.name: Verbatim statement text storage
items.comhairle: Comhairle stores participant utterances verbatim. The polis_statement_aux table was extended (migration 20260612104027) with a NOT NULL statement_text column holding the full submitted text, plus a moderation_status enum (accepted/rejected/pending), and it also retains visible_statement_when_submitted: a verbatim snapshot of what the participant saw at submission time. The model (api/src/models/polis_statement_aux.rs) surfaces these raw strings directly. The stored and served content is the participant's exact words.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine is paraphrase-only. Per its principles-and-commitments spec, participant statements are not served verbatim; quotes are paraphrased before display to reduce re-identification and quotation risk. Storing and serving exact submitted text the way polis_statement_aux does is deliberately outside Civic Intelligence Engine's model.
items.meaning: A principled divergence with an interop implication. Comhairle's verbatim storage is standard for a Pol.is-style tool and enables faithful moderation and audit, but it is exactly the raw-text serving Civic Intelligence Engine avoids. Civic Intelligence Engine should not adopt verbatim serving; more importantly, any pipeline that ingests Comhairle statement_text must run Civic Intelligence Engine's paraphrase step at the boundary, because Comhairle hands over exact words that Civic Intelligence Engine's own surface is committed never to show unmodified.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle stores and serves participant utterances verbatim, with polis_statement_aux holding a NOT NULL statement_text plus a visible_statement_when_submitted snapshot of the exact words shown at submission.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is paraphrase-only and deliberately never serves participant statements verbatim, to reduce re-identification and quotation risk.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should keep diverging from Comhairle's verbatim text storage and must apply its paraphrase step at any boundary that ingests Comhairle's statement_text, since Comhairle hands over exact words Civic Intelligence Engine is committed never to show unmodified.

items.name: Timestamped Structured Query Language migration discipline
items.comhairle: Comhairle carries a disciplined, forward-only schema history: 91 timestamped Structured Query Language migration files in api/migrations/ (e.g. 20260611155735_create_polis_statement_aux_table.sql), applied at startup by db.rs via sqlx::migrate! against Postgres. Each schema change is a small, named, individually reviewable step: creating tables, adding single columns, adding CHECK constraints, adding search indexes, tightening uniqueness, giving a legible, auditable evolution of the production data model over time. The naming convention embeds a sortable timestamp so ordering is unambiguous.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine is a clean-room prototype portfolio (cie-lab) and, per its build-core spec and proof of concept README, is not yet organised around a long-lived, timestamped, forward-only relational migration chain of this scale. Its schema evolution discipline is lighter, matching its earlier build stage.
items.meaning: Watch and borrow the practice as Civic Intelligence Engine hardens. The migration discipline is not a data-model feature per se but an operational capability: 91 reviewable, ordered, startup-applied migrations is what production-grade schema stewardship looks like, and it is the maturity bar Civic Intelligence Engine will need to clear as it moves from prototype to deployed civic infrastructure. Even under append-only storage, Civic Intelligence Engine benefits from the same named, ordered, auditable change log for its own tables.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle maintains 91 timestamped, forward-only Structured Query Language migration files applied at startup via sqlx::migrate!, giving a legible, individually reviewable, auditable history of its production schema.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is a clean-room prototype not yet organised around a long-lived, timestamped relational migration chain of comparable scale.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt Comhairle's named, ordered, startup-applied migration discipline as the schema-stewardship maturity bar to clear when moving from prototype to deployed civic infrastructure.

items.name: Reaction lacks target id and timestamp
items.comhairle: Comhairle's Reaction type (data_model/schema.json) records id, entity_type (the KIND of thing reacted to: Participant/Statement/Group/Reaction), made_by (a Generator), and the reaction payload (ReactionType: SimpleVote / Score / QuadraticVote). Precisely and notably, it carries NEITHER a field identifying WHICH specific entity the reaction targets (only the entity_type, not a target uuid) NOR any timestamp for when the reaction occurred. So at the grammar level a vote knows it is 'a SimpleVote on some Statement by participant X' but not on which statement or when. (Ordering/temporal and target-linkage facts live implicitly in tool-specific tables like polis_statement_aux instead.) This is a real modelling gap in the interchange grammar as written at HEAD.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's vote model is built around a vote matrix in which each vote is intrinsically tied to a specific statement id and is temporally ordered, because clustering (principal component analysis/k-means) and Wilson-gated bridging depend on knowing exactly which statement each vote lands on. A target-less, timestamp-less reaction would be unusable for Civic Intelligence Engine's core math.
items.meaning: A caution for any future adoption of the grammar, and a concrete fix to contribute. If Civic Intelligence Engine ever borrows Comhairle's interchange grammar (CD1), it must first add a target-entity uuid and a timestamp to Reaction, because Civic Intelligence Engine's principal component analysis/k-means/group-informed consensus/Wilson pipeline is meaningless without per-vote target linkage and ordering. This is a specific, HEAD-accurate improvement Civic Intelligence Engine could feed back to Comhairle's team.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Reaction grammar type records the kind of entity reacted to (entity_type), the reactor (made_by), and the vote payload, but carries neither a target-entity uuid identifying which entity is reacted to nor any timestamp of when the reaction occurred.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's vote matrix requires every vote to be tied to a specific statement id and temporally ordered, since principal component analysis, k-means, and Wilson-gated bridging depend on it.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should note that Comhairle's Reaction type omits a target-entity id and timestamp, and would need both added before the grammar could feed Civic Intelligence Engine's clustering and bridging math, making this a concrete improvement Civic Intelligence Engine could contribute back.

items.name: Normalized localized-text indirection
items.comhairle: Comhairle does not store user-facing strings inline on domain rows; instead every localizable field is a TextContentId, a newtype wrapper over a Universally Unique Identifier (api/src/models/translations.rs), that points into a separate translations store (TextContent, carrying a primary_locale, a TextFormat, and per-locale content). The Conversation model shows this throughout: title, short_description, description, privacy_policy, faqs, thank_you_message, call_to_action are all TextContentId references rather than strings, and a Translatable derive macro plus supported_languages[] / primary_locale fields wire multilingual delivery. This content-addressed indirection means one civic conversation can be served in many languages without duplicating or forking the domain row.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's prototype is a single-language listening loop; per its proof of concept README and spec it has no normalized localized-text layer where every display string is a Universally Unique Identifier reference resolved per-locale against a translations table. Multilingual delivery is not a modelled concern at Civic Intelligence Engine's current stage.
items.meaning: A clean adopt candidate if Civic Intelligence Engine ever needs multilingual civic deployments. The TextContentId pattern (store a stable Universally Unique Identifier on the domain row, resolve the actual text per locale in a side table) is a tidy, low-coupling way to add i18n without touching core schema, and it aligns with Civic Intelligence Engine's instinct to keep content indirection clean. It is also compatible with paraphrase-only serving, since the resolved text can itself be a paraphrase. Worth borrowing wholesale if localization enters scope.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle references every user-facing string as a TextContentId Universally Unique Identifier that resolves per-locale against a separate TextContent translations store, so one conversation's title, description, and policies can be served in many languages without duplicating the domain row.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine is a single-language prototype with no normalized localized-text layer resolving display strings per locale.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt Comhairle's TextContentId indirection (stable Universally Unique Identifier on the row, per-locale text in a side table) if multilingual civic deployments enter scope, since it adds i18n without disturbing core schema and stays compatible with paraphrase-only serving.

items.name: Rich reaction union (quadratic/score)
items.comhairle: Comhairle's ReactionType grammar arm (data_model/schema.json) models three distinct vote semantics as a tagged union: SimpleVote (Positive / Negative / Neutral, i.e. agree / disagree / neutral), Score (a generic int32 rating), and QuadraticVote (a QuadVote carrying both an integer 'amount' and a float 'cost'). This means the interchange grammar can, in principle, represent Pol.is-style binary voting, Likert/score rating, AND quadratic voting (where expressing stronger preference costs quadratically more) under one uniform Reaction shape.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's core is a Pol.is-style vote matrix of agree / disagree / pass over statements; per its spec and proof of concept that binary/ternary signal is exactly what principal component analysis, k-means, and group-informed consensus consume. Score-based and quadratic-voting reaction types are not part of Civic Intelligence Engine's modelled elicitation vocabulary.
items.meaning: Watch, situational. Civic Intelligence Engine's clustering math is deliberately tuned to the simple agree/disagree/pass matrix, so richer reaction types would complicate the core pipeline and are not an urgent gain. But the grammar-level demonstration that Score and QuadraticVote can coexist with SimpleVote under one Reaction shape is a useful reference if Civic Intelligence Engine ever wants a preference-intensity signal (e.g. quadratic voting for budget-style prioritisation) as an adjunct to the listening loop. Track it; don't adopt now.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's ReactionType union represents three vote semantics under one shape: SimpleVote (agree/disagree/neutral), Score (a generic integer rating), and QuadraticVote (an amount plus a quadratic cost).
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's core consumes only a Pol.is-style agree/disagree/pass vote matrix, and score-based or quadratic reactions are not in its elicitation vocabulary.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should track Comhairle's unified Score/QuadraticVote/SimpleVote reaction union as a reference for adding a preference-intensity signal later, but not adopt it now since its clustering math is tuned to the simple agree/disagree/pass matrix.

items.name: Typed statement roles & threading
items.comhairle: Comhairle's Statement type (data_model/schema.json) is not a flat opinion string: it carries a StatementRole classifying the statement's argumentative function: Question, Belief, Fact, Evidence, Refutation, or Summary, plus an optional 'in_response_to' uuid that threads one statement as a reply to another, and a 'role_classified_by' Generator recording who/what assigned the role. Together these give the grammar the bones of an argument graph: typed nodes (belief vs fact vs evidence), reply edges (in_response_to), and derived 'Summary' nodes that can represent the output of a grouping or consensus process, all with provenance on the classification.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's statements are essentially untyped opinion units fed into the vote matrix; per its spec the intelligence comes from clustering votes and computing group-informed consensus and bridging, not from typing each statement as question/belief/fact/evidence/refutation or threading statements into an argument graph. Statement-role semantics are not a Civic Intelligence Engine primitive.
items.meaning: Watch, with long-term upside. Civic Intelligence Engine's power is deliberately in the vote-geometry (principal component analysis/k-means/group-informed consensus/bridging), so it does not need statement typing to function, and adding it would be scope creep today. But the typed-role + in_response_to + role_classified_by structure is a compelling reference if Civic Intelligence Engine ever wants to layer argument-structure or evidence-linking on top of its consensus output: notably the 'Summary' role maps neatly onto Civic Intelligence Engine's own group-informed consensus statements, which are exactly algorithm-generated summaries of a grouping. Track it as a future enrichment path.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's Statement type carries a StatementRole (Question, Belief, Fact, Evidence, Refutation, Summary), an in_response_to reply link, and a role_classified_by provenance tag, giving the grammar the bones of a typed, threaded argument graph.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine treats statements as untyped opinion units for its vote matrix, deriving intelligence from vote-clustering rather than from statement typing or argument threading.
items.meaning_s: Civic Intelligence Engine should track Comhairle's typed StatementRole and in_response_to threading as a future enrichment path, noting the 'Summary' role maps neatly onto Civic Intelligence Engine's algorithm-generated group-informed consensus statements, without adopting it now as scope creep.

items.name: Recruitment targets by demographic bucket
items.comhairle: Comhairle lets an admin set explicit recruitment quotas per workflow through a full create, read, update, delete Representational State Transfer surface (api/src/routes/recruitment_targets.rs) backed by a recruitment_target table (api/src/models/recruitment_target.rs). Each target is a (metric, bucket, target_count) triple (e.g. metric 'age', bucket '18-24', target_count 40) with an ON CONFLICT upsert keyed on (workflow_id, metric, bucket) so a host can declare 'I want this many participants of each demographic slice'. This is the data backbone for sample-quota-driven, representativeness-aware recruitment.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately quarantines demographics: its spec (03-principles-and-commitments.md, 08-the-build-core.md) commits to a demographics-free vote matrix and never storing per-participant demographic buckets, so there is no equivalent of a (metric, bucket, target_count) quota table anywhere in cie-lab.
items.meaning: This is a principled divergence, not a gap. Civic Intelligence Engine's bridging/consensus math derives legitimacy from opinion structure (principal component analysis + k-means groups) rather than from demographic weighting, and holding no demographic buckets is what lets it make its no-per-record-egress and consent-minimal promises. The honest tension: quota-based recruitment is a recognised way to defend representativeness claims, so Civic Intelligence Engine trades a recruitment-side representativeness lever for its demographic-quarantine guarantee, and should be able to explain that trade to a host who asks 'how do you know your sample is representative?'.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's recruitment_targets Representational State Transfer surface lets a host set per-workflow demographic quotas as (metric, bucket, target_count) rows, e.g. 40 participants aged 18-24.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine stores no demographic buckets at all, so it has no recruitment-quota table to set or track sample composition against.
items.meaning_s: This is a principled demographic-quarantine divergence: Civic Intelligence Engine gives up quota-based recruitment representativeness in exchange for its demographics-free, low-egress guarantees, and must explain that trade to hosts.

items.name: Localized region reference taxonomy
items.comhairle: Comhairle ships a first-class, admin-managed geographic taxonomy: a regions Representational State Transfer surface (api/src/routes/regions.rs) with paginated list/filter/order, create/update/delete, and locale-aware output via a LocalizedRegionDto and a LocaleExtractor. Regions are reference data that participants and recruitment can be tagged against, giving hosts a controlled vocabulary of places (constituencies, council areas, etc.) to slice reach and target outreach geographically.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has no geographic reference taxonomy in cie-lab; because place-of-residence is a demographic-style attribute, its demographics-quarantine stance (03-principles-and-commitments.md) means it neither stores nor slices participants by region.
items.meaning: A deliberate divergence in the same spirit as CF1: geographic breakdown is exactly the kind of per-participant attribute Civic Intelligence Engine avoids serving or storing. Worth flagging as a watch-adjacent tension, because civic listening buyers often expect 'where are these voices from?' maps; Civic Intelligence Engine's answer is that opinion-group structure, not geography, carries the analytic weight, and any geographic framing would live outside the quarantined core.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle ships an admin-managed, locale-aware regions taxonomy (regions.rs, LocalizedRegionDto) that participants and recruitment can be tagged and sliced against geographically.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine holds no region reference data and never slices participants by place, treating geography as a quarantined demographic attribute.
items.meaning_s: This is a deliberate divergence: Civic Intelligence Engine forgoes geographic breakdowns of participation to keep its demographics-free core, unlike Comhairle's controlled region vocabulary.

items.name: Multi-step conversation design studio
items.comhairle: Comhairle's admin surface is a genuine conversation-authoring studio, not a single-poll form. The design route (ui/.../admin/conversations/[conversation_id]/design/step/[step_id]/+page.svelte) lets a host assemble an ordered sequence of workflow steps, each backed by a different elicitation tool, with dedicated per-tool authoring panels: PolisManage, LearnManage, HeyFormManage, ThinkingSpaceManage, ElicitationBotManage, LivedExperienceManage, Prioritization, plus a shared CommonStepConfig. A Polis step alone exposes Configure / Setup / Statements / Participants / Moderate subtabs. This is a full drag-together participant-journey builder.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine ships a thin participation scaffold around one fixed campaign-listening flow (02-north-star.md, 04-who-we-serve.md); cie-lab has no notion of an admin composing a multi-step journey from a palette of interchangeable elicitation tools.
items.meaning: A clear gain to borrow selectively. Civic Intelligence Engine intentionally stays 'narrow and sharp' (ONE flow), so it should not adopt the whole multi-tool studio. But the pattern of a step-ordered authoring user interface with a per-step config panel and a preview/live split is exactly what Civic Intelligence Engine will need the moment a host wants to bracket its poll with an intro, a consent step, and a close-out. Adopt the authoring scaffold shape; keep the single-method core.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's admin design studio lets a host order multiple workflow steps and configure each with a tool-specific panel (PolisManage, LearnManage, etc.) plus Polis Configure/Setup/Statements/Participants/Moderate subtabs.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine offers only a thin scaffold around one fixed listening flow, with no admin builder for composing a multi-step participant journey.
items.meaning_s: Worth borrowing the step-ordered authoring-panel-with-preview pattern for wrapping Civic Intelligence Engine's poll in intro/consent/close-out steps, while keeping Civic Intelligence Engine's single-method core.

items.name: Curated report authoring with public toggle
items.comhairle: Comhairle treats the results write-up as an authored, publishable artifact. The reports surface (api/src/routes/reports.rs) generates a report for a conversation, lets an admin update it (PartialReport), and exposes a FullReportDto that stitches together a human summary, ordered section_configs (ReportSectionConfigs, one per workflow step, api/src/models/report.rs), facilitator/participant feedback and report_impacts. Crucially the Report carries an is_public flag, so a host explicitly decides when the narrative goes live to the public.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine produces analysis outputs (bridging badges, group-informed consensus, validity cards) but cie-lab has no concept of an editable, host-curated report document with a summary, per-section configuration, and an explicit public/private publish switch.
items.meaning: A strong gain. Civic Intelligence Engine's validity-carded claims are more rigorous than Comhairle's raw statement lists, but rigor without a curated, host-approved narrative is hard to hand to a campaign or council. Adopting an authored report layer (summary + ordered sections + is_public gate) would let Civic Intelligence Engine wrap its gated claims in a publishable story while preserving its 'paraphrase-only, gated-claim' discipline inside each section.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's reports application programming interface produces a host-editable report with a summary, per-step section_configs, feedback, impacts, and an is_public publish toggle.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine emits bridging/validity analysis but has no editable, host-curated report document with sections and a public/private publish switch.
items.meaning_s: Adopt an authored report layer (summary + ordered sections + public gate) so Civic Intelligence Engine can publish its gated claims as a host-approved narrative.

items.name: Participant context and explainer tabs
items.comhairle: Before and during a conversation, Comhairle wraps the participant flow in a set of context tabs at ui/.../(public)/conversations/[conversation_id]/[[preview]]/: faq, privacy, workflow, invite and report sub-routes plus the main join page, all sharing a layout. This mirrors, almost tab-for-tab, Bloom's shipped Open Poll context surface (CONTEXT / HOW IT WORKS / YOUR HOST / WHAT'S NEXT / frequently asked questions from /tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), giving a participant a place to understand what an open deliberation is, who is hosting, how their data is used, and what happens next.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine's spec insists on consent-forward, understandable participation, but cie-lab's thin participation scaffold ships no equivalent participant-facing frequently asked questions / privacy / how-it-works / what's-next context surface.
items.meaning: A clear, low-risk gain that Bloom proves is product-standard. Civic Intelligence Engine already commits to two-tier consent and paraphrase-only quoting; surfacing those commitments to the participant through explicit frequently asked questions/privacy/how-it-works tabs turns Civic Intelligence Engine's principles into visible trust signals. This is content and IA work, not core-engine work, so it can be adopted without touching the quarantined analysis layer.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle wraps each conversation in participant context tabs (frequently asked questions, privacy, workflow, invite, report) mirroring Bloom's CONTEXT/HOW IT WORKS/frequently asked questions surface.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine ships no participant-facing frequently asked questions, privacy, or how-it-works context tabs around its listening flow.
items.meaning_s: Adopt participant context/explainer tabs to turn Civic Intelligence Engine's consent and paraphrase-only principles into visible, Bloom-standard trust signals without touching the core engine.

items.name: Public narrative results page
items.comhairle: Comhairle ships a polished, public-facing results narrative (ui/.../(public)/waves/report/+page.svelte) that reads like a story: engagement stats, consensus / broad-agreement / divisive statement cards, 'emerging opinion groups' with plain-language descriptions, a BeeswarmChart plotting participants by principal component analysis position, statement cards annotated per opinion group, and AiCallout explainer blocks. The underlying report-data.json is built from principal component analysis positions, k-means groups, group_informed_consensus and representative_comments, i.e. it renders the same bridging/consensus family of results Civic Intelligence Engine computes, but as a consumer-readable public page.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine has a candidate bridging dashboard, but cie-lab's surface is analyst-facing; it lacks a public, narrative, plain-language results page that walks a lay reader through 'where we agree, where we diverge, and which groups emerged'.
items.meaning: A gain in presentation, adjacent to what Civic Intelligence Engine already computes. Civic Intelligence Engine's outputs are arguably more defensible (Wilson-gated bridging, validity cards) than Comhairle's raw beeswarm, so the opportunity is to borrow the storytelling IA: engagement → agreement → differences → groups → deeper look, and pour Civic Intelligence Engine's gated claims into it. Bloom's public results page confirms this framing is product-expected.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's public waves/report page narrates results as engagement stats, consensus/divisive statement cards, emerging opinion groups, and a principal component analysis beeswarm chart for lay readers.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine's bridging dashboard is analyst-facing and lacks a public plain-language 'where we agree/diverge/which groups emerged' results narrative.
items.meaning_s: Borrow Comhairle's engagement-to-groups storytelling IA and pour Civic Intelligence Engine's Wilson-gated bridging and validity claims into a public narrative results page.

items.name: Live participation funnel dashboard
items.comhairle: The admin monitor page (ui/.../admin/conversations/[conversation_id]/monitor/+page.svelte) gives a host a live operational dashboard: total users, a DailyStatsChart of signups over time, and per-workflow-step StatProgressIndicator cards showing how many participants started vs completed each step, framed as 'identify any sticking points' and 'check out your reach'. It is a recruitment-and-progress funnel view over the whole participant journey, using workflowStats.stepStats and signupStats.
items.cie: cie-lab focuses on the analysis pipeline (vote matrix → principal component analysis → clusters → bridging) and has no host-facing operational dashboard tracking signup-over-time or per-step start/complete drop-off for a running conversation.
items.meaning: A watch item: valuable but situational, and cleanly separable from Civic Intelligence Engine's core. Because it counts participation events rather than demographic attributes, a funnel dashboard is fully compatible with Civic Intelligence Engine's demographics quarantine: it would just need to source counts from Civic Intelligence Engine's append-only trust/event layer. Worth adopting once Civic Intelligence Engine runs live campaigns and hosts ask 'how is turnout going and where are people dropping off?'.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's admin monitor page shows total users, a daily-signups chart, and per-step started-vs-completed drop-off indicators as a live participation funnel.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no host-facing operational dashboard tracking signups over time or per-step completion drop-off for a running conversation.
items.meaning_s: Track as a demographics-safe funnel dashboard Civic Intelligence Engine can source from its append-only event layer once it runs live campaigns and hosts need turnout and drop-off visibility.

items.name: Invite management with Quick Response open links
items.comhairle: Comhairle has a dedicated invites admin surface (ui/.../admin/conversations/[conversation_id]/invites/+page.svelte, api/src/routes/invites.rs) offering two recruitment channels: targeted email invites (EmailInviteForm / EmailInvitesList) and shareable open invite links rendered as scannable Quick Response codes (svelte-qrcode) with copy-to-clipboard, human-readable invite labels (InviteLabelDialog), and an OpenInviteStatsBarChart tracking uptake per link. This is a real outreach toolkit for driving and attributing participation across print, in-person and digital channels.
items.cie: cie-lab has no invitation or link-attribution surface; its participation scaffold assumes participants simply arrive, with no per-channel invite links, Quick Response codes, or invite-level uptake tracking.
items.meaning: A gain that maps directly to Bloom's 'help bring everyone into the fold' share tier. Invite links and Quick Response codes are pure recruitment plumbing with no demographic content, so they sit comfortably beside Civic Intelligence Engine's principles; adopting labelled open-invite links with per-link uptake stats would give Civic Intelligence Engine hosts a way to run and measure multi-channel recruitment without compromising the quarantined core.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's invites surface offers targeted email invites plus labelled open invite links as scannable Quick Response codes with per-link uptake charts.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no invitation, Quick Response, or per-link attribution surface. Participants are assumed to simply arrive.
items.meaning_s: Adopt labelled open-invite links with Quick Response codes and per-link uptake stats to give Civic Intelligence Engine hosts demographics-free multi-channel recruitment, matching Bloom's share tier.

items.name: Participant knowledge-base documents
items.comhairle: Comhairle lets a host upload background documents to a conversation and expose them to participants. documents.rs (api/src/routes/documents.rs) handles multipart upload, async parsing (parse_status), access control (public+live conversations or participants/owner/admin), and a knowledge-base admin tab; the design authoring user interface filters to documents with parse_status === 'DONE' so a step can be grounded in uploaded material, and those documents feed the retrieval-augmented-generation-backed elicitation bot. It is a content-management layer for briefing participants and grounding artificial intelligence assistance in host-supplied source material.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately avoids per-record external artificial intelligence and mutable document stores; cie-lab has no participant document library or retrieval-augmented generation grounding layer, keeping embeddings local and the pipeline free of per-record egress (08-the-build-core.md, 03-principles-and-commitments.md).
items.meaning: A watch item shading toward divergence. The document-as-content-briefing idea (give participants the background reading) is benign and could be adopted as static content. But the way Comhairle wires documents into a retrieval-augmented-generation-backed bot is precisely the per-record external-artificial-intelligence pattern Civic Intelligence Engine avoids, so Civic Intelligence Engine should adopt at most the briefing-material surface and explicitly not the retrieval-augmented-generation grounding, or it undermines its no-per-record-egress commitment.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle lets hosts upload parsed documents that brief participants and ground its retrieval-augmented-generation-backed elicitation bot (documents.rs, knowledge-base tab).
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine keeps embeddings local and avoids per-record external artificial intelligence, so it has no participant document library or retrieval-augmented generation grounding layer.
items.meaning_s: Watch: Civic Intelligence Engine could adopt the static participant-briefing surface but must avoid Comhairle's retrieval-augmented generation grounding, which is the per-record external-artificial-intelligence pattern Civic Intelligence Engine forbids.

items.name: Per-conversation notification and recontact preferences
items.comhairle: Comhairle gives each participant granular, per-conversation communication controls (api/src/routes/user_conversation_preferences.rs): receive_updates_by_notification, receive_updates_by_email, and, notably, receive_similar_conversation_updates_by_email / _by_notification, an explicit opt-in to be recontacted about related conversations. This is a self-service consent-to-followup tier, stored per user per conversation and editable from the participant settings surface.
items.cie: cie-lab has no participant-managed communication preferences or recontact opt-in; its consent model is about data use, not an ongoing per-conversation notification and re-engagement channel.
items.meaning: A gain that operationalises exactly the recontact tier Bloom ships as 'stay in touch' (bloom-07 in /tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md). It fits Civic Intelligence Engine's two-tier consent ethos well: an explicit, granular, participant-editable opt-in for follow-up and similar-conversation updates is consent-forward by design. Adopting it gives Civic Intelligence Engine a principled re-engagement channel without any demographic capture.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle stores per-conversation participant preferences for email/notification updates plus an explicit opt-in to be recontacted about similar conversations.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no participant-managed notification preferences or recontact opt-in beyond its data-use consent model.
items.meaning_s: Adopt granular participant-editable notification and recontact opt-ins (Bloom's 'stay in touch' tier) as a consent-forward re-engagement channel with no demographic capture.

items.name: Multi-method participant step renderer
items.comhairle: Comhairle's participant workflow-step page (ui/.../workflow/[workflow_id]/s/[workflow_step_id]/+page.svelte) is a polymorphic renderer: a single participant screen dispatches to whichever tool a step is configured with: Polis, HeyForm, Learn, LivedExperience, ThinkingSpace, ElicitationBot or Prioritization, with per-tool loading skeletons and a live/preview split. The tool catalogue (api/src/tools/) additionally includes ranking (basic, quadratic and comparative voting) and stories, so a participant can move through vote-on-statements, ranked/quadratic prioritisation, structured storytelling and guided learning within one journey.
items.cie: Civic Intelligence Engine is intentionally ONE campaign-listening flow (02-north-star.md); cie-lab renders a single Pol.is-style vote/submit surface and has no polymorphic step renderer that swaps in ranked voting, quadratic prioritisation, storytelling or learning modules.
items.meaning: A watch item, held in tension with Civic Intelligence Engine's 'narrow and sharp' identity. Civic Intelligence Engine should not chase feature parity across seven elicitation tools. That breadth is exactly what Civic Intelligence Engine trades away for depth and defensibility. But the client-side pattern (a step contract that a participant renderer dispatches on) is worth noting for the day Civic Intelligence Engine adds even a second method (e.g. a prioritisation pass after bridging), so it can grow without a rewrite.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle's participant step page polymorphically renders whichever tool a step uses (Polis, ranking/quadratic, stories, learning, prioritisation) within one journey.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine deliberately renders a single Pol.is-style flow with no multi-method participant renderer.
items.meaning_s: Watch the step-contract renderer pattern for future extensibility, but do not chase Comhairle's seven-method breadth: depth over breadth is Civic Intelligence Engine's deliberate trade.

items.name: Post-participation feedback and thank-you flow
items.comhairle: Comhairle closes the participant journey with a dedicated thank-you route (ui/.../workflow/[workflow_id]/thank_you/) and a feedback capture surface (api/src/routes/feedback.rs) whose entries flow back into the report as facilitator_feedback / participant_feedback (FullReportDto, api/src/models/report.rs). Together with the report's report_impacts, this gives every conversation an explicit end-of-flow moment for participants to reflect and for the host to gather experience signal.
items.cie: cie-lab has no defined end-of-flow completion surface or post-participation feedback capture; its scaffold ends at the analysis pipeline rather than at a participant reflection/thank-you step.
items.meaning: A gain that lines up with Bloom's completion pattern: the 'thank you' screen and the 1-to-10 experience self-code (bloom-05/-08 in /tmp/bloom/CATALOG.md), which is itself analogous to Civic Intelligence Engine's own 'feeling heard' light self-code. Adopting a thank-you + lightweight feedback step gives Civic Intelligence Engine a natural, low-friction place to capture its feeling-heard signal and route participants to next actions, all without collecting demographics.
items.comhairle_s: Comhairle ends each journey with a thank-you route plus feedback capture that flows back into the report as participant/facilitator feedback.
items.cie_s: Civic Intelligence Engine has no end-of-flow completion surface or post-participation feedback capture beyond its analysis pipeline.
items.meaning_s: Adopt a thank-you plus lightweight feedback step (Bloom's completion + experience self-code) as the natural home for Civic Intelligence Engine's demographics-free 'feeling heard' signal and next-action routing.
